_about: Longer 'More about this place' pages, keyed by destination id. Sections: skiing, beyond, know (plain text; *italic* and **bold** allowed; blank line = new paragraph). Describe the character of the terrain, never route instructions. sources: authoritative or local first; if a vendor is listed, list a second.

nagano.skiing:
Nozawa is a proper mountain above a proper village: about 1,000 m of vertical, from tree runs at the top to long cruisers that end in town. Austrian Hannes Schneider demonstrated skiing here in 1930, and a course still carries his name. Snow arrives from the Sea of Japan in long storm cycles, so January and February bring regular deep days, and the beech glades are the local speciality.

Shiga Kogen, an hour away, is a different animal: a high plateau of interlinked areas that hosted 1998 Olympic events, with the most reliable snow in Honshu and a quieter, more domestic feel.
nagano.beyond:
Nozawa's 13 free public bathhouses (*soto-yu*) are run by the villagers, and bathing your way down the main street after skiing is the real après. At the Ōgama spring, locals boil vegetables and eggs in water hot enough to cook them. Try *nozawana* pickles, the village's namesake greens, and soba at a family counter.

On 15 January the Dōsojin Fire Festival, one of Japan's three great fire festivals, has village men defend a wooden shrine against torch-wielding attackers. Near Shiga, Shibu Onsen's lantern-lit ryokan street and the snow monkeys of Jigokudani are an easy half-day.
nagano.know: Stay in a ryokan at least once: dinner and breakfast are included and the bath is on site. Bathhouse etiquette (wash first, no swimsuits, tattoos may need covering) matters more here than in the resorts. The old village is compact and walkable; you won't need a car.

tahoe.skiing:
A dozen resorts ring North America's largest alpine lake, each with its own character. **Palisades Tahoe** hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics and is famous for the steeps of KT-22 and the cliffs of the Palisades; its sister **Alpine Meadows** is now linked by gondola. **Heavenly** straddles the California–Nevada line with lake views from almost every run. **Kirkwood**, south of the lake, has the highest base and some of the steepest, snowiest terrain in the region. **Sugar Bowl**, **Northstar** and **Mt Rose** round out the big names.

What makes Tahoe unusual is how much **backcountry** sits right beside the resorts. **Donner Summit**, along I-80, has easy-access tours and the Sierra Club's historic huts. **Carson Pass**, to the south, is the classic spring corn tour. The **Mt Rose highlands** and the **Desolation Wilderness** above Emerald Bay round out decades of guidebook coverage and trip reports.

Storms come off the Pacific as heavy "Sierra cement": dense snow that settles fast and is often stable soon after a storm, which makes Tahoe a relatively forgiving backcountry. Spring brings some of the most reliable corn snow in the West, often into May. Between storms, though, it can go weeks without snow under the famous Sierra sun.
tahoe.beyond:
Truckee has a railroad-era downtown with good restaurants. Donner Lake and its pioneer history, told at the Donner Memorial State Park museum, are a sobering stop. Royal Gorge is North America's largest cross-country ski area. In summer-like spring weather, the Emerald Bay overlook and the lake's clear water are spectacular.

On the Nevada side, South Lake Tahoe and Reno have casinos and nightlife, and Reno, 45 minutes away, has a growing food scene.
tahoe.know:
Reno airport is about 1 hour from the north shore; Sacramento and the Bay Area are 2 to 4 hours away by car, depending on traffic. A car is useful, as the resorts are spread around the lake.

Atmospheric rivers can bring 2 m of snow in days, close I-80 and Highway 50, and turn the drive into the crux: carry chains, and check road conditions before leaving. Weekends are busy, with heavy traffic from the Bay Area, so midweek is noticeably better.

Palisades and Alpine Meadows are on the Ikon Pass; Heavenly, Northstar and Kirkwood on the Epic Pass. The Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry daily. Guide services and avalanche courses run all winter.

lyngen.skiing:
Summit to sea: in the Lyngen Alps, steep peaks of around 1,500 to 1,800 m rise straight from the fjords, and many tours end a few steps from salt water. The peninsula is about 90 km long, with a spine of glaciated mountains and dozens of side valleys, and it's a ski-touring destination first: there are no lifts. Descents above the Arctic Circle combine open alpine faces, glaciers, couloirs and wide fjord-side slopes.

The classic way in is from the road that rings much of the peninsula. Around **Lyngseidet**, in the south, popular peaks such as **Rørnestinden** rise directly above the village. The central valleys, reached from **Svensby** on the west side and **Koppangen** on the east, lead to bigger, glaciated objectives. In the north, the area around **Lenangen** has some of the steepest and most dramatic peaks, including **Store Lenangstind**. On the other side of the Ullsfjord, **Lakselvbukt** gives access to the Tromsø mountains with Lyngen views.

Late winter, roughly March and April, brings more stable snow, longer days and the best conditions. By May, the midnight sun lets you ski at 2 a.m., and spring corn runs right down to the shore.
lyngen.beyond:
Lyngen offers northern lights in the dark early season, Sámi reindeer-herding culture, saunas and cold plunges in the fjord, and in midwinter, orcas and humpback whales feeding on herring off Skjervøy, to the north. Tromsø, the gateway, is a lively Arctic city with the striking Arctic Cathedral, a cable car with views over the fjords, and good seafood.

The area's coastal villages are small and quiet, with fishing boats, red wooden houses and ferries linking the peninsulas.
lyngen.know:
There are three ways to do it, from cheapest to priciest. **Camper van or a rented cabin with a car:** most classic tours start from the road along the fjords, so this is the most flexible way to chase the weather, and how many Scandinavians do it. **A lodge with guides:** in the middle, with local knowledge and saunas included. **A sail-and-ski boat:** the top end, more of a tourist experience, using the boat as a floating hut to reach fjords without roads.

Tromsø is about 1.5 hours away, including the Breivikeidet–Svensby ferry. Rent a car with good winter tyres, and allow for ferries that run on a timetable.

Norway's regional avalanche forecast (varsom.no) covers Lyngen. The snowpack is coastal but can be persistent and tricky, especially early in the season, and the weather off the coast changes fast: planning around it is part of the trip. Several of the most famous peaks have glaciers, crevasses and steep summit sections, so go with a guide unless you have the skills.

chamonix.skiing:
Chamonix isn't one ski area but several, strung along the valley under Mont Blanc: **Brévent–Flégère** on the sunny side, the **Grands Montets** above Argentière, **Balme–Le Tour** at the head of the valley, and Les Houches at the bottom. They aren't linked by lift, so you move between them by bus or train.

The pistes are fine, but people come for the high-mountain freeride. The **Aiguille du Midi** cable car climbs to 3,842 m and is the start of the **Vallée Blanche**, a descent of about 20 km over glaciers and past seracs to the Mer de Glace, which most visitors do with a guide. The **Grands Montets** is the steep, glaciated freeride hill, with big lines down toward the Argentière glacier; its top cable car burned in 2018, and access to the highest terrain has depended on what's been rebuilt since, so check before you go.

The ski touring is world-class too. From the top of the lifts, classic tours lead to cols like the **Col du Passon** and the **Col du Chardonnet**, and Argentière is the traditional start of the Haute Route to Zermatt. Brévent–Flégère has easier, sunnier off-piste and views across to the whole Mont Blanc massif.

The terrain is huge and much of it is serious mountaineering ground, with crevasses, seracs and exposure.
chamonix.beyond: A real mountain town with year-round life: climbing history (the Compagnie des Guides was founded here in 1821), museums, good bars and restaurants, and the Montenvers rack railway to the Mer de Glace. The Mont Blanc tunnel puts Courmayeur and Italian food about 20 minutes away. On a clear day, the Aiguille du Midi terrace is one of the great viewpoints in Europe, even if you don't ski down.
chamonix.know:
Geneva airport is about an hour away by road. A guest card usually gives free valley buses and trains. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass also covers Courmayeur across the tunnel and the Aiguille du Midi.

The off-piste here is glaciated: if you don't have glacier skills, hire a guide. The Compagnie des Guides and many independent guides offer the Vallée Blanche and touring days. Bad weather closes the high lifts often, so build spare days into the trip.

Midwinter is cold and shady on the valley floor; spring brings long days and the classic glacier runs. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

lagrave.skiing:
La Grave is the purest lift-served freeride in the Alps. A single old cable car, in two sections, climbs from the village to about 3,200 m on the Girose glacier, below La Meije (3,983 m). From there, it's roughly 2,000 m of vertical back down to the village, and almost none of it is groomed, marked or patrolled.

The terrain is high mountain in every sense: open bowls, steep couloirs, cliffs, seracs and crevasses. The two classic descents are the **Vallons de la Meije** and the **Vallon de Chancel**, long, wild runs through big glacial terrain to the village, but there are dozens of variations, many of them steep, exposed or only in condition a few days a year. On the glacier at the top, a short drag lift serves gentler slopes, and in good conditions it's possible to ski over the Girose glacier toward Les Deux Alpes.

There are no pistes to fall back on, which is the point. On a good powder day, La Grave is one of the best freeride experiences in the world; on a bad one, the lift stays shut and the village waits. The resort has been at the centre of a long debate about replacing its ageing cable car and extending it higher onto the glacier, so check the latest before you plan.
lagrave.beyond:
La Grave is a small, quiet village of stone houses, set on a steep hillside facing the north side of La Meije, one of the great peaks of the French Alps and one of the last major Alpine summits to be climbed, in 1877. The Écrins National Park surrounds it. The hamlets of Les Terrasses and Le Chazelet, just above the village, have some of the best views of the mountain.

For groomed skiing, **Serre Chevalier** (on the Briançon side of the Col du Lautaret) and **Les Deux Alpes** are both close. The **Col du Lautaret** itself is a classic ski-touring area, with gentle and moderate tours above the road. Briançon, France's highest town, has Vauban fortifications that are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
lagrave.know:
Treat La Grave as guided terrain unless you have strong avalanche, glacier and route-finding skills: getting lost here can mean cliffs or crevasses, and rescues are common. The local guides' office in the village runs daily outings, and hiring a guide for your first days is the norm, even for strong skiers.

Wind closes the cable car regularly, so plan flexible days and have a backup (Serre Chevalier is about 40 minutes away). The best months are usually February to April, when the glacier is well covered and days are longer.

Access is via Grenoble (about 1.5 to 2 hours) or Briançon (about 40 minutes). The road over the Col du Lautaret is kept open in winter but can close in storms or for avalanche risk. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin for the Oisans and Écrins massifs.

3vallees.skiing:
The world's largest linked ski area, about 600 km of pistes across three valleys: **Courchevel**, **Méribel**, and **Les Menuires–Val Thorens**, plus Orelle and Saint-Martin-de-Belleville. You can ski valley to valley all day without repeating a run, and a single pass covers it all.

**Val Thorens**, at about 2,300 m, is the highest resort in Europe and the most snow-sure, with lifts reaching around 3,200 m. **Courchevel** has long, beautifully groomed runs, good tree skiing lower down and some of the area's steepest marked runs in its couloirs. **Méribel**, in the middle, is the hub, with a chalet village and runs in every direction. **Les Menuires** is broad and family-friendly.

Off-piste is extensive between the lifts, and well-known itineraries like the **Vallon du Lou**, between Val Thorens and Les Menuires, see many skiers after storms. None of it is controlled, though, so the usual off-piste rules apply.
3vallees.beyond: The villages range from very luxurious (Courchevel 1850's hotels and Michelin-starred restaurants) to simple, car-free apartment blocks. Saint-Martin-de-Belleville is the traditional Savoyard village among the purpose-built resorts, with a church and old stone houses. Méribel's Olympic ice rink and Courchevel's Aquamotion pool are good bad-weather options.
3vallees.know:
Moûtiers is the train station for the valley, with direct TGV and seasonal trains from Paris and further afield; buses run up to each resort. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the airports, all a couple of hours away.

Costs vary a lot by village: Courchevel 1850 is among the most expensive places to ski in the world, while Les Menuires and Saint-Martin are much cheaper on the same lift pass. A cheaper single-valley pass is available if you don't need the whole area.

French school holidays (February in particular) are very busy. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

valisere.skiing:
Val d'Isère and Tignes share one big, high area of about 300 km, known as Espace Killy after the triple Olympic champion Jean-Claude Killy, with lifts up to around 3,450 m on the **Grande Motte** glacier above Tignes. It's one of the most snow-sure places in the Alps, with a season from late November to early May.

Pistes range from long cruisers to the **Face de Bellevarde**, the 1992 Olympic downhill, a steep, sustained black above Val d'Isère. The high areas of **Pissaillas** glacier and the **Col de l'Iseran** are good in spring, and **Le Fornet** is a quieter sector at the end of the valley.

The off-piste is legendary for its variety and is reachable straight from the lifts: big bowls, couloirs and long descents to the valley, with famous runs like the **Tour du Charvet** and the descents from the **Grande Motte**. That makes it popular, and it's involved in accidents every winter. Ski touring into the Vanoise National Park starts right from the lifts.
valisere.beyond: Val d'Isère is an old village with a stone church and a lively après scene, including the famous La Folie Douce on the slopes. Tignes is a set of purpose-built, mostly car-free stations around a lake, with an aquatic centre and ice diving under the frozen lake. Both are self-contained and very ski-focused.
valisere.know:
The nearest train station is Bourg-Saint-Maurice, about 45 minutes away by bus. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the usual airports, about 3 hours away.

The off-piste is uncontrolled and the terrain is big: hire a guide or join a group with the local ski schools if you're new to it. Altitude makes it cold in midwinter; spring here is long and reliable.

Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin. Weekends and French holidays are busy.

paradiski.skiing:
Paradiski joins Les Arcs and La Plagne across a valley with the **Vanoise Express**, a double-decker cable car that swings 380 m above the ground. Together they make around 400 km of pistes, mostly above 1,600 m.

**Les Arcs** has the more interesting terrain: the **Aiguille Rouge** (3,226 m) starts a 7 km run with about 2,000 m of vertical down to Villaroger, and the trees above **Peisey-Vallandry** are a storm-day refuge. The off-piste around the Aiguille Rouge and the Grand Col is big and varied. **La Plagne** is broad, high and gentle, ideal for families and mixed groups, with the **Bellecôte** glacier on top and long off-piste descents to the valley villages of Champagny and Montchavin.

The area is huge and mostly above the treeline, which means great views and lots of snow but also flat light in bad weather. On those days, head to the trees of Peisey or Montchavin.
paradiski.beyond: The villages are purpose-built, but some have real character: architect Charlotte Perriand designed much of Arc 1600 and 1800, and they're now protected as 20th-century heritage. In La Plagne you can ride the 1992 Olympic bobsleigh track in a bob-raft with a pilot. Peisey and Champagny are traditional villages with a quieter feel.
paradiski.know:
This is one of the easiest big areas to reach by train: from Bourg-Saint-Maurice station, a funicular climbs straight to Arc 1600 in about 7 minutes. Geneva and Chambéry are the nearest airports.

Apartments are the norm, and they can be small, so check the size before booking. French school holidays (February especially) are packed. Off-piste is uncontrolled; Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

portesdusoleil.skiing:
A cross-border circuit of about 12 resorts between France and Switzerland, with around 600 km of pistes. You can ski a big loop through both countries in a day, crossing passes and dropping into villages that feel very different from each other.

**Avoriaz** is the highest and most snow-sure part, with good parks and access to the Swiss side. **Morzine** and **Les Gets** are lower and wooded, good in storms. **Champéry**, on the Swiss side, has the famous **Swiss Wall** (Le Mur Suisse), a long, steep mogul face that's one of the best-known runs in the Alps. **Châtel**, to the north, is a traditional village with a big local scene.

Much of the area sits between about 1,000 and 2,300 m, so low snow and rain are real risks in a warm winter. When it snows, though, the tree skiing between the villages is excellent, and the off-piste around Avoriaz and Champéry is extensive.
portesdusoleil.beyond: Morzine and Châtel are year-round mountain towns with plenty of life. Avoriaz is a car-free village built into the cliff, with sleigh rides and an aquatic centre. Lake Geneva is about an hour away, and the Swiss side has thermal baths and chocolate.
portesdusoleil.know:
Geneva airport is about 1 to 1.5 hours away, which makes this one of the easiest big areas to reach for a short trip.

Check the snow before you book, especially in early season or a warm spell: the lower villages can be green while Avoriaz is still good. Weekends bring day-trippers from Geneva. Both French and Swiss avalanche bulletins apply.

alpedhuez.skiing:
Alpe d'Huez calls itself the "island in the sun": the slopes face south and get sunshine most of the day. Around 250 km of pistes link it with **Oz-en-Oisans**, **Vaujany** and **Auris**, and the **Pic Blanc** (3,330 m) is the high point, with huge views on a clear day.

From the top starts the **Sarenne**, at about 16 km one of the longest black runs in the world. It's long rather than terrifying, and it passes through empty, wild terrain. Off-piste from the Pic Blanc is big and varied, and guides know lines that most visitors never see, including long descents into the valleys around the massif.

Vaujany and Oz are quieter, wooded bases connected by big cable cars, and good on storm days. The Pic Blanc also has the Tunnel, a steep black that starts by passing through the mountain.
alpedhuez.beyond: Road cyclists know Alpe d'Huez for its 21 hairpins, made famous by the Tour de France, and each bend has a sign with the winners' names. In winter there's an ice-driving circuit, a big sports centre and plenty of nightlife.
alpedhuez.know:
Grenoble is about 1.5 hours away, Lyon a little more. The road up is the famous hairpin climb, so carry chains.

The sun has a downside: south-facing snow turns slushy in the afternoon and icy in the morning, so ski the high, shady runs early and the sunny ones late. Les Deux Alpes and La Grave are nearby for a day of glacier or freeride.

Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

courmayeur.skiing:
The Italian side of Mont Blanc. The resort itself is mid-sized, with sunny, tree-lined pistes that are good on storm days, and a mountain base at **Plan Checrouit** with excellent restaurants.

The big draw is the **Skyway Monte Bianco**, a rotating cable car that climbs to **Punta Helbronner** at about 3,466 m. From there, glaciated freeride runs drop back towards Italy, including the **Toula glacier**, a steep classic, and the **Marbrées**, a long descent with big views. The **Vallée Blanche** descends to Chamonix from the same place, often in better conditions than from the Aiguille du Midi.

Treat everything off the Skyway as glacier terrain, with crevasses and changeable conditions. The resort side also has good off-piste among the trees and in the Val Veny, with views across to the Mont Blanc glaciers.
courmayeur.beyond: A handsome, very Italian mountain town with excellent food, long lunches on the mountain and good coffee. The Aosta Valley adds Roman ruins and castles. Chamonix is about 20 minutes away through the tunnel, and the Pré-Saint-Didier thermal baths are a great rest day.
courmayeur.know:
Turin and Geneva are both about 1.5–2 hours away. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass covers Courmayeur, the Skyway and Chamonix.

The Skyway closes in strong wind. Hire a guide for the glacier descents unless you have glacier skills and gear. Courmayeur often catches storms from the south that miss the French side, so it's a good backup when Chamonix is dry.

hautroute.skiing:
The classic Haute Route links Chamonix and Zermatt over about six to seven days of high, glaciated terrain, staying in mountain huts each night. Most days involve long climbs on skins, some crampon sections and big glacier descents, mostly between about 2,500 and 3,800 m.

The classic route starts in Argentière, crosses the **Col du Chardonnet** and the **Fenêtre de Saleina** into Switzerland, then passes the **Trient** hut and reaches Champex or Verbier. From there it crosses the high ground of the Grand Combin and the Val des Dix, via huts like the **Cabane des Dix** and the **Cabane des Vignettes**, with the **Pigne d'Arolla** as an optional summit. The last day, from the Vignettes to Zermatt, crosses three cols in a long day ending under the Matterhorn.

It's a demanding trip: you need solid skiing in all snow conditions, good fitness for several long days in a row, and glacier travel skills. Most people do it with a guide.
hautroute.beyond: Few trips in the Alps match it for scenery: Mont Blanc at one end, the Matterhorn at the other, and a week of high mountain huts in between, each with its own character and a shared dinner.
hautroute.know:
The main season is roughly April to mid-May, when days are long and the snowpack is usually more stable. Huts fill up and need booking well ahead.

Plan for weather: storms can pin you in a hut or force a change of plan, so leave spare days at the end. The SLF bulletin covers the Swiss section and Météo-France the French start.

granparadiso.skiing:
Gran Paradiso (4,061 m) is the only 4,000 m peak entirely in Italy, and one of the most skiable in the Alps. The classic plan is two days: climb from **Pont**, at the head of the Valsavarenche, to the **Vittorio Emanuele II** hut, then set off before dawn up the long glacier to just below the summit, and enjoy around 2,000 m of descent back down.

The last part to the summit is a short rocky ridge with a Madonna statue on top, done on foot with crampons. Most people leave their skis at the bergschrund.

The area around the hut has other good objectives for a longer stay: the **Ciarforon** and the **Tresenta**, two neighbouring peaks, are classic ski summits with big glacier descents. The **Chabod** hut, on the other side of the valley, is the start of a different route up Gran Paradiso, with a steeper approach.
granparadiso.beyond: The Gran Paradiso National Park was Italy's first, created from a royal hunting reserve that saved the Alpine ibex from extinction. You'll almost certainly see ibex. Cogne, on the other side of the massif, is famous for ice climbing and cross-country skiing, and the Aosta Valley has fontina cheese and Roman ruins.
granparadiso.know:
The usual approach is from Pont. The Vittorio Emanuele hut, with its distinctive rounded metal roof, is staffed in spring and needs booking.

The glacier has crevasses, and the summit ridge is exposed. Go with a guide unless you have glacier and crampon experience. Turin and Geneva are both around 2 hours away.

ecrins.skiing:
The Écrins massif is the wilder, quieter alternative to Mont Blanc: big glaciers, jagged peaks and few lifts. The **Barre des Écrins** (4,102 m) is the southernmost 4,000 m peak in the Alps, and the neighbouring **Dôme de Neige des Écrins** (4,015 m) is one of the classic ski 4,000ers, reached from the Écrins hut via the long Glacier Blanc.

The classic plan is to climb from Vallouise to the **Refuge du Glacier Blanc** or the **Refuge des Écrins**, then spend a few days on the summits around the glacier: the Dôme, the **Roche Faurio** and others, with big descents on wide glaciers under steep rock walls.

Around the massif, dozens of other tours go from huts and valley villages, from gentle glaciers to steep couloirs. For quieter, easier touring, the **Névache** valley near Briançon has gentle terrain and cosy refuges, and the Col du Lautaret has roadside tours with big views of the Meije.
ecrins.beyond: Briançon, the highest town in France, has Vauban fortifications that are a UNESCO World Heritage site. Vallouise and the hamlet of Ailefroide are climbing villages. La Grave and Serre Chevalier are close for lift-served days.
ecrins.know:
The usual start for the Glacier Blanc is above Vallouise, from Ailefroide or, once the road opens in spring, Pré de Madame Carle. Huts are staffed in spring and need booking. The Vénéon valley, on the western side, was badly damaged by floods in 2024, so check access there.

Grenoble and Turin are about 2 hours away. The glaciers have crevasses and the terrain is big: go with a guide unless you have glacier skills. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

vanoise.skiing:
The Vanoise Haute Route crosses France's first national park, from **Pralognan-la-Vanoise** to Val d'Isère or **Bonneval-sur-Arc**, linking glaciers and passes over about five to six days. The **Grande Casse** (3,855 m) dominates the start, and the route crosses the big, gentle Vanoise glaciers, with optional summits like the **Dôme de Chasseforêt** and the **Dôme de l'Arpont** along the way.

It's less committing than the Chamonix–Zermatt Haute Route, with friendlier glaciers and easier days, which makes it a good first big traverse. The landscape is open and wide, with long views across to the Écrins and Mont Blanc.

The huts along the way, like the **Col de la Vanoise** and **Arpont** refuges, can also be used as bases for a few days of day tours, without doing the whole traverse.
vanoise.beyond: The huts are traditional and welcoming, and there's a good chance of seeing ibex and chamois. Bonneval-sur-Arc, at the end, is one of the most beautiful stone villages in the French Alps. Beaufort cheese comes from these valleys.
vanoise.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season, when huts are staffed. Book ahead. The start is about 2.5 hours from Geneva or Chambéry; arrange the return from the finish in advance.

You need glacier travel skills and gear, or a guide. Météo-France publishes the avalanche bulletin.

maira.skiing:
Valle Maira, in Piedmont near the French border, has no lifts at all and hundreds of mapped ski tours. From each hamlet, you can choose open slopes, wooded ridges and steeper couloirs, mostly between about 1,500 and 3,000 m.

The valley catches storms from the south and the Mediterranean, so its snow can be very different from the northern Alps, for better or worse. In a good year it's a touring paradise. Classic summits include **Monte Chersogno**, a big, open pyramid, and **Rocca la Marchisa**, and the upper valley around **Chiappera** and **Acceglio** has some of the best terrain, under the limestone towers of the Rocca Provenzale.

Most visitors stay a week in one guesthouse and tour in different directions each day, often with a local guide who knows where the snow is best.
maira.beyond:
Valle Maira is part of the Occitan world, with its own language, music and food. Small guesthouses (*locande*) in stone hamlets offer half-board, and the cooking is a big part of the trip: local ravioli, polenta, cheeses and Piedmont wines like Barolo.

The valley lost most of its population in the 20th century, and its revival is partly thanks to slow, low-impact tourism like this.
maira.know:
Turin is about 2 hours away, and Cuneo is the nearest town. A car is the easiest way to get around.

Snow varies a lot from year to year. Check the Piedmont avalanche bulletin (ARPA Piemonte). Local guides know the best tours for the conditions.

verbier.skiing:
Verbier is the hub of the **4 Vallées**, a linked area of about 400 km that also takes in **Nendaz**, Veysonnaz, Thyon and La Tzoumaz. The pistes are good, but Verbier's reputation is freeride: steep, varied off-piste is reachable straight from the lifts, from the top of **Mont Fort** (3,330 m) down.

The **Bec des Rosses** face hosts the Xtreme Verbier, the final of the Freeride World Tour. Much of the best terrain is ungroomed itinéraire runs and off-piste, and classics like the **Vallon d'Arbi**, a long descent toward La Tzoumaz, and the steep slopes of **Mont Gelé** draw skiers from all over the world. Conditions vary a lot day to day.

Verbier is also a great base for ski touring. From the top of the lifts, tours lead toward the **Rosablanche** and the Grand Combin massif, and the area is a stage on the Haute Route. **Bruson**, across the valley, is a quieter little area with good trees and no crowds.
verbier.beyond: A chalet village with a big international crowd and one of the liveliest nightlife scenes in the Alps. Quieter villages around the 4 Vallées are cheaper bases. The Rhône valley below has vineyards and the thermal baths at Saillon and Lavey.
verbier.know:
Le Châble, in the valley, has a train station and a cable car up to Verbier, so you can arrive by train from Geneva (about 2 hours). Verbier is expensive, especially in high season; staying in Le Châble or Nendaz saves money.

The off-piste is popular, which means tracked out fast after storms and involved in accidents every winter. A local guide finds the good snow and keeps you out of trouble. The SLF publishes the Swiss avalanche bulletin.

zermatt.skiing:
Zermatt is skiing under the Matterhorn, and the mountain is in view from almost every run. Three sectors (**Sunnegga–Rothorn**, **Gornergrat** and the **Matterhorn Glacier Paradise**) climb to 3,883 m, the highest cable-car station in Europe, with glacier skiing even in summer. Across the Theodul glacier, the lifts connect to **Cervinia** in Italy, so you can ski over the border for lunch, and on to Valtournenche for a very long day.

The pistes are long and high, with lots of vertical: the run from the glacier to Zermatt drops more than 2,000 m. Off-piste around the **Stockhorn** and Schwarzsee is excellent but glaciated in places, so a guide is a good idea.

Zermatt is also a great base for ski mountaineering. From the top of the glacier lifts, the **Breithorn** (4,164 m) is one of the easiest 4,000 m peaks in the Alps to climb on skis, and the Monte Rosa huts and the Haute Route are close by.
zermatt.beyond:
The village is car-free, with electric taxis and horse-drawn sleighs. The mountain restaurants are some of the best in the Alps, and long lunches on a sunny terrace are part of the culture. The Matterhorn Museum tells the story of the first ascent in 1865, which ended in tragedy on the way down.

The Gornergrat railway, opened in 1898, climbs to a famous viewpoint over the Monte Rosa glaciers.
zermatt.know:
Arrive by train: change at Visp, or park in Täsch and take the shuttle train. Zurich and Geneva are about 3.5 hours away. The Glacier Express connects to St. Moritz.

Zermatt is expensive. The international pass is needed for Cervinia. High winds close the top lifts and the link to Italy. The SLF publishes the Swiss avalanche bulletin.

saasfee.skiing:
Saas-Fee sits in a bowl surrounded by thirteen peaks over 4,000 m, with the Fee glacier hanging right above the village. The skiing is high and snow-sure, reaching about 3,500 m on the Allalin glacier via the **Metro Alpin**, an underground funicular. National ski teams train on the glacier in autumn, and the season runs from late autumn to spring.

The pistes are mostly intermediate, with long, scenic runs and around 1,800 m of vertical from the glacier to the village. The off-piste is limited by crevasses, so most of it is guided. **Saas-Grund**, down the valley, has its own smaller area, **Hohsaas**, with big views and quieter slopes.

For tourers, Saas-Fee is a superb base. The **Allalinhorn** (4,027 m) is one of the most accessible 4,000 m summits in the Alps, starting from the top of the Metro Alpin. The **Alphubel** and the **Strahlhorn**, from the Britannia Hut, are classic glacier ski tours, and the valley is the end point of many Haute Route variations.
saasfee.beyond: The village is car-free and quieter than Zermatt. At the top of the Metro Alpin, the Mittelallalin has a revolving restaurant and an ice pavilion carved into the glacier. The other villages of the Saas valley (Saas-Grund and Saas-Almagell) are cheaper and calmer. Sledging and winter walks are popular.
saasfee.know:
Take the train to Visp, then the bus up the valley. Geneva and Zurich are around 3 hours away. A guest card often includes the valley buses and, in some years, the lift pass for overnight guests.

Altitude gives a long season, from November to April. The glacier has crevasses, so stay on the pistes unless you're with a guide. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

engelberg.skiing:
Engelberg is a low village under a high mountain: the **Titlis** (3,020 m) rises about 2,000 m above town, and its glaciated north face and big open slopes are the reason to come.

The **Laub** is a huge, steep open face of about 1,000 m vertical, visible from town, and the **Galtiberg** is a long descent of around 2,000 m from the glacier to the valley. The **Steinberg** run drops off the glacier through seracs and rock bands. All are classic big-mountain lines reachable by lift, and they make Engelberg one of the most famous freeride destinations in Europe.

The pistes are modest, mostly on the Titlis side, with some good long runs. **Brunni**, across the valley, is a small, sunny family area, good for a quiet day and for beginners. Ski touring is also popular, with routes from the Titlis and from the Jochpass area.
engelberg.beyond: A strong Scandinavian freeride community (mostly Swedish) has settled here, bringing bars, guides and a lively scene. The Benedictine abbey, founded in the 12th century, has a show cheese dairy. Lucerne is about 45 minutes away by train, with its old town and lake.
engelberg.know:
Zurich is about 1.5 hours away by train. The Rotair, a rotating cable car, climbs to the Titlis summit.

The low village means rain is possible at the bottom when it snows at the top. The big lines are serious avalanche and glacier terrain, with crevasses on the upper slopes. Go with a guide, and check the SLF bulletin. The Laub is often closed or heavily tracked; timing matters.

andermatt.skiing:
The **Gemsstock** (2,961 m) above Andermatt is one of the best freeride mountains in Switzerland, with steep north-facing bowls and couloirs and about 1,500 m of vertical. Andermatt sits at a weather crossroads near the Gotthard, catching storms from both north and south, so it often gets snow when other areas don't.

The off-piste from the Gemsstock is the main draw. The **Guspis** valley, a long, wild descent toward Hospental, is one of the classic lines, and there are big faces and couloirs right below the top station.

The **Oberalp pass** links Andermatt with **Sedrun** and **Disentis** into one area, with good off-piste on the Disentis side too, and a train runs over the pass alongside the slopes. The Oberalp is also a popular ski-touring base, with tours like the **Pazolastock** starting right from the pass.
andermatt.beyond: Andermatt used to be a quiet army garrison town. In recent years, a big resort development, now partly owned by Vail Resorts, has added hotels and apartments. The old village still has charm, and the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen gorge is linked to a famous Russian army crossing in 1799.
andermatt.know:
Zurich is about 2 hours away by train. The Matterhorn Gotthard railway, including the Glacier Express, links the area, and the train over the Oberalp also works as a lift between the sectors.

The Gemsstock is serious avalanche terrain, and the snowpack can be tricky after big storms. Go with a guide, and check the SLF bulletin. Andermatt is on the Epic Pass at the time of writing.

engadin.skiing:
The Engadin is a high, sunny valley at around 1,800 m, with St. Moritz and Pontresina as its main villages. **Corviglia** has wide, sunny pistes above St. Moritz; **Corvatsch** is higher, steeper and more snow-sure, with lifts to about 3,300 m; and **Diavolezza** offers a long run down the **Morteratsch glacier**, about 10 km, under the peaks of the Bernina range.

The climate is dry and sunny, so the snow is often cold and fast, but the snowpack can be weak. Corvatsch also offers night skiing and the **Hahnensee** run, a long descent from the top of the area down to St. Moritz Bad.

Piz Bernina, above Pontresina, is the easternmost 4,000 m peak in the Alps, and the area is a great base for ski touring and ski mountaineering, from easy tours on the Bernina Pass to big glacier objectives around **Piz Palü**.
engadin.beyond:
St. Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics in 1928 and 1948, and has an extravagant winter culture: the Cresta Run toboggan, the natural-ice bobsleigh track and horse racing on the frozen lake (White Turf). The Engadin Ski Marathon in March is one of the biggest cross-country races in the world.

Romansh is spoken here, and the valley's villages have beautiful painted houses.
engadin.know:
Zurich is about 3 to 3.5 hours away by train, via the UNESCO-listed Albula line. The Bernina Express runs south to Italy.

St. Moritz is very expensive, but Pontresina and the smaller villages are better value. The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak, so be careful off-piste and check the SLF bulletin. The Morteratsch glacier run is a marked route; the glacier itself is crevassed.

davos.skiing:
Davos and Klosters share five ski areas, and the best is the **Parsenn**, with long runs to valley villages like **Küblis**, a descent of about 12 km. **Jakobshorn** has parks and a young scene; **Pischa** has been given over largely to freeride; **Rinerhorn** is quiet and family-friendly; and **Madrisa**, above Klosters, is sunny and good for families.

The off-piste is big and varied, and the long runs to the valley are a highlight. The terrain around the Parsenn, especially toward Klosters and the Gotschna, has some of the best lift-served off-piste in Graubünden.

The ski touring is excellent too. The side valleys of **Sertig**, **Dischma** and **Flüela** have many classic tours, from short half-day climbs to bigger peaks like the **Flüela Schwarzhorn**.
davos.beyond:
Davos is the highest town in Europe and home to the World Economic Forum. Thomas Mann set *The Magic Mountain* in one of its sanatoriums. Klosters is a smaller, quieter village, a favourite of the British royal family. The Spengler Cup ice hockey tournament takes place over Christmas.

The SLF, Switzerland's avalanche research institute, is based here, and publishes the Swiss bulletin.
davos.know:
Zurich is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by train. The ski areas aren't linked, so you move between them by bus or train.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak. Check the SLF bulletin and go with a guide off-piste. The Flüela Pass road closes in winter at times, so check before planning tours there.

laax.skiing:
Laax is Europe's freestyle capital, with huge terrain parks and one of the biggest halfpipes in the world. It hosts the Laax Open, a major snowboard and freeski event. Beyond the parks, **Laax**, **Flims** and **Falera** share around 225 km of pistes, with wide open slopes up to the **Vorab glacier** at about 3,000 m.

The freeride is good and varied, with lots of terrain between the lifts and some long, quiet descents toward the valley. Laax has also experimented with freeride areas that are avalanche-controlled but not groomed, a good step between piste and true off-piste.

Laax is known for its innovations, from early adoption of snowboarding to its app-based lift system. The parks are open to all levels, with lines for beginners and experts, and the area is big enough for a week even if you never touch a rail.
laax.beyond: The Flims rockslide, one of the biggest in the Alps, shaped the landscape and carved the Rhine Gorge (Ruinaulta), sometimes called the "Swiss Grand Canyon". The Caumasee lake is beautiful year-round. The Rocks Resort, at the Laax base, has a modern, urban vibe.
laax.know:
Zurich is about 1.5 to 2 hours away, by train to Chur then bus.

The Vorab glacier has crevasses off-piste. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

jungfrau.skiing:
Wengen, Grindelwald and Mürren sit under the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau, and the scenery is the point. The pistes are mostly intermediate and fairly low, but the views are among the best in the Alps.

Wengen hosts the **Lauberhorn**, the longest downhill on the World Cup circuit. Mürren is home to the **Inferno**, one of the biggest amateur ski races in the world, held since 1928. **Grindelwald–First** has long, sunny runs, and **Kleine Scheidegg** links Wengen and Grindelwald right under the Eiger's north face.

Off-piste is limited but good above Mürren, around the **Schilthorn**, where steep lines lead down from the summit. For ski tourers, the Jungfraujoch railway is the start of classic glacier tours, including the descent of the **Aletsch glacier** to the Lötschental via the **Lötschenlücke**, a long, beautiful trip best done with a guide.
jungfrau.beyond: The Schilthorn's revolving restaurant, Piz Gloria, appeared in the James Bond film *On Her Majesty's Secret Service*. The Jungfraujoch railway climbs through the Eiger to the highest railway station in Europe. Sledging is a big part of the culture here, with long runs from the Faulhorn and elsewhere.
jungfrau.know:
Wengen and Mürren are car-free. Take the train from Interlaken; Zurich and Bern are 1.5 to 2.5 hours away. The Eiger Express gondola links Grindelwald to the ski area.

The lower slopes can be thin in a warm winter. The Jungfraujoch is very expensive. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

monterosa.skiing:
Monterosa Ski links three valleys (**Alagna** in the Valsesia, **Gressoney** and **Champoluc**) on the Italian side of Monte Rosa. Alagna is the freeride mecca: few pistes, but huge, lift-served off-piste with long descents through steep faces and couloirs.

The classic Alagna lines drop from the **Passo dei Salati** area and the high lifts into wild valleys, like the **Vallone d'Olen**, often with more than 1,500 m of descent back to the village. The terrain is big, varied and often empty.

Heli-skiing is legal in Italy (unlike in France), so heli drops reach glaciers on Monte Rosa that would otherwise take hours to climb. The 4,000 m peaks of the massif, like **Castor**, are also popular ski-mountaineering objectives, best in spring with a guide.
monterosa.beyond: Alagna is a Walser village, settled centuries ago by German-speaking farmers who built distinctive wooden houses. The Capanna Margherita, on a 4,554 m summit of Monte Rosa, is the highest hut in Europe. The food is hearty: polenta, fontina and Piedmont wines.
monterosa.know:
Milan and Turin are about 2 hours away. Alagna is the place for freeride; Gressoney and Champoluc are better for pistes and families.

The terrain is big and the glaciers have crevasses: go with a local guide. Storms from the south can bring heavy snow that the northern Alps miss.

bernese.skiing:
The Bernese Oberland Haute Route starts with a train ride through the Eiger to the **Jungfraujoch** (3,454 m), then tours across the Aletsch glacier world: the largest glacier in the Alps and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Huts such as **Konkordia**, **Finsteraarhorn** and **Hollandia** are bases for big summits like the **Finsteraarhorn** (4,274 m), the highest in the Bernese Alps, the **Gross Fiescherhorn** and the **Mönch**. The glaciers are huge and the scale is vast: the Konkordiaplatz, where several glaciers meet, holds ice hundreds of metres thick.

The usual exit is over the **Lötschenlücke** into the Lötschental, or down the long Fiescher glacier to Fiesch. A typical trip lasts four to six days, with summits on most days.
bernese.beyond: The Konkordia hut sits on a cliff high above the glacier, reached by hundreds of metal steps, because the glacier has thinned so much since the hut was built. It's a striking reminder of how fast the Alps are changing.
bernese.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Book huts ahead.

The train takes you straight to 3,454 m without acclimatisation, so the first night can be hard. You need glacier skills and gear, or a guide. The SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

arlberg.skiing:
The Arlberg links **St. Anton**, St. Christoph, **Stuben**, **Lech**, **Zürs** and **Warth-Schröcken** into one of the biggest areas in Austria, with around 300 km of runs. It's known for steep, challenging terrain and for its **ski routes**: marked, avalanche-controlled runs that are never groomed, somewhere between a piste and off-piste. The **Run of Fame**, a marked circuit of about 85 km, links the whole area in one long day.

The off-piste from the **Valluga** and around Lech and Zürs is huge, varied and among the best lift-served freeride in the Alps. The top of the Valluga, at about 2,800 m, can only be reached with skis if you're with a guide, and leads to the big north-side descents toward Zürs and Lech.

Stuben is a small, old village with cold, shady slopes that often hold the best snow in the area. Warth-Schröcken, at the far end, is one of the snowiest places in the Alps.
arlberg.beyond: The Arlberg is where modern ski technique and teaching began, in the early 20th century. St. Anton has one of the liveliest après scenes in the Alps; Lech and Zürs are quieter and more exclusive, with excellent hotels and restaurants.
arlberg.know:
St. Anton has its own train station on the main line between Zurich and Innsbruck, about 2.5 hours from Zurich and 1 hour from Innsbruck.

Lech limits how many day passes it sells, which keeps it uncrowded. The ski routes aren't patrolled like pistes, and the off-piste is uncontrolled: go with a guide to explore. It's a very snowy area, and avalanche danger can be high after storms. The Tyrol and Vorarlberg avalanche services publish bulletins.

ischgl.skiing:
The Silvretta Arena links **Ischgl** in Austria with **Samnaun** in Switzerland into about 240 km of pistes, almost all above 2,000 m. The hub is the **Idalp**, a broad high basin, and from there long, wide reds fan out in every direction, including over the border to Switzerland. It's a confident intermediate's playground, with good off-piste between the lifts on a powder day.

Altitude is the selling point: the season runs reliably from late November to early May. The terrain is mostly open and above the trees, with big views and long runs, but few real steeps.

The rest of the Paznaun valley has its own smaller areas. **Kappl** is a family area with sunny, wooded slopes, and **Galtür**, at the head of the valley, is quiet and traditional, with a small ski area and a big ski-touring tradition. From Galtür, the **Jamtal Hut** is one of the classic touring huts in the Silvretta, with glacier peaks all around.
ischgl.beyond:
Ischgl is famous for partying, from afternoon après to clubs that run late, and for the free "Top of the Mountain" concerts that open and close the season. Samnaun, on the Swiss side, is duty-free, and people ski over to stock up.

In 1999 a huge avalanche hit Galtür and killed 31 people; the Alpinarium, built into the new protection wall, tells the story.
ischgl.know:
Innsbruck is about 1.5 hours away; Landeck is the nearest train station, with buses up the valley. Ischgl is busy and not cheap, especially in high season. Staying in Galtür or Kappl and taking the bus is calmer and better value.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak in thin winters, so be careful off-piste and check the Tyrol avalanche bulletin.

otztal.skiing:
Two very different resorts share one long valley. **Sölden** is big, lively and high, with two glaciers (Rettenbach and Tiefenbach) and its "Big 3": three peaks above 3,000 m, each with a viewing platform. The World Cup season opens on the Rettenbach glacier every October, and the area's long runs drop nearly 2,000 m to the village.

**Obergurgl-Hochgurgl**, at the head of the valley, sits at about 1,900 m and is one of the most snow-sure resorts in Austria. The terrain is mostly easy and intermediate, quiet and sunny, with good touring right from the lifts.

The Ötztal is also one of the great ski-touring valleys of the Alps. From **Vent**, a small village in a side valley, tours climb toward the **Wildspitze**, Austria's second-highest peak, and the huts of the Ötztal glaciers, the start of multi-day hut-to-hut trips.
otztal.beyond:
Sölden is a party town; Obergurgl is calm and family-oriented. On the Gaislachkogl summit, the glass-walled ice Q restaurant was a set for the Bond film *Spectre*, and the 007 Elements exhibition sits next to it. Hochgurgl has a motorcycle museum at the top of the closed Timmelsjoch pass road. The Aqua Dome thermal spa in Längenfeld is the classic rest day.

Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old iceman, was found on a glacier above Vent in 1991.
otztal.know:
About 1 hour from Innsbruck by car or bus. Obergurgl and Sölden are on different lift passes, though combined passes exist.

The glaciers make early and late season possible, but they close in strong wind. Off-piste is uncontrolled and the inner-Alpine snowpack is often weak; check the Tyrol bulletin.

kitzbuhel.skiing:
Kitzbühel's KitzSki area covers around 230 km of pistes on several mountains around a medieval town, and the neighbouring **SkiWelt Wilder Kaiser–Brixental** adds a similar amount more. The runs are long, varied and mostly intermediate, with mountain huts at every turn.

The **Streif**, home of the Hahnenkamm downhill each January, is the most famous race course in the world: the Mausefalle jump at the top drops racers onto an 85% slope. You can ski most of it yourself, on a gentler route around the steepest sections.

The **Kitzbüheler Horn**, across the valley, is quieter and sunnier, and **Pass Thurn–Resterhöhe**, to the south, is higher and holds snow better. The grassy Kitzbühel Alps are also popular for gentle ski touring, and many resorts here allow uphill skiing on marked routes beside the pistes.

The area is fairly low, mostly under 2,000 m, so snowmaking matters and the season can be short in a warm winter.
kitzbuhel.beyond: The pedestrian old town has painted houses, good shops, restaurants and nightlife. Toni Sailer, who won three Olympic golds in 1956, was a local hero. Hahnenkamm weekend is one of the biggest parties in skiing.
kitzbuhel.know:
Salzburg and Innsbruck are about 1 hour away, Munich about 1.5 hours, and the town has its own train station.

Check the snow before booking early or late in the season. January race week is busy and expensive. Uphill rules on pistes vary by resort, so check before skinning up.

zillertal.skiing:
The Zillertal is a valley of several ski areas covered by one pass, with more than 500 km of pistes in total. **Mayrhofen** has the Penken and the **Harakiri**, with a gradient of 78%, the steepest groomed run in Austria. **Hintertux**, at the head of the valley, has glacier skiing up to about 3,250 m, open all year.

The **Zillertal Arena**, **Hochfügen** and **Hochzillertal** add plenty of variety. Hochfügen, at the end of a side valley, is especially good for freeride, with open bowls and easy access to off-piste, and it often gets more snow than the main valley.

The Tux and Zillertal Alps also offer good ski touring, from short tours above the valley to glacier peaks around Hintertux. Many tourers use the lifts to get high before skinning on.
zillertal.beyond: The valley towns are lively, with lots of après. Inside the Hintertux glacier, the Natur Eis Palast is a cave you can tour, with ice formations and an underground lake. The Snowbombing festival takes over Mayrhofen each April. Innsbruck is close for a city day.
zillertal.know:
Jenbach is the main train station, about 1 hour from Innsbruck, with the Zillertalbahn running up the valley. Ski buses link the areas, but a car helps.

The lower areas can be thin in a warm winter, but Hintertux almost always has snow. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Tyrol bulletin.

saalbach.skiing:
The Skicircus links **Saalbach**, **Hinterglemm**, **Leogang** and **Fieberbrunn** into about 270 km of pistes. You can ski a full circuit around the valley in either direction, which makes it great for intermediates who like to cover distance and never repeat a run.

**Fieberbrunn**, linked in more recently, catches more snow than the rest and hosts a Freeride World Tour stop on the **Wildseeloder**, a steep, rocky face. Its terrain has some of the best lift-served off-piste in the area, with marked freeride routes and open bowls.

Saalbach hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships in 2025, and its race slopes are steep and well prepared. Leogang has long runs, a bike park in summer, and a quieter feel. The grassy mountains of the area also offer easy ski touring, with many marked uphill routes.
saalbach.beyond: This is one of the great après valleys of Austria, with busy mountain huts, umbrella bars and live music from mid-afternoon. Zell am See, with its frozen lake and the Kitzsteinhorn glacier above Kaprun, is close for a change of scenery.
saalbach.know:
Salzburg is about 1.5 hours away. The area is mid-altitude, mostly below about 2,100 m, so conditions vary with the winter; snowmaking is extensive. If the Skicircus is thin, the Kitzsteinhorn glacier nearby is a good backup.

Good value for a big area, and popular with groups. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Salzburg and Tyrol bulletins.

dolomiti.skiing:
Dolomiti Superski is one pass covering about 12 valleys and around 1,200 km of pistes, including **Val Gardena**, **Alta Badia**, **Arabba** and **Cortina d'Ampezzo**. The **Sella Ronda** is the classic: a loop of about 40 km around the Sella massif, skiable in either direction in a day.

The skiing is mostly groomed and intermediate, among dramatic pale limestone towers. The **Marmolada** glacier, the highest point of the area at about 3,265 m, has a long descent to Malga Ciapela, and the run through the **Hidden Valley** from **Lagazuoi**, past frozen waterfalls, ends with a horse tow back to the lifts.

For experts, the Dolomites have famous couloirs. The **Val Mezdì**, a narrow gully that cuts through the Sella massif from near Sass Pordoi down to Colfosco, is one of the best-known off-piste lines in Italy. Ski touring is excellent too, with classic tours on the Sella plateau and in the Fanes area.
dolomiti.beyond: The food is a big part of the trip: mountain huts serve excellent South Tyrolean and Italian cooking, and Alta Badia has several Michelin-starred restaurants. The Ladin culture, the open-air WWI museums along the old front line, and Cortina (an Olympic host in 1956 and 2026) add depth.
dolomiti.know:
Venice, Verona and Innsbruck are 2 to 3 hours away. A car helps, though buses link the valleys.

Natural snowfall can be thin, but snowmaking is excellent and the pistes are usually in great shape. Off-piste is limited and often steep and rocky: the Dolomites are a groomed-skiing and touring destination more than a freeride one. Go with a guide for the couloirs.

livigno.skiing:
Livigno sits at about 1,800 m in a remote valley near the Swiss border, so it's cold and snow-sure. Two sides of the valley, **Mottolino** and **Carosello 3000**, offer about 115 km of mostly wide, open intermediate pistes, and Mottolino's terrain park is one of the best in Europe.

Carosello is the bigger, higher side, reaching about 3,000 m, with long runs and some off-piste in its upper bowls. Mottolino is steeper and catches the morning sun, with the park and the area's freeride terrain. A free bus links the two sides along the valley floor.

Livigno hosted the freestyle and snowboard events of the 2026 Winter Olympics, and the town has grown into a serious freestyle centre. The surrounding mountains are also good for gentle ski touring, and the valley has one of the best cross-country tracks in Italy along the valley floor.
livigno.beyond: Livigno has long been duty-free, so fuel, alcohol and electronics are cheap, and the long main street is lined with shops. It's a lively, young town. Bormio, over the pass, has thermal baths dating back to Roman times.
livigno.know:
Remote to reach: about 3 to 3.5 hours from Milan or Zurich. From Switzerland, a narrow, one-lane toll tunnel (the Munt la Schera) runs in alternating directions; from Italy, a high pass can close in storms.

The altitude makes it bitterly cold in midwinter, and spring is pleasant. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Lombardy avalanche bulletin.

silvretta.skiing:
Gentle, glaciated hut touring on the border between Austria and Switzerland, with lots of peaks around 3,000 m. Big huts such as the **Jamtalhütte** and **Wiesbadener Hütte** make good bases, and **Piz Buin** (3,312 m), the peak that gave the sunscreen its name, is the best-known summit. The **Dreiländerspitze**, where Tyrol, Vorarlberg and Switzerland meet, is another classic.

The terrain is friendlier than many high Alpine areas, which makes it a good first hut trip, though the glaciers still need care. A **Silvretta traverse**, linking several huts over four to six days, is a popular plan, and day tours from a single hut work too.

The **Rätikon**, to the west, adds limestone peaks, the Drei Türme and the frozen **Lünersee**, with a different, more Dolomite-like feel, and its own huts.
silvretta.beyond: The huts are comfortable by Alpine standards, with good food and a sociable atmosphere. The Montafon valley, on the Vorarlberg side, has traditional villages and its own ski areas for a rest day.
silvretta.know:
The usual starting points are Galtür, in the Paznaun valley, and the Montafon. The Silvretta high road is closed in winter. Huts are staffed in spring (roughly February to May) and need booking, especially at Easter.

Glacier skills or a guide are needed for the higher tours. Check the Tyrol and Vorarlberg avalanche bulletins.

otztalhuts.skiing:
High, glaciated hut touring from **Vent**, a small village at about 1,900 m at the head of the Ötztal. The huts (the **Breslauer**, the **Vernagthütte**, the **Hochjochhospiz** and the high **Brandenburger Haus**) sit among some of the biggest glaciers in Austria. The **Wildspitze** (3,768 m), Austria's second-highest peak, is the classic summit.

Days are long, with big glacier crossings, and the terrain is more serious than the Silvretta or Stubai, with greater distances and altitude. A popular plan is to cross into Italy via the **Similaun**, with a night at the Similaun hut on the border and a descent to the Schnals valley.

Other classic summits include the **Fluchtkogel**, the **Weisskugel** and the many peaks around the Gepatsch and Kesselwand glaciers. The landscape is vast, white and open, with few signs of people.
otztalhuts.beyond: Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old iceman, was found on a glacier pass near the Similaun hut in 1991. Every summer, shepherds still drive sheep across the glaciers between Italy and the Ötztal, a tradition recognised by UNESCO. Vent is tiny and quiet, and the Aqua Dome spa down the valley is a good finish.
otztalhuts.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Book huts ahead. You need glacier skills, crampons and good fitness, or a guide.

About 1.5 hours from Innsbruck. The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak; check the Tyrol bulletin daily.

stubai.skiing:
The Stubai Alps have one of the densest hut networks in Austria, and they're the classic place for a first hut-touring week. The **Franz-Senn-Hütte**, named after a priest who helped found the Alpine Club, and the **Amberger Hütte** are bases for many 3,000 m peaks. You can tour from one hut for several days or link several huts together.

From the Franz-Senn-Hütte, tours lead to peaks like the **Ruderhofspitze** and the Wildes Hinterbergl, with glaciers and open slopes in every direction. From the Amberger Hütte, the **Schrankogel** (3,497 m) is one of the big objectives. The **Zuckerhütl** (3,507 m) is the highest summit in the range.

The **Stubai Glacier**, Austria's largest glacier ski area, is close for a warm-up day on lifts, and its top lifts also give quick access to touring terrain.
stubai.beyond: Innsbruck is less than an hour away, so a city day is easy. The huts are traditional and welcoming, with hearty Tyrolean food like Kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings).
stubai.know:
Spring is the main season. Book huts ahead, especially at weekends and Easter. Buses run from Innsbruck into the Stubai valley.

The terrain mixes glaciers and steep slopes, so glacier skills or a guide are needed. The Tyrol bulletin covers the area.

ortler.skiing:
High, glaciated touring in the Stelvio National Park, around the Ortler and Cevedale groups. The **Casati hut**, at about 3,250 m on the pass below the Cevedale, and the **Branca hut** in the Forni valley are the classic bases. From them, big rounded glacier summits like the **Cevedale** (3,769 m) and **Palon de la Mare** (3,703 m) make some of the best ski 3,000ers in the Alps.

The Forni glacier, once one of the largest valley glaciers in Italy, is the heart of the area, and a classic loop links several summits around it. The Ortler itself (3,905 m) is more of a mountaineering objective.

The altitude keeps the snow good late into spring. **Santa Caterina Valfurva** and **Solda** are the main bases, both with small lift-served areas.
ortler.beyond: This area was on the front line of the First World War, the so-called "White War" fought on glaciers, and the melting ice still reveals traces of it. Bormio, with its Roman thermal baths, is the place to recover.
ortler.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Access is from Santa Caterina Valfurva or Solda. Milan is about 3.5 hours away; the Stelvio pass is closed in winter.

You need glacier skills, crampons and acclimatisation for the altitude, or a guide. Check the Lombardy and South Tyrol avalanche bulletins.

fanes.skiing:
Quieter Dolomites touring through the Fanes-Senes-Braies nature park, between Cortina and Alta Badia: high limestone plateaus, gentle valleys and some steeper peaks. Rifugi such as **Fanes**, **Lavarella** and **Sennes** make bases for day tours or a multi-day traverse.

The terrain is mostly moderate, which makes it a good introduction to Dolomites touring, though some peaks are steep and rocky. Summits like **Col Becchei** and **Piz Lavarella** offer big views over the plateau, and the **Sennes** plateau is a wide, open area of gentle slopes.

The usual start is the **Pederü** hut, at the end of the road from San Vigilio di Marebbe, from where a track climbs to the plateau. A traverse can continue to the Braies valley or toward Cortina.
fanes.beyond: The rifugi serve excellent South Tyrolean and Ladin food, and Lavarella brews its own beer. The area is full of Ladin legends about the lost Kingdom of Fanes, and the famous Lago di Braies is on the edge of the park.
fanes.know:
Access is from San Vigilio di Marebbe and the Pederü hut, with snowcat taxis to some rifugi. Rifugi open in winter and spring; book ahead. Venice and Innsbruck are about 2.5 hours away.

The Dolomites' snowpack is often thin and weak: check the South Tyrol avalanche bulletin carefully.

julianalps.skiing:
Slovenia's Julian Alps catch heavy snowfall from the Adriatic and offer limestone karst terrain unlike anywhere else in the Alps: bowls, sinkholes and steep gullies. **Kanin**, above Bovec, is the highest ski area in Slovenia and links to **Sella Nevea** in Italy, giving access to touring and freeride terrain on the high karst plateau. Its lifts have had long closures in recent years, so check before you go.

**Triglav** (2,864 m), Slovenia's highest peak and a national symbol on its flag, is a more serious objective, usually a spring tour. **Vogel**, above Lake Bohinj, is a small ski area with one of the best lake views in the Alps, and it gives access to easy touring on the plateau behind.

The Italian side of the range, around Sella Nevea and Tarvisio, has steep, snowy couloirs and big north faces, with a strong local freeride scene.
julianalps.beyond: The Soča valley is famous for its emerald river. Kobarid has an excellent museum about the First World War front on the Soča, the setting for Hemingway's *A Farewell to Arms*. Planica, near Kranjska Gora, has the world's biggest ski-flying hill. Ljubljana and Lake Bled are close for days off.
julianalps.know:
Many mountain huts are closed in winter, so tours are often day trips from the valley. Ljubljana is about 2 hours away; Trieste and Venice are close too. The Vršič pass is closed in winter.

The karst terrain hides holes and drops, so go with a local guide. Slovenia's avalanche bulletin is published by ARSO.

whistler.skiing:
Two big mountains, **Whistler** and **Blackcomb**, linked at the top by the Peak 2 Peak gondola, make this the largest ski area in North America, with more than 200 marked runs, over 3,300 hectares of terrain and about 1,600 m of vertical. Above the trees are wide alpine bowls, glaciers and steep chutes; below them, long groomers and some of the best storm-day tree skiing in the West.

Each mountain has its own character. Whistler's alpine has big open bowls (Harmony, Symphony, Whistler Bowl) and is the place to be on a clear powder morning. Blackcomb has the Horstman and Blackcomb glaciers, and famous steep entrances like the couloirs off the top of the 7th Heaven area. With so much terrain, even busy days have quiet corners.

The coastal location brings lots of snow, often more than 10 m a season up high, but also mild storms: it can rain at the village while it dumps above about 1,500 m. Freezing level is the number to watch.

Whistler is also the gateway to the **Spearhead Traverse**, a classic hut-to-hut tour linking the two ski areas through the glaciers behind them, and to the **Duffey Lake Road**, an hour north, where roadside touring reaches big peaks in a colder, drier climate.
whistler.beyond:
The pedestrian village is busy and lively, with every kind of restaurant, bar and shop, and a strong après culture. The Scandinave Spa, in the forest outside town, is a classic rest day, and the Audain Art Museum has a fine collection of West Coast and First Nations art. The Squamish Lil'wat Cultural Centre tells the story of the two nations whose shared territory this is.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway from Vancouver, along Howe Sound and past the granite walls of the Stawamus Chief, is one of the most scenic drives anywhere, and Vancouver itself is easy to add to the trip.
whistler.know:
Whistler is about 2 hours by road from Vancouver airport, with regular shuttle buses, so you don't need a car. It's busy and expensive, especially at weekends and during holidays, when lift lines at the village gondolas can be long; the Creekside base is often quieter. It's on the Epic Pass.

Check the freezing level each day: when it's high, ski the alpine and avoid the lower runs. Avalanche Canada's Sea-to-Sky forecast covers the backcountry; the resort's own terrain is controlled, but the gates to the backcountry lead to uncontrolled, glaciated terrain. The Spearhead's huts are run by the Spearhead Huts Society and need booking.

mammoth.skiing:
Mammoth Mountain is a dormant volcano rising to about 3,370 m above the Eastern Sierra, and one of the biggest ski areas in California, with more than 1,400 hectares of terrain and about 950 m of vertical from the summit to the lowest lift. The terrain covers everything: wide groomers and some of the best terrain parks in North America lower down, and a summit ridge of steep chutes and open bowls, reached by gondola, that open when the wind allows.

Its altitude and big Sierra storms give one of the longest seasons in North America, usually from November and often into June; in big years, skiing continues to July 4th. The snow is often deep but dense, and the sun is strong, so spring brings excellent corn.

Dave McCoy started Mammoth with a portable rope tow in the 1940s and grew it into one of America's great ski mountains. **June Mountain**, about 30 minutes north, is the quieter sister: small, steep in places, uncrowded, with views of the Sierra crest.

The Eastern Sierra's backcountry, from the Mammoth Crest to the big couloirs of Rock Creek and Convict Lake, is right next door.
mammoth.beyond:
The Eastern Sierra is a spectacular road trip: natural hot springs in the desert below town, the tufa towers of Mono Lake and, when roads allow, the basalt columns of Devils Postpile. The town of Mammoth Lakes has plenty of restaurants and breweries, and the village at the base of the gondola keeps things lively.

Further afield, Bishop has famous bouldering, and Death Valley and the Alabama Hills are a long day's drive.
mammoth.know:
Los Angeles is about 5 to 6 hours by car; flights to the small local airports are limited and change from year to year. Tioga Pass, the shortcut from the Bay Area through Yosemite, is closed in winter, so from the north you come via Lake Tahoe and Highway 395.

Weekends and holidays bring crowds from Southern California. Wind closes the upper lifts often, so have a plan for lower-mountain days. The altitude is high: the base is about 2,400 m, so take it easy on the first day.

Mammoth and June are on the Ikon Pass. The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry.

cottonwoods.skiing:
Two canyons above Salt Lake City hold four resorts with some of the deepest, driest snow in North America, the basis of Utah's "Greatest Snow on Earth" slogan. Storms crossing the desert arrive cold, then stall against the Wasatch, and the canyons can get more than 13 m of snow in a season.

In **Little Cottonwood**, **Alta** is skiers-only (no snowboards), with legendary traverses, steep chutes and old-school charm; it has been run with a famously light touch since the 1930s. **Snowbird**, next door and linked by a shared pass, has a 125-person aerial tram, steep north-facing terrain, more than 1,000 m of vertical and one of the longest seasons in the US, often into May or June.

In **Big Cottonwood**, **Brighton** and **Solitude** are smaller, cheaper and more local. Brighton has night skiing and a strong snowboard culture; Solitude has quiet tree runs and the steep, wild terrain of Honeycomb Canyon.

The backcountry between and around the canyons is one of the most popular in the US. Trailheads along both canyon roads lead to famous tours such as **Mount Superior**, **Grizzly Gulch**, **Cardiff Fork** and **Days Fork**, and on powder mornings the parking lots fill before dawn.
cottonwoods.beyond:
Salt Lake City is a 40-minute drive, so you can stay in town and ski the canyons, with restaurants, breweries and a big airport close by. Or stay at a classic lodge such as the Alta Lodge or Snowbird's Cliff Lodge for the full mountain experience, including being snowed in.

On days off, Park City and its old mining town are an hour away, and Salt Lake City has the Great Salt Lake, Temple Square and good hot springs in the nearby mountains.
cottonwoods.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 40 minutes away. Little Cottonwood Canyon's road is one of the most avalanche-exposed highways in the US, and closes for control work after big storms. During "interlodge", guests at the top have to stay indoors until it's safe, sometimes for a day or more.

Traffic on powder mornings can be severe, with queues backing down into the valley, and paid parking or reservations are now required at some resorts on busy days. Take the ski bus or start very early. Alta and Snowbird sell a joint pass; all four resorts are on the Ikon Pass (Alta, Snowbird, Brighton and Solitude, with varying days).

The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry daily. The Wasatch snowpack can be very unstable, and the backcountry here sees some of the most avalanche accidents in the US: carry gear, check the forecast, and consider a local guide.

parkcity.skiing:
Since Canyons and Park City were linked in 2015, **Park City Mountain** has been one of the largest ski areas in the US, with more than 7,000 acres (about 2,900 hectares) and over 300 trails. It has lots of terrain for every level: long groomers, open bowls along the ridgeline, and trees. The two sides of the mountain feel different, with the Canyons side slightly snowier and more spread out.

**Deer Valley**, next door, is skiers-only and famous for immaculate grooming, limited ticket sales and a level of service unusual in skiing. It's in the middle of a major expansion that is adding new lifts and terrain on its eastern side, so it will keep growing over the next few seasons.

The snow is dry Utah powder, though Park City sits a little lower and less in the storm track than the Cottonwoods, so it gets less: roughly 8 to 9 m a season versus 13 m at Alta. The trade-off is a real town at the bottom, easy access and lots of sunshine. When the Cottonwoods are on, they're under an hour away.

**Guardsman Pass**, between Park City and Big Cottonwood, is the local backcountry road access, open only part of the winter.
parkcity.beyond:
Park City is an old silver-mining town with a lively Main Street of bars, restaurants and galleries in restored 19th-century buildings. Several events of the 2002 Winter Olympics were held here, and at the Utah Olympic Park you can ride the bobsled track with a pilot and watch ski jumpers train. The Sundance Film Festival has made January famous here, though it's moving to Boulder from 2027.

Salt Lake City, under an hour away, has good restaurants and the Great Salt Lake.
parkcity.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 40 minutes away. Free buses run around town and between the resorts, so you don't need a car. Holidays and weekends are busy, and Park City Mountain's main base areas can have long lift lines on peak days.

Park City Mountain is on the Epic Pass; Deer Valley is on the Ikon Pass. Deer Valley caps daily ticket sales, so buy in advance.

The Utah Avalanche Center covers the backcountry; the Park City zone has its own daily forecast.
