jackson.skiing:
Jackson Hole is America's big-mountain resort: around 1,260 m of continuous vertical, served by the red Aerial Tram to the top of Rendezvous Mountain. **Corbet's Couloir**, a cliff drop into a narrow chute right under the tram, is one of the most famous runs in the world. The rest of the mountain is steep too, with chutes, cliffs, big bowls like Rendezvous and Cheyenne, and long fall-line runs. Even the groomers tend to be pitched.

The resort pioneered open backcountry gates in the US, and the terrain beyond them, toward Granite Canyon and Rock Springs, is huge and serious: uncontrolled, avalanche-prone and easy to get lost in. Jackson is also one of the best places in the country to learn steep skiing, with steep camps and guided days.

**Grand Targhee**, on the Wyoming side of the Tetons but reached through Idaho, gets more snow, often lighter and deeper, and has a gentler, family feel with cat skiing on its own peak. Many skiers combine the two.

**Teton Pass**, between Jackson and Victor, Idaho, is one of the busiest backcountry roads in the US, and Grand Teton National Park offers serious ski mountaineering.
jackson.beyond:
The town of Jackson is a Western mountain town with good food, galleries and the Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, where the bar stools are saddles. Sleigh rides go through the National Elk Refuge, where thousands of elk spend the winter. Snowcoach and snowmobile tours run into Yellowstone, and wildlife tours in Grand Teton National Park often see moose, bison and sometimes wolves.

Teton Village, at the base, is small and convenient; Jackson itself has more life in the evenings.
jackson.know:
Jackson's airport is inside Grand Teton National Park, with direct flights from many US hubs, especially in winter. Teton Village is at the base of the resort; the town is about 20 minutes away, with regular buses. Grand Targhee is about 1.5 hours away over Teton Pass.

The terrain is steep. If you're new to it, ski with a guide or join a steep-skiing camp before heading into the bigger lines. Jackson and Targhee are on the Ikon Pass, with limited days.

Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry daily. Don't go through the gates without avalanche gear, a partner and the skills to use them.

bigsky.skiing:
Big Sky is huge and uncrowded, with about 2,350 hectares of terrain and **Lone Peak** at its centre, a pyramid of a mountain at about 3,400 m. A tram climbs to the summit, and from there steep, exposed terrain drops in every direction, with around 1,300 m of vertical. The **Big Couloir**, a long, sustained chute off the summit, requires a partner, avalanche gear and a check-in with patrol.

Below the peak, the resort has long cruisers, open bowls, glades and wide-open terrain on Andesite Mountain and the Southern Comfort area, with rarely a lift line, even on busy days. New high-speed lifts and a new tram in recent years have made getting around much faster.

The snow is cold and dry, from a continental snowpack, and the season is long. Montana's other mountains add variety: **Bridger Bowl**, a community-run hill near Bozeman, is famous for its steep Ridge terrain, reached by a hike from the top lift. Further south, **Cooke City**, near Yellowstone's northeast gate, is a remote mountain town known for its deep snow and backcountry, mostly reached by snowmobile.
bigsky.beyond:
Yellowstone National Park is close: snowcoach tours run to Old Faithful in winter, and the wildlife is spectacular, with bison, elk and, if you're lucky, wolves in the Lamar Valley. Bozeman has a lively college-town feel, with good restaurants and breweries, and the Museum of the Rockies, known for its dinosaur fossils.

Chico Hot Springs, in Paradise Valley, is a classic soak.
bigsky.know:
Bozeman airport is about 1 hour away, with flights from many US cities. The resort is remote, so most people stay on the mountain or in the small Big Sky town. The canyon road from Bozeman is long and can be icy.

Big Sky is pricier than most of Montana, and lodging on the mountain books up in holiday weeks. Staying in Bozeman and driving up is cheaper. Big Sky is on the Ikon Pass.

The Gallatin Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry, including the Bridger Range and Cooke City. Cooke City's backcountry is big and remote, and many accidents there involve snowmobiles: go with local knowledge.

aspen.skiing:
Aspen Snowmass is four very different mountains on one lift pass. **Aspen Mountain**, known as Ajax, rises right from the edge of town, with steep, fall-line runs, mogul lines and no beginner terrain at all. **Aspen Highlands** is the locals' favourite, with the **Highland Bowl**, a hike-to bowl at about 3,780 m whose steep, open faces are some of the best inbounds expert skiing in Colorado. The hike takes 30 to 60 minutes, and the views of the Maroon Bells are a reward in themselves.

**Snowmass**, about 20 minutes away, is the big one, with more than 1,300 hectares and around 1,300 m of vertical, from long groomers and family terrain to the steep Hanging Valley and Cirque. **Buttermilk** is gentle, with excellent beginner terrain and the terrain park that hosts the Winter X Games.

The snow is dry and light, but Colorado's continental snowpack is often weak, with buried layers that can persist all season. Inbounds is controlled; the backcountry, including the classic tours from the Braun and 10th Mountain huts, needs real avalanche skills. In late spring, when Independence Pass opens, the high peaks around it become a well-known corn-skiing objective.
aspen.beyond:
Aspen was a silver-mining boomtown in the 1880s, then nearly a ghost town, until veterans of the 10th Mountain Division and the industrialist Walter Paepcke helped turn it into a ski resort and cultural centre after the Second World War. Today it's known for luxury and celebrities, but the Victorian town, the Hotel Jerome and the Wheeler Opera House still give it real character.

The Aspen Art Museum, good restaurants at every price, and the Maroon Bells (reached by snowmobile tour or on skis in winter) fill rest days.
aspen.know:
Aspen has its own airport, with flights from US hubs, though weather sometimes diverts them. Denver is about 3.5 to 4 hours by car, since Independence Pass is closed in winter. Free buses link the four mountains and the town.

It's expensive, especially in town; Basalt, Carbondale and Glenwood Springs are cheaper bases. Aspen Snowmass is on the Ikon Pass, with limited days.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts the backcountry daily.

vail.skiing:
Vail is one of the biggest ski areas in North America, with more than 2,000 hectares of terrain. The front side is classic groomed skiing, with long, rolling runs down to the village. Behind it, the **Back Bowls** stretch for about 11 km along the ridge: wide open, treeless and superb on a powder day. Further back still, **Blue Sky Basin** has more remote-feeling terrain, with gladed trees, small cliffs and natural half-pipes.

Vail was founded in 1962 by Pete Seibert and Earl Eaton, and Seibert was one of the many veterans of the 10th Mountain Division who trained at nearby Camp Hale during the Second World War. **Beaver Creek**, about 15 minutes west, is smaller and more upscale, with immaculate grooming, warm cookies at 3 p.m. and the Birds of Prey downhill course, one of the hardest on the World Cup.

The snow is dry Colorado powder. **Vail Pass**, just east of the resort on I-70, is a popular backcountry and snowmobile area, and **Shrine Pass** is a classic, gentle tour from it.
vail.beyond:
The village is built in a Tyrolean style, with pedestrian streets, covered bridges, restaurants and shops. The Colorado Snowsports Museum, in the village, tells the story of the 10th Mountain Division and Colorado skiing. Beaver Creek is more upscale and calm. Both are expensive.

The old mining town of Leadville, about 45 minutes away, is the highest incorporated city in the US and a good contrast. Camp Hale, now a national monument, is on the way.
vail.know:
Eagle County airport is about 40 minutes away; Denver is about 2 hours, but I-70 traffic on weekends can make it much longer, and storms close Vail Pass. Free buses run through the village and between the towns of the valley.

Vail is on the Epic Pass, and buying a pass ahead is far cheaper than walk-up tickets, which are among the most expensive in the world. Staying in Avon, Edwards or Minturn is cheaper than the village.

The Colorado snowpack is often weak, so be careful in the backcountry. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

summit.skiing:
Summit County is a cluster of big resorts within about 2 hours of Denver, at some of the highest elevations in North America. **Breckenridge** spreads across five peaks above a Victorian mining town, and its Imperial Express is one of the highest chairlifts on the continent, reaching about 3,900 m. **Keystone** has night skiing and big intermediate terrain on three mountains. **Copper Mountain** separates its terrain neatly by difficulty, from easy on one side to steep on the other.

**Arapahoe Basin** is high, steep and old-school, with the hike-to terrain of the East Wall and the expert chutes of the Steep Gullies; it's often open from October into June. **Loveland**, right on the Continental Divide, is a no-frills locals' favourite with free cat rides to the ridge.

Everything is high, with bases at around 2,900 m, so the snow is dry and the season long. The trade-off is wind and cold: the upper lifts are exposed, and January can be bitter.

The passes are the local backcountry: **Loveland Pass** is famous for short, road-accessed laps, and **Berthoud Pass**, a former ski area, has lots of easy-access terrain.
summit.beyond:
Breckenridge is an old gold-mining town with a pretty Victorian main street, good restaurants and breweries. Frisco and Dillon, on the Dillon Reservoir, are cheaper and quieter. At A-Basin, the parking lot by the slopes, known as "the Beach", is famous for spring tailgating and barbecues.

Denver is close enough for a city day.
summit.know:
Denver airport is about 2 hours away, but I-70 traffic on weekends can be very slow, especially after big storms; leave early or ski midweek. Free buses (the Summit Stage) link the towns and most resorts.

The resorts are on different passes: Breckenridge and Keystone are on the Epic Pass; Copper and A-Basin on the Ikon Pass. Check which one you need.

The altitude is high: drink lots of water and take it easy the first day. The Colorado snowpack is weak and often dangerous; check the CAIC forecast before going near the passes.

steamboat.skiing:
Steamboat is known for its tree skiing and for "Champagne Powder", a name it trademarked for its unusually light, dry snow. Aspen glades and open terrain cover a big, rolling mountain with about 1,100 m of vertical, and the resort is good for everyone, from families on long cruisers to tree skiers in famous glades like Shadows, Closet and the Twilight area. A major expansion in recent years added the Fish Creek Canyon terrain and a long new gondola.

Steamboat sits a little further north and west than most of Colorado's resorts, so it catches storms well and gets around 8 m of snow a season. It's colder than the I-70 resorts too, which keeps the snow dry.

**Howelsen Hill**, in town, is one of the oldest ski areas in the US, operating since 1915. It has ski jumps, night skiing and a big role in producing Olympians.

The backcountry nearby is famous for deep snow: **Buffalo Pass**, north of town, gets some of the most snow in Colorado and has cat skiing and touring, and **Rabbit Ears Pass**, to the south-east, is gentler.
steamboat.beyond:
Steamboat is a real ranching town with a Western feel, rather than a purpose-built resort. Strawberry Park Hot Springs, in the hills above town, has natural rock pools and is a beautiful place to soak in the snow at night. In town, the Old Town Hot Springs is a family-friendly alternative.

The town has produced more Winter Olympians than almost any other in the US, earning it the nickname "Ski Town USA". Cowboys in the lift line are not a costume: ranching is still part of daily life in the Yampa Valley.
steamboat.know:
Yampa Valley airport, at Hayden, is about 30 minutes away, with seasonal direct flights. Denver is about 3 hours by car, over Rabbit Ears Pass. A free bus links town and the mountain.

Steamboat is on the Ikon Pass. It's busy in holiday weeks but rarely as crowded as the I-70 resorts.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry, including Buffalo and Rabbit Ears passes.

telluride.skiing:
Telluride is a former mining town in a box canyon in the San Juan Mountains, with a ski area rising right behind it and 13,000-foot peaks all around. The terrain is big and varied: long groomers for all levels, including the famous See Forever run along the ridge, plus serious expert terrain. **Palmyra Peak**, at about 4,000 m, and the chutes of **Gold Hill** are hike-to lines among the best inbounds steeps in Colorado, and the bumps of the Plunge and Spiral Stairs drop straight toward town.

It's remote, so even on busy days the lift lines are short, and the scenery, with the Wilson Range and the San Juans in every direction, is some of the best in North American skiing.

The San Juans are big, steep and wild, but they have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America, and the backcountry here demands respect. **Lizard Head Pass**, south of town, is the classic local backcountry, with Black Face a popular tour. Helitrax runs heli-skiing in the surrounding peaks, and Red Mountain Pass, near Silverton, is about 2 hours away.
telluride.beyond:
The town is a National Historic Landmark, with Victorian buildings and a main street that feels untouched by mass tourism. Butch Cassidy robbed his first bank here in 1889. A free gondola links the town to Mountain Village, running until late in the evening, and is one of the nicest commutes in skiing.

Ouray, about 1.5 hours away by road, has hot springs and a famous ice park.
telluride.know:
Montrose airport is about 1.5 hours away; the small Telluride airport is often affected by weather. Denver is about 6 hours by car. Once there, you don't need a car.

Telluride is on the Epic Pass (with limited days). The town is expensive, though less so than Aspen or Vail.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America; check the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecast carefully before going out of bounds.

crestedbutte.skiing:
Crested Butte is famous for its **Extreme Limits**: steep, rocky, inbounds terrain that hosted some of the first extreme skiing competitions in the US in the early 1990s. The North Face, Headwall and Teocalli areas are full of chutes, cliffs and tight trees, and many of them need a lot of snow before they open. Below the steeps, the mountain has good intermediate runs and a relaxed, uncrowded feel.

It's often called the last great Colorado ski town, because it's so remote and still feels like a small community. Crested Butte is quiet midweek, and on a powder day the locals know which steep zones open first. It's a mountain that rewards a few days to learn its secrets, rather than a single visit.

The backcountry is right on the doorstep. **Kebler Pass** and **Washington Gulch**, just west and north of town, lead to classic tours, including the famous Red Lady Bowl on Mount Emmons, which dominates the view from town. **Snodgrass Mountain**, next to the ski area, is a popular short tour. Crested Butte is also the start of the Grand Traverse, an overnight ski-mountaineering race over the Elk Mountains to Aspen.
crestedbutte.beyond: The town of Crested Butte, an old coal-mining town, has a colourful main street (Elk Avenue) with good restaurants and bars, and a strong community feel. Cross-country skiing and fat biking are popular, with lots of groomed trails. The Alpenglow concert series and the big Al Johnson Memorial Uphill/Downhill telemark race in March are local institutions.
crestedbutte.know:
Gunnison airport is about 45 minutes away, with seasonal flights. Denver is about 4.5 hours by car. A free bus links town and the mountain.

Crested Butte is on the Epic Pass. It's one of the coldest places in Colorado in midwinter.

The snowpack is often weak; the Crested Butte Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry daily.

taos.skiing:
Taos Ski Valley, founded by Ernie Blake in 1955, has some of the steepest inbounds terrain in North America, tucked into a narrow valley in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The **Kachina Peak** lift, added in 2014, reaches about 3,800 m, one of the highest lift-served points in North America, and the **Highline Ridge** and **West Basin Ridge** are hikes to steep chutes like Stauffenberg and Juarez. Al's Run, the steep mogul run right above the base, sets the tone from the first chairlift.

The resort has a European feel, with a small village at the base and strong ski-school traditions; the week-long Ski Week lessons are a local institution. Snowboarding has been allowed since 2008. New owners have invested heavily in new lifts and lodging, and the resort became one of the first certified B Corps in skiing.

The snow in New Mexico varies a lot from year to year: in good seasons, the steeps are superb; in dry ones, coverage can be thin. Above the valley, **Wheeler Peak**, the highest summit in New Mexico at about 4,010 m, is a classic spring tour.
taos.beyond: Taos is a fascinating town with adobe buildings, art galleries and New Mexican food. Order your chile "Christmas" (red and green). Taos Pueblo, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has been lived in for about 1,000 years. The Rio Grande Gorge Bridge and the natural hot springs along the river are nearby, and Santa Fe is easy to add.
taos.know:
Albuquerque is about 2.5 hours away; Santa Fe is about 1.5 hours. Taos Ski Valley is a small, high village at the end of a winding canyon road. Staying in the valley gives you the full experience; staying in the town of Taos gives you more food and culture, about 30 minutes away.

The altitude is high, so take it easy at first. Taos is on the Ikon Pass.

The snowpack in New Mexico is often thin and weak; check the Taos Avalanche Center forecast before going outside the resort.

sunvalley.skiing:
Sun Valley was America's first destination ski resort, built in 1936 by the Union Pacific railroad's chairman, Averell Harriman, who wanted a European-style resort to fill his trains. It's also where the world's first chairlifts were installed, based on a design for loading bananas onto ships.

**Bald Mountain** (Baldy) has about 1,000 m of steady, consistent fall-line vertical, with very little flat terrain, few lift lines and some of the best grooming in the world, which makes it a dream for skiers who love speed and carving. The bowls on the back side, like Easter and Christmas bowls, can be excellent after a storm, and the Seattle Ridge area has long, gentle runs with big views. **Dollar Mountain**, next to the village, is the gentle beginner's hill, with good terrain parks.

The snow is often thin by Western standards, and Sun Valley's snowmaking system is one of the biggest in the country, which keeps Baldy reliable. The backcountry is excellent: **Galena Summit**, north of town, is the local touring spot, and the **Sawtooth Mountains** beyond, around Stanley, have yurt-based touring in wild, granite terrain.
sunvalley.beyond:
Sun Valley has a long Hollywood history, from Clark Gable and Marilyn Monroe to today's celebrities, and the Sun Valley Lodge still has old-school glamour, with photos of famous guests on the walls. Ernest Hemingway lived in nearby Ketchum, finished *For Whom the Bell Tolls* at the lodge and is buried in Ketchum's cemetery. The town has excellent restaurants, good galleries and a relaxed feel.

The outdoor ice rink at the lodge and the Nordic trails of the Wood River Valley fill rest days, and the hot springs around Stanley are a beautiful drive away.
sunvalley.know:
Friedman Memorial airport, in Hailey, is about 20 minutes away, but flights are limited and weather can divert them to Twin Falls or Boise, 2 to 3 hours away.

Sun Valley is on the Epic Pass (with limited days). It's quiet by Western standards, except over the holidays.

The Sawtooth Avalanche Center forecasts the backcountry, including Galena Summit and the Sawtooths. Sun Valley Trekking and other operators run guided yurt trips.

mtbaker.skiing:
Mt. Baker Ski Area holds the world record for snowfall in a single season: about 29 m in 1998–99, and it averages more than 16 m a year. It sits not on Mount Baker itself but on the ridges between Baker and **Mount Shuksan**, whose glaciers and rock spires make some of the most dramatic views in North American skiing.

The terrain is steep and varied, with natural halfpipes, cliffs, gullies and trees, and the deep, heavy Cascade snow sticks to slopes that would be rock in drier places. There's no lodging at the mountain, no village and no real resort scene. It's all about the snow and the terrain, and the lifts are mostly old fixed-grip chairs.

The backcountry beyond the gates is excellent and easily reached. The **Shuksan Arm**, a long ridge running toward Shuksan, has classic steep descents, and **Table Mountain** and **Artist Point** at the top of the access road are popular touring areas. Mount Baker itself, a glaciated volcano, is a separate spring objective from Heliotrope Ridge or the Easton Glacier.
mtbaker.beyond: The Legendary Baker Banked Slalom, held each February since 1985, is one of the most loved events in snowboarding, and Baker played a big role in snowboarding's early culture. The small town of Glacier, at the bottom of the road, has a couple of places to eat and stay; Bellingham is a pleasant college town with breweries and good food, and the San Juan Islands are close.
mtbaker.know:
Bellingham is about 1.5 hours away; Seattle is about 2.5 to 3 hours; Vancouver about 2.5 hours, plus the border. The road up is winding and snowy, so carry chains. Most visitors stay in Glacier, Maple Falls or Bellingham.

The Pacific snowpack is heavy and wet. Storm slabs, tree wells and deep-snow immersion are serious hazards, and the Shuksan Arm and other gated terrain have seen many accidents. The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts the area.

silverton.skiing:
Silverton Mountain is unlike any other US ski area: a single old chairlift serving steep, ungroomed, avalanche-controlled terrain, with a base at about 3,200 m and hike-to terrain reaching around 4,000 m. For much of the season, skiing is guided only, in small groups, and the hikes from the top of the lift, along the ridges of Storm Peak, open even more terrain: chutes, open bowls and big alpine faces.

It's expert-only, with no groomed runs or easy way down, and the vibe is closer to a backcountry operation than a resort. There's no lodge on the mountain: the base is a heated tent and a school bus. Heli drops are available too, for big lines on the surrounding peaks. In spring, the resort usually offers unguided skiing for a short period, once the snowpack has settled.

The San Juans get less snow than the coastal ranges, but it's often light and dry, and the terrain is some of the most dramatic in Colorado. Red Mountain Pass, just north of town, is one of the state's most famous backcountry roads.
silverton.beyond: Silverton is a former mining town with a Wild West feel, high in the San Juans at about 2,800 m, with a main street of Victorian buildings and old saloons. In summer, the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad steams up the canyon, and in winter a shorter trip runs from Durango. Ouray, over Red Mountain Pass, has hot springs and a famous ice-climbing park.
silverton.know:
Durango is about 1.5 hours away by road, over high mountain passes that can close in storms. Book guided days well ahead, as group sizes are small.

The town is small, with a handful of hotels, cafés and bars, many open only in season. Pack layers: the cold and altitude can hit hard.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America; listen to your guide. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

revelstoke.skiing:
Revelstoke Mountain Resort has the biggest lift-served vertical in North America, about 1,710 m, from the top of Mount Mackenzie down to the edge of town. The snow in the Selkirks and Monashees is deep and frequent, and the terrain is steep: old-growth trees, open alpine bowls like North Bowl and Greely Bowl, hike-to terrain and long runs that test your legs from top to bottom.

The resort also has easier terrain, but the mountain is at its best for strong skiers. Lift lines are short by big-resort standards, though powder days have become busier as the resort's reputation has grown.

Revelstoke is also the hub of BC's "Powder Highway": heli-skiing (including the world's largest heli operations), cat skiing and backcountry touring all run from town. **Rogers Pass** is about an hour east. Closer, **Mount Revelstoke National Park** has touring from the Meadows in the Sky Parkway, and **Mount Begbie**, the glaciated peak across the valley, is a classic spring ski-mountaineering objective.
revelstoke.beyond: The town of Revelstoke is a real railway town with a historic downtown, good restaurants, cafés and breweries. The Railway Museum tells the story of the transcontinental railway through the mountains, and the Last Spike, where it was completed in 1885, is a short drive west at Craigellachie. Hot springs at Halcyon and Canyon are a drive away.
revelstoke.know:
Kelowna airport is about 2.5 to 3 hours away; Calgary is about 5 hours. The roads, especially the Trans-Canada over Rogers Pass and Highway 23, can be difficult in winter and close for avalanche control.

Stay in town rather than at the base for the restaurants and better value; the gondola is a short drive or bus ride away. Revelstoke is on the Epic Pass (with limited days).

Interior BC's snowpack often has persistent buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily, and Mount Revelstoke National Park requires the same care as Rogers Pass.

kickinghorse.skiing:
Kicking Horse, above the town of Golden, is a steep, serious mountain with over 100 chutes, four big bowls and about 1,260 m of vertical from a single gondola. The terrain includes wide open bowls like Crystal and Feuz, rocky ridges and steep, narrow chutes off the ridgelines, many reached by short hikes. There are fewer easy runs than at most resorts, though the gondola and some long groomers make it skiable for intermediates.

It sits in the Purcell Mountains, with views across the Columbia Valley to the Rockies, and the snow is usually drier and lighter than at the coastal resorts. It's a favourite of freeriders who like to work for their turns, and has hosted Freeride World Tour events.

Golden is surrounded by backcountry operations: heli and cat skiing in the Purcells, and huts in the Selkirks and Rockies. Rogers Pass is about an hour west and the Icefields Parkway's touring is a few hours north.
kickinghorse.beyond: The Eagle's Eye restaurant, at the top of the gondola, is the highest restaurant in Canada. Golden is a working town on the railway and the Trans-Canada Highway, with a long timber-frame pedestrian bridge over the Kicking Horse River and a growing restaurant scene. Yoho National Park, just east, has frozen waterfalls and Emerald Lake.
kickinghorse.know:
Calgary airport is about 3 hours away by road, through Banff and Yoho national parks. The Trans-Canada Highway can close in storms or for avalanche control.

Golden is a good base for a road trip: Revelstoke, Rogers Pass and Lake Louise are all within about 1.5 hours. Stay in town for more food choices, or at the base for ski-in access. Kicking Horse is on the Epic Pass (with limited days).

The terrain is steep and avalanche-prone beyond the boundary. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

fernie.skiing:
Fernie Alpine Resort has five big bowls (Cedar, Lizard, Currie, Timber and Siberia) that catch deep snow from storms coming over the Rockies. The Lizard Range funnels moisture from the west, so Fernie often gets more snow than its neighbours, around 9 m a season. The terrain is varied, with open bowls, steep chutes along the ridges, and good tree skiing that holds up in storms.

It's one of the best powder resorts in the Canadian Rockies, with around 1,000 m of vertical and a relaxed, local feel. Its lower slopes sit low enough that rain at the base is possible in warm spells, but the bowls usually hold good snow.

**Island Lake Lodge**, in the next valley, runs famous cat-skiing trips in old-growth forest and open alpine, and the area has good touring in the Lizard Range. The wider region, from Kimberley to Panorama, makes a good road trip.
fernie.beyond: Fernie is an old coal-mining town with a pretty historic centre of brick buildings, good bars and the Fernie Brewing Company. Locals celebrate the "Legend of the Griz", a mythical mountain man who brings the snow, each winter. The Elk River valley is beautiful, and the town is a real community rather than a resort.
fernie.know:
Cranbrook airport is about 1 hour away; Calgary is about 3 hours. Lodging ranges from slopeside condos to cheaper motels and hostels in town, about 10 minutes away.

Fernie is on the Epic Pass (with limited days).

The snowpack can have buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada's South Rockies forecast covers the area daily.

kootenays.skiing:
Two small, deep-snow resorts in the West Kootenays, about an hour apart: **Whitewater**, above Nelson, and **RED Mountain**, above Rossland. Whitewater has steep bowls and gladed trees off a ridge at the top of a narrow valley, a small day lodge, and is famous for its food. RED has steep tree skiing on several peaks, including Grey Mountain, added in 2013, and the lifts open more than 1,600 hectares of terrain.

Both are uncrowded, local and full of character, and both get a lot of snow, with long periods of powder. The area is the heart of BC's "Powder Highway", and the region has one of the highest concentrations of cat-skiing operations in the world.

**Kootenay Pass**, on Highway 3 between Creston and Salmo, is the classic road-accessed backcountry, with popular tours like Ripple Ridge and Lightning Strike. Whitewater also has easy access to backcountry touring from its boundary, and several ski-touring lodges sit in the Selkirks and Valhallas around Nelson.
kootenays.beyond: Nelson is a colourful heritage town, known for its arts, cafés and counterculture, and the setting for the film *Roxanne*. Rossland is a gold-mining town that hosted the first ski races in Canada in the 1890s, with a strong local ski culture. The Ainsworth hot springs, in a horseshoe-shaped cave, are a classic stop.
kootenays.know:
Castlegar is the nearest airport, nicknamed "Cancelgar" because flights are often cancelled by weather. Spokane, in the US, is about 2.5 to 3 hours away; Trail has a small airport too.

The two resorts are about 1 hour apart, so a week can easily combine both. Cat-skiing operators around Nelson and Rossland offer excellent days.

The snowpack often has buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts the Kootenay Boundary region daily.

banff.skiing:
Banff National Park has three resorts on one pass, sold together as SkiBig3, in some of the most spectacular scenery in skiing. **Lake Louise** is the biggest, with about 1,700 hectares across four faces: groomers on the front with views of the Victoria Glacier, and big back bowls and steep chutes like the Paradise and Whitehorn areas. **Sunshine Village** is high and snowy, straddling the Continental Divide, with a long gondola from the valley and the famous **Delirium Dive**, a steep, hike-in bowl where avalanche gear and a partner are required. **Mt Norquay**, small and steep, is just above town and good for half days and night skiing.

The terrain is big, the season long (Sunshine often runs from November to May), and the snow light and cold. The trade-off is the Rockies' continental snowpack, which is often thin and weak.

The backcountry is world-class. The **Icefields Parkway**, north of Lake Louise, has road-accessed touring and huts, with Bow Summit a popular spot, and **Skoki Lodge**, a historic backcountry lodge built in the 1930s, is reached on skis from Lake Louise. The Wapta Icefield traverse starts nearby.
banff.beyond: The town of Banff sits inside a national park, with elk wandering through it and mountains rising on every side. The Banff Upper Hot Springs and the Fairmont Banff Springs hotel are classics, and skating on the frozen Lake Louise in front of the Château is magical. Johnston Canyon's frozen waterfalls make a good ice walk, and the Whyte Museum tells the story of the Rockies' early guides and artists.
banff.know:
Calgary airport is about 1.5 hours away. January can be bitterly cold, sometimes below −25 °C, so pack properly.

The three resorts are spread out, so a car or the SkiBig3 shuttle buses are needed. Staying in Banff gives you restaurants and nightlife; Lake Louise village is quieter. Book the shuttle or plan parking for weekends, when Calgary skiers arrive. A national park pass is required.

The Rockies' snowpack is often thin and weak. Avalanche Canada and Parks Canada forecast daily.

bigwhite.skiing:
Big White, near Kelowna, is known for its light Okanagan powder and its "snow ghosts": trees near the top coated in rime ice until they look like frozen sculptures. The terrain is mostly intermediate, with long groomers, gentle glades and good tree skiing among the ghosts, plus some steeper runs and bowls on the edges. The resort covers about 1,100 hectares, one of the biggest in BC.

The village is the biggest ski-in, ski-out village in Canada, and very family-friendly: almost everything is reachable on skis.

The Okanagan has two more resorts within about 2 hours: **SilverStar**, near Vernon, with a colourful, Victorian-style village and lots of cross-country skiing, and **Apex Mountain**, near Penticton, smaller and steeper, with a loyal local following. A road trip linking the three is easy.
bigwhite.beyond: The Okanagan Valley is wine country, and Kelowna has good restaurants, wineries and a lakeside downtown. The resort is very popular with Australians, many of whom work there for the season, which gives it a lively après scene. Night skiing, a tube park and an ice-skating rink keep families busy.
bigwhite.know:
Kelowna airport is about 1 hour away, with flights from Vancouver, Calgary and further afield. Everything is in the village, so most people stay a week without a car.

The top of the mountain is often in cloud, earning it the nickname "Big White-out"; the trees help on those days.

Avalanche Canada forecasts the backcountry.

wolfcreek.skiing:
Wolf Creek gets the most snow in Colorado, on average more than 10 m a year, thanks to its spot right on the Continental Divide, where southwesterly storms stall and unload. It's a family-owned ski area, run by the Pitcher family for decades, with no village and no lodging at the base: just good terrain, deep snow and reasonable prices.

The terrain covers about 650 hectares, from gentle groomers to steep trees and open bowls. **Alberta Peak** and the **Knife Ridge** offer hike-to steeps, and the Waterfall area has some of the best tree skiing in the state. Because it gets so much snow, it's often one of the first resorts in Colorado to open, sometimes in October, and it often has the deepest base in the state through the season.

The pass itself is a backcountry and Nordic spot, though the terrain around it is avalanche-prone and the highway is regularly closed for control work. The San Juans' weak snowpack applies here too.
wolfcreek.beyond: Pagosa Springs, about 30 minutes away, has hot springs along the San Juan River, including the Mother Spring, one of the deepest geothermal springs in the world. Durango is a lively college town with a narrow-gauge railway and good food, and the Great Sand Dunes, on the other side of the pass, are a spectacular detour.
wolfcreek.know:
Durango airport is about 1.5 hours away; Alamosa is closer but has few flights. Wolf Creek Pass can close in storms. There's no lodging at the ski area, so most people stay in Pagosa Springs or South Fork.

Lift tickets are good value by Colorado standards, and Wolf Creek isn't on the big multi-resort passes, so it stays relatively uncrowded except on powder weekends.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts the area.

winterpark.skiing:
Winter Park is the closest big resort to Denver and is owned by the City of Denver, which bought it in the 1930s as a city ski area. It's run by a private company today, but the city still owns it. It covers about 1,250 hectares across several connected areas.

**Mary Jane**, its sister mountain, is famous for steep, relentless bumps, and its motto is "no pain, no Jane". Winter Park's side has long groomers and family terrain; Vasquez Ridge and Cirque have more spread-out runs; and the high, treeless **Parsenn Bowl** and the hike-to **Vasquez Cirque** have big open terrain with views of the Continental Divide.

The snow is cold and dry, and the resort usually gets around 8 m a season. The Winter Park Express ski train runs from Denver's Union Station through the Moffat Tunnel, one of the only ski trains in the US.
winterpark.beyond: The town of Fraser, nearby, calls itself the "Icebox of the Nation" for its cold winters. The area has good cross-country skiing (Devil's Thumb Ranch and Snow Mountain Ranch), snowmobiling, and Hot Sulphur Springs further down the valley. Denver is close enough for a city day.
winterpark.know:
Denver is about 1.5 to 2 hours away by car, over Berthoud Pass, which can close in storms. The ski train runs on weekends in season and drops you at the base.

Winter Park is a good choice for a short trip from Denver, and it's popular with locals on weekends. Staying in the base village or in Fraser avoids the drive. The resort is on the Ikon Pass.

The Colorado snowpack is weak. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily; Berthoud Pass is the nearest backcountry.

ogden.skiing:
Two very different resorts in the mountains above Ogden. **Snowbasin** hosted the downhill and super-G races at the 2002 Winter Olympics, and has grand day lodges, fast gondolas and long, steep runs from the top of Mount Ogden, with around 1,000 m of vertical. It's famously uncrowded for a resort of its quality.

**Powder Mountain** is huge and very different: the lifts sit on top of the mountain, so you ski down and ride up, and it covers several thousand acres of tree skiing and open terrain, with cat skiing and a limit on daily ticket sales to keep it uncrowded. It has changed hands several times in recent years, and its access rules and ticket policies have changed with it.

Together they offer a quieter alternative to the Cottonwoods and Park City, with the same dry Utah snow. The peaks around the Ogden Valley, like **Ben Lomond**, also have good backcountry, reached from the valley's trailheads.
ogden.beyond: Ogden was a railway town, and its historic 25th Street, once notorious for its saloons, now has good bars and restaurants. Salt Lake City is about 1 hour away. Nordic Valley, a small local hill, offers night skiing, and the Ogden Valley's small towns, Huntsville and Eden, are quiet bases.
ogden.know:
Salt Lake City airport is about 1 hour away. Both resorts are about 30 to 45 minutes from downtown Ogden, and lodging in town is cheaper than in Park City or the canyons.

Powder Mountain's rules about tickets and access have changed often, so check before you go. Snowbasin is on the Ikon Pass.

The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts the Ogden area daily.

rogerspass.skiing:
Rogers Pass, in Glacier National Park, is the most famous road-accessed backcountry in Canada. The Trans-Canada Highway crosses the Selkirk Mountains here, right through some of the heaviest snowfall in the country, and you can be skinning within minutes of leaving the car. On storm days, skiers stay in the steep old-growth forest, where huge cedars and hemlocks hold the snow and give some protection from the wind. On clear days, the big alpine terrain opens up: glaciers, long couloirs and peaks like **Sir Donald**, whose pointed summit dominates the pass.

There are no lifts, and no grooming. The terrain falls into a handful of drainages, each with its own character. South of the highway, the **Illecillewaet** and **Asulkan** valleys lead to glaciers and to the Alpine Club of Canada's huts, so you can stay up high for several days. West of the summit, **Balu Pass** and **Connaught Creek** reach the most popular day-touring terrain, with tree runs and open bowls on both sides of the valley. North of the highway are steeper, more committing objectives.

The snowpack in the Selkirks is deep and maritime-influenced, usually more stable than in the Rockies to the east, but it can still produce very large avalanches, and the slide paths above the highway are some of the most active in the world. That's why the whole area runs on a permit system, described below.
rogerspass.beyond:
The pass has a dramatic history. Surveyor Major A.B. Rogers found it in 1881, and the Canadian Pacific Railway crossed it a few years later. Avalanches buried the line again and again, and in 1910 one killed 58 railway workers who were clearing an earlier slide. The railway then tunnelled under the pass, and the old grade is now a walking trail.

Today, Rogers Pass is home to one of the world's largest mobile avalanche-control programs: the Canadian Armed Forces fire howitzers from fixed gun positions along the highway to bring down slides before they reach the road. The **Rogers Pass Discovery Centre**, built in the style of the old railway snowsheds, tells the story.

Revelstoke, about an hour west, is a lively ski town with good food and a big lift-served resort for stormy days. Golden, about an hour and a half east, is smaller and quieter.
rogerspass.know:
You need a free **winter permit** from Parks Canada to ski in the restricted areas, which include most of the popular terrain. Getting one involves a short online quiz on the rules. Each morning, Parks Canada declares areas open or closed depending on its avalanche control work, and the status is posted online and at the Discovery Centre. Entering a closed area is illegal and genuinely dangerous: the artillery may be firing.

Avalanche Canada publishes a specific forecast for Glacier National Park. The huts (Wheeler Hut near the Illecillewaet campground, the Asulkan Cabin and others) need booking through the Alpine Club of Canada, often well in advance for February and March.

The season runs from December to May. Midwinter brings the deepest snow and the shortest days; spring brings longer days, glacier tours and corn snow. Calgary is about 4 hours away and Kelowna about 3. There are no services at the pass itself, so most skiers stay in Revelstoke or Golden.

bcheli.skiing:
Heli-skiing was born in the Interior of British Columbia: the mountain guide Hans Gmoser flew his first guests into the Bugaboos in 1965, and the company he founded, CMH, still runs lodges across the region. Today, operators in the Selkirks, Monashees, Purcells and Cariboos fly skiers into old-growth trees on storm days and onto alpine glaciers when it clears. Mike Wiegele's operation at Blue River, in the Cariboos and Monashees, is another pioneer.

The snow is deep and frequent: the Columbia Mountains catch Pacific storms before they reach the Rockies, and the snow arrives cold enough to stay light. A week can bring an enormous amount of vertical, often 20,000 to 30,000 m for strong groups, though it depends on weather and the package.

Cat skiing offers similar terrain, often in the trees, at a lower price. The Kootenays have dozens of cat operations, from rustic to luxurious, and **Baldface**, near Nelson, is one of the best known.
bcheli.beyond: Lodges range from comfortable to luxurious, with food, saunas and massage included. Many are reached only by helicopter, and the evenings, with fellow guests swapping stories by the fire, are part of the experience. Some operators also offer ski-touring weeks from the same lodges.
bcheli.know:
This is among the most expensive skiing in the world, and popular weeks book up a year or more ahead. Most operators sell trips by the week, with day trips and cat skiing as cheaper ways in. Fat skis are usually provided.

Operators run professional avalanche programs, with guides trained by the Association of Canadian Mountain Guides, but weather can ground helicopters for days. Strong powder skiing and good fitness help you get the most out of it. Practise tree-well safety: always ski with a partner in sight.

tetonpass.skiing:
Teton Pass, on the road between Jackson, Wyoming, and Victor, Idaho, is one of the most popular road-accessed backcountry areas in the US. From the top of the pass, at about 2,560 m, tours go in every direction, from mellow tree laps on the south side to big, steep descents like **Glory Bowl**, a famous slide path above the highway that runs right down to the road. Many runs end at the highway lower down, so laps with a shuttle car are common.

In spring, **Grand Teton National Park** offers some of the most serious ski mountaineering in North America. The Grand Teton itself was first skied by Bill Briggs in 1971, and its steep couloirs, along with those on Mount Moran, Mount Owen and the South Teton, are classics for experienced ski mountaineers. Gentler tours lead up the canyons from the park road, like the approaches from Taggart Lake.

The snow is usually dry and light, and the Tetons get plenty of it, but the snowpack often has persistent weak layers, and the terrain is steep and consequential.
tetonpass.beyond: Jackson is close, with good food and a Western feel. Jackson Hole and Grand Targhee are nearby for lift-served days. On the Idaho side, Victor and Driggs are quieter, cheaper bases, with views of the Tetons' west face. Yellowstone is a few hours north.
tetonpass.know:
The parking at the top of the pass fills early on good days. Respect the road: slides can reach it, so never trigger slopes above the highway, and follow local etiquette and closures, especially around Glory Bowl.

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts daily, and the snowpack often has persistent weak layers. Local guides and avalanche courses are easy to find in Jackson. Grand Teton National Park requires registration for some overnight trips.

tenthmountain.skiing:
The 10th Mountain Division Hut Association runs a network of around 30 backcountry huts in the Colorado Rockies between Vail, Aspen and Leadville, linked by trails through forest and over high passes. It's named after the army's mountain troops, who trained at Camp Hale nearby during the Second World War and later helped found Colorado's ski industry. Several huts honour soldiers who died in the war.

Most of the touring is moderate: long approaches, often 8 to 13 km, through forest to huts at around 3,000 to 3,500 m, with good tree skiing and open slopes nearby. It's more about the hut experience than big descents, though some huts have excellent terrain close by. Classic trips include the **Shrine Mountain Inn** near Vail Pass, the **Uncle Bud's** and **Skinner** huts near Leadville, and **Margy's Hut** above the Fryingpan Valley.

The Braun and Friends hut system, near Aspen, has huts with steeper terrain closer to the door.
tenthmountain.beyond: The huts are cosy, with wood stoves, bunks, solar lighting and kitchens. You bring your own food and sleeping bag. Evenings with friends in a hut far from any road are the highlight. Camp Hale is now a national monument, with the ruins of the training camp visible from the highway.
tenthmountain.know:
Popular dates book up fast, with a booking lottery for peak dates. The altitude is high, so acclimatise first, and expect long days with heavy packs. Navigation can be challenging in storms; carry a map and GPS.

The Colorado snowpack is weak; the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily. Many routes avoid avalanche terrain, but not all, and the slopes near some huts need care.

sanjuans.skiing:
Road-accessed touring around **Red Mountain Pass**, between Silverton and Ouray, in the high San Juan Mountains. The pass is at about 3,350 m, so tours start high, and the terrain is big and alpine, with steep slopes above old mines and avalanche paths that cross the highway. Popular objectives include the Red Mountains (No. 1, 2 and 3) and **McMillan Peak**, with options from gentle tree runs to big couloirs.

Huts and old mining buildings allow multi-day trips: the San Juan Hut System runs huts in the area, and others sit near the pass. **Molas Pass**, south of Silverton, and **Ophir Pass** offer more road-accessed terrain.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America: shallow, cold and full of faceted layers. Conservative decisions are essential, and many experienced locals stick to low-angle terrain for much of the winter, waiting for spring for the big lines. Silverton Mountain, just outside Silverton, offers guided lift-served steeps.
sanjuans.beyond:
Ouray has natural hot springs and a famous ice-climbing park, built in a gorge in town. Silverton is a historic mining town at about 2,800 m, and its avalanche school is one of the oldest in the US. Both towns are small and full of character.

The old mines and ghost towns scattered across the mountains give the area a haunted, historic feel, and many hut trips use restored mining buildings.
sanjuans.know:
The pass road, known as the Million Dollar Highway, is steep, narrow, has few guardrails and can close in storms or for avalanche control. Silverton and Ouray are the bases; Durango and Montrose have the nearest airports, each about 1.5 hours away.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily for the Northern and Southern San Juans. Going with a local guide is a good idea, especially early in the season.

cascadevolcanoes.skiing:
A spring road trip to ski the big Cascade volcanoes is one of North America's classic ski adventures. From north to south, **Mount Baker**, **Mount Rainier**, **Mount St. Helens**, **Mount Adams** and **Mount Hood** rise in isolation above forested foothills, each a long day's drive or less from the next. Each offers a long climb on skins and crampons, then a descent of around 1,500 to 2,000 m on smooth corn snow, with the other volcanoes lined up along the horizon.

They are very different mountains. **Mount St. Helens** (2,549 m) is the most accessible, and lets you ski from the rim of the crater left by the 1980 eruption, looking straight down at the lava dome. **Mount Adams** (3,743 m) has broad, gentle slopes on its south side and the famous **Southwest Chutes**, long, sustained gullies for strong skiers. **Mount Hood** (3,429 m) has the most convenient access, starting from Timberline Lodge, and is the closest to a city.

**Mount Rainier** (4,392 m) and **Mount Baker** (3,286 m) are heavily glaciated, and skiing them from the top is a serious mountaineering trip, with crevasses and seracs. Many skiers stick to their lower snowfields instead, like the Muir Snowfield on Rainier, which offers a huge descent without glacier travel.
cascadevolcanoes.beyond:
Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood was built by the Works Progress Administration in the 1930s, with hand-carved wood and ironwork, and you may recognise its exterior from *The Shining*. Paradise, on Rainier, has the historic Paradise Inn and is one of the snowiest places on Earth where snowfall is regularly measured.

Between mountains, the Pacific Northwest offers great food, coffee and breweries in Portland and Seattle, hot springs, and endless forest camping. The Columbia River Gorge, between Hood and Adams, is a spectacular drive, and Hood River is a good base for both mountains.
cascadevolcanoes.know:
The best season is roughly April to July, once the snowpack has consolidated and the long access roads have melted out. Before then, many trailheads are still snowed in, or reached only from winter sno-parks with longer approaches. A Washington or Oregon sno-park permit is needed for winter parking.

Permits vary by mountain: **St. Helens** needs a climbing permit, sold in limited numbers in spring; **Adams** needs a Cascade Volcano Pass in summer; **Rainier** requires registration and a climbing fee above 3,000 m or on glaciers. Check the rules for each before you go.

Glacier travel skills, or a guide, are essential on the higher peaks. Start very early, so you ski the snow as it softens rather than after it turns to slush, and watch for afternoon wet slides and cornice falls. The weather on the volcanoes can change fast, and whiteouts on the broad upper slopes have led many parties astray. The Northwest Avalanche Center covers Hood, Rainier, Baker, Adams and St. Helens.

easternsierra.skiing:
Huge couloirs and open faces rise straight above Highway 395 between Bishop, Mammoth and Lone Pine, with some of the biggest vertical from the road in the lower 48. In spring, the Eastern Sierra is one of the best places in the world for corn snow on big, steep lines, and peaks like **Mount Tom**, which towers more than 2,000 m above Bishop, dominate the views from the desert.

The range is a long wall, and each canyon leads to its own playground. **Rock Creek**, at high elevation, has gentle terrain and the snowiest road access. **Convict Lake** sits under Mount Morrison and Laurel Mountain, whose **Mendenhall Couloir** is a famous line. **June Lake** has Carson Peak's big north face, and when the **Tioga Pass** road opens in late spring, it gives access to the **Dana Couloir** and the high terrain near Yosemite's east entrance.

Midwinter brings big storms and powder, but spring is the classic season, when the snow settles and freeze-thaw cycles create smooth corn on huge faces.
easternsierra.beyond: Natural hot springs, desert landscapes and the small towns of Bishop and Lone Pine make it a great road trip. The Alabama Hills, near Lone Pine, have been the backdrop for many westerns. Bishop is famous for bouldering, and its bakery, Erick Schat's, is a road-trip institution. Death Valley and Yosemite are within reach.
easternsierra.know:
The season runs roughly from January to June, with the best corn in March to May. Some peaks, like Mount Whitney, need permits. Mammoth Lakes has the most lodging; Bishop and Lone Pine are cheaper.

Long approaches and big vertical mean early starts, so the snow softens while you're on the descent, not after. The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the area.

wapta.skiing:
The Wapta Icefield traverse is the Canadian Rockies' classic hut-to-hut glacier trip, starting from the Icefields Parkway north of Lake Louise. It links the **Bow**, **Peyto**, **Balfour** and **Scott Duncan** huts across glaciers and passes over about four to six days, with optional summits like Mount Gordon, Mount Olive and Mount Rhondda along the way, many of them easy ski ascents with huge views.

The terrain is glaciated and high, mostly between 2,300 and 3,100 m, with crevasses, icefalls and exposure to weather. The route itself isn't technically hard, but navigating across featureless glaciers in a whiteout is a real challenge, and the descent off the Balfour high col and the exit toward Sherbrooke Lake need care.

The neighbouring **Waputik Icefield** can be added for a longer trip, and the Bow Hut alone makes a great base for a few days of glacier touring if you don't want to do the full traverse.
wapta.beyond: The Icefields Parkway is one of the most scenic roads in the world, with frozen lakes, waterfalls and glaciers along the way. Num-Ti-Jah Lodge, at Bow Lake, built by the pioneer guide Jimmy Simpson, has a long history in the Rockies. Lake Louise and Banff are close for a rest day.
wapta.know:
The main season is roughly March to May, when the days are long and the snowpack more settled. Huts are run by the Alpine Club of Canada, are self-catered and need booking; they have stoves, pots and foam mattresses, so you need only food and a sleeping bag.

Most parties start at Bow Lake and finish on the Yoho side near Sherbrooke Lake, so plan a car shuttle. Glacier travel skills and good navigation are essential, or go with a guide.

The Rockies' snowpack often has weak layers; Avalanche Canada and Parks Canada forecast daily.

sierrahr.skiing:
A committing multi-day ski traverse across the high Sierra Nevada, from the Eastern Sierra near Mount Whitney to Sequoia National Park, through wilderness with no huts for most of the way. The classic route climbs from the desert at **Symmes Creek** over Shepherd Pass, then crosses high passes and alpine basins, mostly above 3,000 m, to finish near the **Pear Lake Ski Hut** and Wolverton, in the giant sequoias. It takes about six to eight days.

The terrain is some of the wildest in the lower 48: granite peaks, frozen lakes, the headwaters of the Kern River, and long days far from any road. The skiing ranges from easy glides to steep passes, and the route-finding is part of the challenge.

You carry everything, camp in the snow and need strong navigation, skiing and winter-camping skills. Spring snow is usually stable and fast in the morning, but storms can arrive with little warning, and there's no easy way out once you're in the middle.
sierrahr.beyond: The scenery is spectacular: granite peaks, frozen lakes and giant sequoias on the western side, including the General Sherman Tree, the largest tree on Earth by volume. The Pear Lake Ski Hut in Sequoia is a welcome stop near the end. On the east side, Lone Pine and the Alabama Hills make a great start.
sierrahr.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. A wilderness permit is needed, and quotas may apply. Bear-resistant food storage is required in some areas, even in spring. Plan the logistics carefully: the start and finish are far apart by road, about 8 hours' drive.

The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center covers the eastern side. Go with a guide unless you're experienced in multi-day backcountry travel.

shasta.skiing:
Mount Shasta is a lone volcano, about 4,320 m high, rising far above the forests and lava plains of northern California. It offers long corn-snow descents of around 2,000 m on several sides, from the popular **Avalanche Gulch**, the standard route on the south side above Bunny Flat, to quieter routes on the north and east sides, like the **Hotlum-Wintun** ridge from Brewer Creek.

It's a classic spring and early-summer objective, when the snowpack has consolidated and the roads to the trailheads open. The climb is long and the summit high, so altitude and weather matter: many people split it over two days, camping at Helen Lake or near Horse Camp.

**Lassen Peak**, about 1.5 hours south in Lassen Volcanic National Park, is another volcano with good spring skiing, especially when the park road is open but still snowbound.
shasta.beyond: The town of Mount Shasta has a quirky, spiritual reputation, with crystal shops and stories of a hidden city inside the mountain. The Sierra Club's stone Horse Camp cabin, from the 1920s, sits on the main route. McCloud and Dunsmuir have waterfalls and old railway towns, and Lassen's hydrothermal areas are fascinating.
shasta.know:
A summit pass and wilderness permit are required, and you must carry out your human waste in bags provided at the trailhead. The best season is roughly May to June. Guided climbs are available in town.

The Mount Shasta Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Weather on the summit can change very fast, with strong winds and lenticular clouds, and the descent from the summit plateau in a whiteout has led many parties astray.

bclodges.skiing:
Backcountry lodges in the Selkirks, Purcells, Monashees and Valhallas offer a week of touring from the door. You fly in by helicopter to a timber lodge near treeline, then tour each day on terrain that ranges from old-growth tree runs to alpine bowls and glaciers, with no lifts and no other people.

The Interior BC snowpack is deep and the snow usually light, and the skiing is some of the best in the world. Lodges are spread across the region: the **Valhalla Range**, near Nelson, has several; the **Battle Range** in the northern Selkirks is wild and remote; and the **Kokanee and Kaslo** area has lodges and huts close to towns. The Alpine Club of Canada's **Fairy Meadow** hut, in the Adamants, is one of the most famous huts in North America, with big glaciated terrain right outside.

Most lodges are guided, with small groups led by certified guides, but some are self-guided for experienced parties.
bclodges.beyond: Lodges are cosy, with saunas and good food. The isolation, far from any road, is a big part of the appeal. Many lodges have a long history, built by ski pioneers in the 1970s and 1980s, and guests often return to the same lodge year after year. A week with the same small group of people builds strong friendships.
bclodges.know:
Lodges can be guided or self-guided, and catered or self-catered. Trips usually run Saturday to Saturday, with helicopter flights from towns like Golden, Revelstoke or Nelson. Popular weeks book up a year ahead.

The Interior snowpack has persistent buried weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily, and guides at each lodge run their own observations. Self-guided groups need strong avalanche skills.

wapass.skiing:
Each spring, the North Cascades Highway (State Route 20) reopens after its winter closure, giving road access to steep granite couloirs and glaciers around **Washington Pass**. Peaks like Liberty Bell and the Early Winters Spires tower above the road, and lines like the **Early Winters Couloir** are classics. The terrain is big, steep and dramatic, and the access, straight from the car on a newly cleared road, is unusual for terrain of this scale.

The most famous outing is the **Birthday Tour**, a loop that links several passes and descents around Washington Pass in a long day. **Silver Star Mountain**, to the east, has a well-known couloir and big views.

The season is short, usually from the road opening in spring until the snow melts in early summer. Before the opening, the area is reached only by long approaches from the closed road, and in winter, North Cascades Heli in Mazama flies skiers into the surrounding peaks.
wapass.beyond: The Methow Valley, to the east, has one of the largest cross-country ski networks in North America, and Winthrop has a Western-style main street with wooden boardwalks. Mazama is a small, friendly base for climbers and skiers, with a famous store and bakery.
wapass.know:
The highway is closed all winter and usually reopens between April and May; check the reopening date before planning. There are no services at the pass. Seattle is about 4 hours away; lodging in Mazama and Winthrop fills up quickly in spring, so book ahead.

The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Wet slides, cornices and rockfall are the main spring hazards, so start early and finish before the afternoon heat.

gudauri.skiing:
Gudauri sits high on the Georgian Military Highway in the Greater Caucasus, with lifts climbing above 3,000 m over wide, treeless slopes. The pistes are simple and uncrowded, but the draw is the open freeride terrain between and beyond them, plus heli-skiing at prices far below the Alps or Canada.

The lift-served off-piste is huge, with long, open descents into side valleys, some ending at the highway where taxis wait to bring you back. Heli operators fly into the surrounding peaks of the Kazbegi region, with long runs on open faces.

With no trees, storm days and flat light are hard, and the big open slopes are serious avalanche terrain. Further up the highway, **Kazbegi** (Stepantsminda) is a base for ski touring, and **Mount Kazbek**, at about 5,050 m, is a serious spring ski ascent.
gudauri.beyond: Georgian food and wine are a highlight of any trip: khachapuri, khinkali, and wine made in clay qvevri jars. Kazbegi, with the Gergeti Trinity Church under Mount Kazbek, is a short drive further up the highway, and Tbilisi is a lively, beautiful capital.
gudauri.know:
Tbilisi is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by road. The highway is the main route to Russia, so expect truck traffic, and the pass above Gudauri can close in storms.

There's no full public avalanche forecast like in the Alps, and off-piste accidents happen every winter: hire a local guide. It's very good value.

svaneti.skiing:
Upper Svaneti sits under the highest peaks of the Caucasus, with mountains of 4,000 to 5,000 m, including the twin-peaked **Ushba** and **Shkhara**, Georgia's highest. Two small ski areas near Mestia, **Hatsvali** and **Tetnuldi**, give lift access to big terrain, and from them you can tour into wild, rarely skied mountains.

Tetnuldi is the bigger and higher of the two, with lifts to about 3,150 m and long, open descents. Hatsvali, just above Mestia, is small, with a few lifts and tree skiing. The touring is the real draw, with big, untracked faces and long descents in every direction.

The terrain is big and remote; this is a place for touring with a guide rather than a resort trip.
svaneti.beyond: The medieval stone defensive towers of Svaneti are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and **Ushguli**, a cluster of tower villages further up the valley, is one of the highest permanently inhabited villages in Europe. Svan food, music and hospitality make the trip.
svaneti.know:
Mestia has a small airport with flights from Tbilisi that depend on the weather; by road it's a long drive from Kutaisi or Zugdidi. Plan extra days.

There's no public avalanche forecast: go with a local guide who knows the snowpack. Facilities are simple, and English is less common than in Tbilisi.

kackar.skiing:
The Kaçkar Mountains, the highest part of Turkey's Pontic Alps, rise steeply from the Black Sea coast to about 3,940 m at **Kaçkar Dağı** and catch the sea's moisture as deep, maritime snow. Heli-skiing here means steep, treeless ridges and long descents into valleys of stone villages and summer pastures, often with the sea glinting on the horizon.

The terrain is big and largely unskied, and operators run small groups from lodges in the valleys. Descents of 1,000 to 1,500 m are common, on open faces and in couloirs, ending among wooden houses and forests.

The valleys around **Ayder** are also good for ski touring, with big, open terrain and few people.
kackar.beyond: This is the land of the Laz and Hemşin peoples, with their own languages, music and food. Rize, on the coast, is the heart of Turkey's tea country, and tea terraces climb the hillsides. Ayder, a mountain village with hot springs, is a classic stop. Near Trabzon, the Sumela Monastery clings to a cliff face.
kackar.know:
Trabzon is the nearest airport, with flights from Istanbul. Most visitors book a heli-ski week through an operator, which arranges transfers.

The maritime snowpack brings storm slabs and wet slides in spring. Weather can ground the helicopter for days, so allow for down days.

gulmarg.skiing:
Gulmarg's two-stage gondola climbs from a meadow town at about 2,650 m to the **Apharwat** ridge at nearly 4,000 m, one of the highest lift-served points in the world. Below it lies a huge freeride playground: open bowls up high, long descents through pine and fir forests lower down, and very few people.

There are only a few pistes. Gulmarg is about freeride, and the snow can be superb, though storms are heavy and conditions change fast. From the top, short hikes along the ridge open more bowls, and long descents on the back side lead to villages like **Drung**, with a taxi ride back to town.

The lower gondola stage, through the trees, is the storm-day option, with excellent tree skiing when the top is closed.
gulmarg.beyond: Gulmarg was a British hill station, and has one of the highest golf courses in the world under the snow. Srinagar, 1.5 hours away, is famous for its houseboats and wooden shikara boats on Dal Lake, and for Kashmiri cooking: try a *wazwan*, a multi-course feast, and *kahwa*, a saffron and almond tea.
gulmarg.know:
Srinagar has flights from Delhi and Mumbai. Kashmir is a sensitive region, with a heavy security presence; check your government's travel advice before booking, and expect checkpoints.

Rescue services are limited and the terrain is avalanche-prone, so ski with a local guide. Costs are low compared with almost anywhere else with this terrain.

karakol.skiing:
Karakol, in the Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan, has a small ski resort with a few lifts and wide open slopes in the forest, and around it a huge range of backcountry. Yurt camps and small guesthouses are bases for touring, and cat-skiing operators take skiers deep into the mountains. The snow is dry and continental, often light and cold.

Nearby, the **Jyrgalan** valley has developed a community-based touring scene, with marked tours and local guides, and yurts or guesthouses as bases. The terrain is open and rolling, with peaks around 3,500 to 4,000 m.

**Altyn-Arashan**, a valley with hot springs above Karakol, is another base for touring, with big, empty terrain all around.
karakol.beyond: Lake Issyk-Kul, one of the largest mountain lakes in the world, never freezes. Karakol itself has a wooden Russian Orthodox cathedral and a Chinese-style wooden mosque built by the Dungan community. Try *ashlyan-fu*, the local cold noodle soup.
karakol.know:
Bishkek is about 6 hours away by road. Infrastructure is simple and prices are low. Pack for real cold.

The continental snowpack is often weak, with persistent layers. There's no public avalanche forecast, so go with a local guide or operator.

iranresorts.skiing:
Iran's Alborz Mountains rise just north of Tehran, and their resorts sit high, at around 2,500 to 3,600 m, with dry, light snow. **Dizin**, opened in 1969, is big and open, with long descents and some of the best snow in the region. **Shemshak** is steep and known for moguls, and it offers night skiing. **Tochal**, reached by a long gondola from the northern edge of Tehran, has some of the highest pistes in the region.

The off-piste around Dizin and Shemshak is extensive, with big, open slopes and few skiers. The resorts are popular with locals, and weekends (Thursday and Friday) are busy; weekdays are quiet.

The Alborz also offers ski touring, and the area around Dizin and Shemshak has many peaks over 4,000 m.
iranresorts.beyond: Tehran has excellent museums, the Grand Bazaar and the Golestan Palace. Persian food is a highlight: kebabs, saffron rice, stews and fresh bread. The Chalus road, north over the Alborz to the Caspian, is one of Iran's most scenic drives.
iranresorts.know:
Check your government's travel advice carefully before planning a trip. A visa is required for most nationalities, and international bank cards don't work because of sanctions, so bring cash. Local laws on dress and behaviour apply on the slopes as elsewhere.

Tehran's airport is about 2 to 3 hours from the resorts. Off-piste is uncontrolled; ski with a local guide.

damavand.skiing:
Mount Damavand, at 5,610 m, is the highest volcano in Asia and a near-perfect cone rising above the Alborz. In spring, it offers a huge descent from the summit, where sulphur fumes rise from the crater, down broad slopes to the **Bargah-e Sevom** hut at about 4,150 m and beyond.

The skiing itself isn't steep. The challenge is the altitude, the wind and the cold near the top. The standard south route starts from **Polour**, at the foot, with a drive to the trailhead, then a climb on foot or skis to the hut, and the summit day takes 8 to 12 hours.

The descent, of around 1,500 m from the summit to the hut and more below, is one of the longest volcano descents in the world.
damavand.beyond: Damavand is central to Persian mythology: in the *Shahnameh*, the national epic, a tyrant is chained inside the mountain. The village of Polour is the gathering point for climbers, and Tehran is a few hours away.
damavand.know:
Check your government's travel advice before planning a trip. Climbers register and pay a fee at the Iranian Mountaineering Federation camp in Polour. Mules can carry gear to the hut.

Spring (roughly May and June) is the season. Acclimatise properly, ideally on nearby peaks first. There's no avalanche forecast.

lebanon.skiing:
Lebanon is one of the few places where you can ski in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean in the afternoon. **Mzaar Kfardebian**, about an hour from Beirut, is the largest resort, with wide open slopes up to about 2,465 m, with runs spread over several peaks.

**The Cedars**, in the north, is smaller and higher, above a grove of ancient cedar trees, with open bowls and good off-piste. **Zaarour** and **Laqlouq** are smaller local areas closer to Beirut.

The snow can be excellent after storms but varies a lot from year to year. The treeless Mount Lebanon range also offers spring ski touring, with long, open descents and views to the sea.
lebanon.beyond: The Cedars of God, a grove of ancient trees in the Qadisha valley, is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Lebanese food is one of the great cuisines of the world, from mezze to grilled fish, and Byblos and Batroun are beautiful coastal towns. Beirut has a lively restaurant and nightlife scene.
lebanon.know:
Beirut's airport is about 1 to 2 hours from the resorts. Check your government's travel advice before planning a trip, since the security situation can change quickly.

Weekends are busy with Beirut skiers. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

almaty.skiing:
Almaty is a big, green city at the foot of the Tian Shan, and its ski resort, **Shymbulak**, is reached by a gondola from Medeu, just above town. The lifts climb to the **Talgar pass** at about 3,200 m, with freeride terrain off both sides and a wall of 4,000 m peaks behind.

It's lift-served freeride with a city at the bottom, and prices are low. The pistes are short but steep, and the off-piste from the Talgar pass is big and varied, with descents into the side valleys.

**Ak Bulak**, a smaller area outside the city, is a quieter option, and the mountains above both resorts are a base for touring.
almaty.beyond: Medeu, at the gondola base, is a huge outdoor ice rink where many Soviet speed-skating records were set. Almaty means "father of apples": wild apple forests here are the ancestors of the apples we eat today. The Green Bazaar is the place to try Kazakh food like *beshbarmak* and horse-meat sausage.
almaty.know:
Almaty's international airport is about 45 minutes from the gondola. Many nationalities can visit Kazakhstan without a visa.

The continental snowpack can be weak. Kazakhstan has a local avalanche service, but information in English is limited, so go with a local guide off-piste.

almatytouring.skiing:
Above Almaty, the Trans-Ili Alatau range offers multi-day touring from yurts, mountain huts and old Soviet scientific stations. The **Bogdanovich** and **Tuyuksu** glaciers, above Shymbulak, give high, glaciated terrain; the Tuyuksu glacier is one of the most closely studied in the world.

The area around **Big Almaty Lake** has more high touring, with peaks around 4,000 m and an old Soviet observatory as a base. Further east, the **Turgen gorge** and the Ketmen ridge are wilder and quieter.

The terrain ranges from gentle glaciers to big, steep faces. Trips usually last a few days to a week, with yurts or huts as bases.
almatytouring.beyond: The Tien Shan Astronomical Observatory, near the Big Almaty Lake, is an old Soviet observatory that now hosts visitors. The turquoise Big Almaty Lake is beautiful even in winter. Almaty is close for city days.
almatytouring.know:
Almaty's airport is 1 to 2 hours from the trailheads. Local guides and operators arrange yurts, huts and transport.

The snowpack is continental and often weak, and there's limited avalanche information in English. Go with a local guide.

mera.skiing:
Mera Peak (6,476 m) is the classic Himalayan ski objective: a broad, gentle glacier that allows a ski descent from near the summit. From the top, on a clear day, you can see five of the world's 8,000 m peaks, including Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu and Kangchenjunga.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude makes every turn hard work. The usual plan is to climb from **Khare**, the last settlement, to a high camp on the glacier, then summit early and ski the long, gentle glacier back down, with some of the best views in the Himalaya.

Most skiers are on expeditions with guides and porters, and the ski descent is a highlight of a longer trek through the Hinku valley.
mera.beyond: The trek in, through the remote Hinku valley, passes forests, Sherpa villages and teahouses. The journey and the people are as memorable as the summit.
mera.know:
Fly from Kathmandu to Lukla; flights are often delayed by weather. A climbing permit is required. Most trips take about two to three weeks, including acclimatisation.

Spring (April to May) has the best snow for skiing. Altitude sickness is the main risk. Crevasses exist on the glacier, so rope up.
