tremblant.skiing:
Mont-Tremblant, in the Laurentians, is the flagship resort of eastern North America, with runs on several sides of the mountain and a colourful pedestrian village at the base. The summit is at about 875 m, with roughly 645 m of vertical, big for the East, and around 100 runs.

The **South Side** gets the sun and the views over Lac Tremblant; the **North Side** is colder but often has better snow, with steeper runs and glades. The **Edge** has some of the best glades in eastern Canada, and the **Soleil** side has long, sunny cruisers. The terrain is mostly intermediate, with a few steep runs and lots of tree skiing for experts.

It's cold, often very cold, and the snow can be firm, but snowmaking is extensive and the village and atmosphere make it special. In a good winter, powder days in the glades are excellent.
tremblant.beyond: The village has a French-Canadian feel, with Québécois food like poutine and tourtière. The Scandinave Spa, nearby, offers outdoor Nordic baths in the forest. In March, sugar shacks (*cabanes à sucre*) serve maple-syrup feasts. Dogsledding, snowshoeing and ice skating on the lake are popular, and Montréal is close enough for a city day.
tremblant.know:
Montréal is about 1.5 hours away; Mont-Tremblant also has a small airport with seasonal flights. Pack for real cold: windchill below −30 °C is common in January. Facemasks and handwarmers are not optional.

The resort is on the Ikon Pass at the time of writing. Weekends and Québec holidays are busy.

vermont.skiing:
Northern Vermont has the best snow in the US Northeast, with classic New England tree skiing. **Stowe**, on Mount Mansfield, the highest peak in Vermont, has the famous "Front Four", steep, narrow trails, plus long cruisers and glades. **Jay Peak**, near the Canadian border, gets the most snow in the East, thanks to the "Jay Cloud", and has some of the region's best glades. **Sugarbush** has varied terrain and a laid-back vibe, and **Mad River Glen** next door is a skiers-only cooperative with a single chair: "Ski it if you can". **Smugglers' Notch**, across the notch from Stowe, is a family favourite with surprisingly steep terrain.

The snow can be icy, but powder days in the trees are excellent, and the region's skiing culture runs deep.

The backcountry has grown fast in recent years. Community groups, working with landowners and the Forest Service, cut and maintain backcountry glades, like the well-known zone at **Brandon Gap** in the Green Mountain National Forest, and the Vermont Backcountry Alliance coordinates much of this work.
vermont.beyond: The Trapp Family Lodge, near Stowe, was founded by the family from *The Sound of Music*. Ben & Jerry's factory, maple syrup, Vermont cheddar and craft beer are local highlights, and the small towns, with covered bridges and white churches, are classic New England.
vermont.know:
Burlington airport is about 1 hour away; Montréal is about 2 hours. Freeze-thaw cycles make conditions variable, so watch the forecast and chase storms.

Pass affiliations change: Stowe is on Epic, Sugarbush on Ikon, and Jay and Mad River Glen are independent at the time of writing.

The backcountry is mostly in the trees; respect the landowner agreements that keep the glades open.

tuckerman.skiing:
Tuckerman Ravine, on Mount Washington, is the classic Eastern spring pilgrimage. Each spring, skiers hike up from Pinkham Notch to ski the ravine's steep **Headwall**, with slopes of around 50° near the top, while crowds watch from a pile of boulders called **Lunch Rocks**.

In 1939, Toni Matt famously schussed the headwall in the American Inferno race, and the ravine has drawn skiers since the 1930s. Beyond the Headwall, gullies like **Left Gully**, **Right Gully** and **Hillman's Highway** offer slightly gentler options, and the **Gulf of Slides**, in the next valley, is a quieter alternative.

The atmosphere on a sunny spring weekend is part party, part pilgrimage. Snow usually lingers into May or June in good years, long after the surrounding forests are green.
tuckerman.beyond: Mount Washington held the world record for the highest wind speed measured at the surface for decades, about 372 km/h in 1934. The Appalachian Mountain Club's Joe Dodge Lodge, at Pinkham Notch, is the base. North Conway has outlet shopping, restaurants and other White Mountains activities.
tuckerman.know:
Portland and Boston are the nearest major airports. The hike up from Pinkham Notch takes about 2 to 3 hours.

The ravine has serious hazards: falling ice, crevasses, undermined snow and avalanches. The Mount Washington Avalanche Center forecasts the ravine daily. The weather can change fast, and the summit is famous for some of the worst weather on Earth.

Camping is limited; most people come up for the day.

chicchocs.skiing:
The Chic-Chocs, in Gaspésie National Park, get eastern Canada's best snow, with open alpine bowls and glades above the St. Lawrence River. Peaks like **Mont Albert** and **Mont Jacques-Cartier**, the highest in southern Québec at about 1,270 m, offer big terrain by eastern standards, and huts and lodges make multi-day trips possible.

The terrain is surprisingly alpine, with treeless summits, open bowls and long descents. Storms from the St. Lawrence often bring deep snow.

The **Chic-Chocs Mountain Lodge** offers guided touring and cat skiing from a lodge in the park, while the park's huts allow independent trips. Outside the park, the Haute-Gaspésie has other popular touring areas, and local outfits run guided trips there.
chicchocs.beyond: The Gaspésie is a beautiful, remote corner of Québec, with fishing villages, seafood and the famous Percé Rock. The park is home to the last herd of woodland caribou south of the St. Lawrence, and some areas are closed to protect them.
chicchocs.know:
The drive from Montréal is long, around 8 hours; Mont-Joli has the nearest airport. The Chic-Chocs Mountain Lodge and the park's huts need booking.

Avalanche Québec forecasts the Chic-Chocs. Weather can be severe, with strong winds and whiteouts. Caribou closures change from year to year, so check the park's current rules before planning a route.

grosmorne.skiing:
Gros Morne National Park, on Newfoundland's west coast, has fjords, tablelands and treeless bowls with big, open terrain. The snow can be deep, and the setting is wild and remote, with very few people.

The backcountry ranges from the barren, orange-rock **Tablelands**, near Trout River, to steep gullies above the fjords of **Bonne Bay** and the high plateau of the **Long Range Mountains**. Many slopes run down toward the sea, and on clear days the views across the ice-dotted water are spectacular.

**Marble Mountain**, in the Humber Valley near Corner Brook, offers lift-served skiing for stormy days, with about 500 m of vertical and some good glades. It's one of the biggest ski areas in Atlantic Canada.
grosmorne.beyond: Gros Morne is a UNESCO World Heritage site, partly because the Tablelands expose rock from the Earth's mantle. Newfoundland is famous for its hospitality, kitchen parties and "screech-in" ceremonies for visitors. Moose are everywhere, so drive carefully at night.
grosmorne.know:
Deer Lake airport is about 1 hour from the park. A car is essential.

There's no regular public avalanche forecast for the area. The weather is maritime and can change quickly. Go with a local guide, who will know where the snow is best.

Rocky Harbour and Woody Point are small villages in the park; lodging is limited in winter, so book ahead.

maunakea.skiing:
Mauna Kea, on Hawaii's Big Island, rises to about 4,200 m and gets snow after rare winter storms. Skiing here means driving up in a 4x4 and skiing short runs on thin snow over volcanic rock, then surfing the same day.

It's an opportunistic trip: you go only when it snows, and conditions are often thin. The snow can last days or weeks, depending on the storm and the sun. Most people come for the novelty and the views of the Pacific and Mauna Loa.

The slopes are open cinder cones and broad faces near the summit, with short runs and sharp lava rocks under the snow, so bring old skis. There are no lifts or services: locals shuttle each other back up in trucks.
maunakea.beyond: Mauna Kea is sacred to Native Hawaiians, and the summit has world-class observatories. Respect the cultural significance of the mountain and stay on established routes. Below, the Big Island has beaches, volcanoes (including active Kīlauea), coffee farms and great snorkelling.
maunakea.know:
Kona and Hilo are about 2 hours away. A 4x4 is needed beyond the visitor station. The road can close in storms or ice, and rental car agreements often forbid driving the summit road.

The altitude is high and you drive up from sea level quickly, so altitude sickness is a real risk. Stop at the visitor station at about 2,800 m to acclimatize.

antarctica.skiing:
Ski touring on the Antarctic Peninsula, from expedition yachts or small ships, among icebergs, penguins and whales. Peaks rise straight from the sea, and descents end at the shoreline, where zodiacs wait to take you back to the boat.

Days are spent touring from anchorages, with short to medium climbs and long descents back to the sea. Areas like **Paradise Harbour** and the **Lemaire Channel** are among the most famous, with steep walls of ice and peaks on every side.

It's the trip of a lifetime, and the scenery is unlike anywhere else on Earth. Small groups and expert guides keep it safe.
antarctica.beyond: Gentoo and Adélie penguins, seals and humpback whales are common. Port Lockroy, a former British base, has a museum and post office.
antarctica.know:
Most trips leave from Ushuaia and cross the Drake Passage, about two days each way, which can be rough. Some trips fly to King George Island instead.

Visitors follow strict rules set by IAATO, including biosecurity and keeping distance from wildlife. Crevasses are a real hazard, and rescue is very far away. Trips are expensive and book up a year or more ahead. November offers the best snow; later in the season, the snow becomes wetter.

grandvalira.skiing:
Grandvalira is the biggest ski area in the Pyrenees, spread across Andorra from **Pas de la Casa** on the French border to **Soldeu** and **El Tarter**. With around 210 km of pistes, it's bigger than many Alpine areas. The terrain is mostly wide, rolling intermediate runs above the treeline, with good tree skiing lower down and some off-piste.

Soldeu hosted the World Cup Finals in 2019, and the ski schools are known for teaching in English. Pas de la Casa is the party town by the French border, with steep runs on its north-facing side; Soldeu and El Tarter are quieter, with good tree runs; and **Grau Roig**, in the middle, is a sheltered bowl that's good in bad weather.

For freeride, **Ordino Arcalís**, in the north of Andorra, has big, open terrain and hosts a Freeride World Tour stop. It's under the same ownership and has its own pass options.
grandvalira.beyond: Andorra is a small, mountainous country with duty-free shopping in Andorra la Vella. The Caldea spa is a huge thermal complex with outdoor pools. Catalan is the official language.
grandvalira.know:
Barcelona and Toulouse are about 3 hours away; there's no major airport in Andorra. Prices are reasonable compared with the Alps.

Snowmaking is extensive. Andorra's weather service publishes avalanche information. Lift passes and lodging are good value, and the ski-school packages are popular with British families. Easter and February holidays are busy.

baqueira.skiing:
Baqueira-Beret, in the Val d'Aran, is Spain's best ski resort, on the Atlantic-facing side of the Pyrenees, so it gets more snow than most of the range. With around 170 km of pistes, the terrain is big and varied, with wide pistes and lots of off-piste across three areas: **Baqueira**, **Beret** and **Bonaigua**.

The off-piste is the highlight, with big, open terrain off the Baqueira and Beret areas and quieter slopes on the Bonaigua side. The **Escornacrabes** couloir, near the top of Baqueira, is the area's best-known steep line, and the Bonaigua sector has long descents into empty valleys.

It's a favourite of the Spanish royal family. Spanish skiers come for long weekends, and the slopes are quietest midweek. The **Port de la Bonaigua**, a pass at the eastern end, is also the start of ski tours into the Pyrenees.
baqueira.beyond: The Val d'Aran has its own language, Aranese (a form of Occitan), and its own culture. Try the *olla aranesa*, a hearty stew. Dinners start late, Spanish style. Vielha is the main town, and the valley has beautiful Romanesque churches.
baqueira.know:
Toulouse is about 2.5 hours away; Barcelona about 4 hours. Spanish holidays and weekends are busy.

The Val d'Aran has its own avalanche service (Lauegi). Off-piste is uncontrolled.

pyreneeshr.skiing:
The Pyrenees Haute Route crosses the central Pyrenees from **Gavarnie** to the **Aneto**, the highest peak in the range at 3,404 m, staying in mountain huts on both sides of the French-Spanish border. The route passes peaks like the **Vignemale** and **Monte Perdido**, and is much quieter than its Alpine cousin.

The glaciers are small, so it's less technical than the Alpine Haute Route, but the terrain is big and wild, and the days are long. The route crosses the border several times, from green French valleys to drier, sunnier Spanish ones, with big views of the range.

The classic finish is the Aneto from the **Renclusa** hut, above Benasque, with a short, exposed ridge (the Pont de Mahoma) to the summit on foot. Many people also do shorter sections, or day tours from a single hut.
pyreneeshr.beyond: The Cirque de Gavarnie, a huge amphitheatre of cliffs, and the Ordesa canyon are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. Spanish huts serve late, hearty dinners, and Benasque, at the end, is a lively mountain town.
pyreneeshr.know:
Toulouse, Zaragoza and Barcelona are about 3 hours from the start. Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Some huts have only self-service winter rooms, so check before you go.

Météo-France and Spain's weather service publish avalanche bulletins.

tatras.skiing:
The High Tatras are a compact granite range on the border between Slovakia and Poland, with steep couloirs, sharp ridges and alpine lakes. They're small, but steep and dramatic for their size, with couloirs and big faces that feel alpine.

On the Polish side, the cable car to **Kasprowy Wierch** gives access to classic terrain: the Gąsienicowa and Goryczkowa valleys below it are some of the most popular freeride spots in Poland. On the Slovak side, the **Lomnický štít** cable car climbs to one of the highest peaks, and **Štrbské Pleso** has a small resort by a lake.

Touring from mountain huts (*chaty*) is a classic way to explore, with tours to cols and summits above frozen lakes. National park rules restrict ski touring to certain areas and times on both sides, so it's important to check before you go.
tatras.beyond: Zakopane, on the Polish side, is a lively mountain town with wooden architecture and *góral* culture, including smoked sheep's cheese (*oscypek*). Kraków is about 2 hours away. On the Slovak side, the villages are quieter, and Poprad has thermal baths.
tatras.know:
Kraków and Poprad are the nearest airports. National park rules restrict ski touring to certain areas and times, so check them first.

The Slovak and Polish rescue services publish avalanche bulletins.

popova.skiing:
Popova Šapka, in the Šar Mountains above Tetovo, runs one of Europe's longest-running cat-skiing operations. The terrain is wide and wild, with open bowls and long descents across a range of peaks reaching over 2,700 m.

The resort itself is small and old-fashioned, with a few lifts and a sleepy feel, but the cats climb to ridges well above it, opening long, open descents with views across the Polog valley. The operation offers good value, and groups are small.

The Šar Mountains stretch along the border with Kosovo and Albania, and the highest peaks, like **Titov Vrv**, are serious ski-touring objectives with big, empty terrain. Snow is variable, but in a good year it's deep.
popova.beyond: Tetovo's Painted Mosque is one of the most beautiful in the Balkans. Skopje, the capital, has an old bazaar, and Lake Ohrid, a UNESCO site, is a few hours away. Macedonian food is hearty: try *tavče gravče* (baked beans) and *ajvar* (pepper relish).
popova.know:
Skopje airport is about 1 hour away. Prices are low. Lodging at Popova Šapka is simple, with a few hotels; Tetovo and Skopje are close for city days.

There's no public avalanche forecast, so ski with the operators' guides.

pirin.skiing:
Bansko sits at the foot of the Pirin Mountains, a UNESCO-listed national park with alpine limestone and marble peaks up to **Vihren** (2,914 m). The resort has a gondola from town and around 75 km of pistes, with long, wooded runs and a long ski road back down to town at the end of the day. It has hosted women's World Cup races.

For tourers, the mountains above are the real draw. Vihren's marble faces and the cirques around the **Vihren** and **Banderitsa** huts are the highlights, with steep gullies and wide, open bowls. The area feels wild and quiet, with few other tourers.

Bansko is cheap and lively, and the touring is quiet and wild, a rare combination.
pirin.beyond: Bansko's old town has stone houses and traditional taverns (*mehanas*) serving hearty dishes like *kapama* (slow-cooked meat). The Rila Monastery, a UNESCO site, is about 1.5 hours away.
pirin.know:
Sofia is about 2.5 hours away. Prices are low compared with the Alps.

Bansko gets busy in February, and the gondola queues from town can be long in the morning; staying near the lift or starting early helps. Guides in Bansko can arrange hut-to-hut tours in the national park. The Bulgarian mountain rescue service publishes avalanche information.

scotland.skiing:
Scotland's Highlands have wild, wind-scoured plateaus and gullies, with five ski areas (**Cairngorm**, **Glenshee**, **The Lecht**, **Nevis Range** and **Glencoe**) and backcountry touring when conditions allow. The snow is unpredictable, but when it's on, Scottish skiing can be brilliant.

Ski touring on the **Cairngorms plateau** feels closer to the Arctic than to the Alps: vast, rounded, and often swept by wind into hard snow and cornices. On the west coast, Glencoe, Scotland's oldest commercial ski area, sits at the edge of Rannoch Moor, and the Nevis Range gondola gives access to the steep back corries of Aonach Mòr.

**Ben Nevis**, the highest peak in the UK, has steep gullies on its north face, and **Number Four Gully** is a classic ski descent in good conditions. Glenshee, the biggest of the five ski areas, has the most lifts and gentle terrain.
scotland.beyond: Whisky distilleries, bothies (simple mountain shelters) and Highland hospitality. The Cairngorms have the only free-ranging reindeer herd in the UK.
scotland.know:
Inverness and Glasgow are the nearest airports. The weather is notoriously windy; Cairngorm summit has recorded gusts of about 280 km/h.

There are several ways to do it: chase forecasts and drive up for a weekend when snow arrives, base yourself in Aviemore or Fort William with a local guide, or combine a lift day with a touring day. Navigation skills matter: on the plateau, whiteouts and cornices catch people every winter.

The Scottish Avalanche Information Service forecasts six areas daily.

oukaimeden.skiing:
Oukaïmeden, in Morocco's High Atlas, has the highest lift-served slopes in Africa. A chairlift climbs to about 3,200 m near the summit of **Jbel Oukaïmeden**, and a handful of drag lifts serve the lower slopes around the village, which sits at about 2,600 m on a high plateau.

The terrain is open, wide and treeless, mostly gentle to intermediate on the pistes. After a good storm, the off-piste on the surrounding slopes and gullies can be excellent, with long, open runs and views across the Atlas. Ski tourers use the top of the chairlift as a starting point for the nearby ridges.

The lifts and rental gear are basic, grooming is limited, and the snow varies a lot from year to year: some winters bring plenty, others almost none. Local men offer donkey rides back up the slopes, and others rent out wooden sledges, which is part of the charm. It is best treated as an adventure rather than a ski holiday.
oukaimeden.beyond: Prehistoric rock engravings, thought to be several thousand years old, are scattered around the plateau. Marrakech, about 1.5 hours away, has the Jemaa el-Fna square, the souks and riads. The Ourika valley, on the way up, has waterfalls and Berber villages.
oukaimeden.know:
Marrakech airport is about 1.5 hours away by road; taxis and tours run up from the city. The road can close after heavy snow.

Check the snow before going: the season is short and unreliable, usually from January to March. There is no avalanche forecast, so off-piste skiers should assess conditions themselves or go with a local guide. Bring your own gear if you can.

highatlas.skiing:
Ski touring in the High Atlas centres on **Toubkal** (4,167 m), the highest peak in North Africa. Trips start from the Berber village of **Imlil**, at about 1,740 m, with mules carrying the gear up the valley to the **Toubkal refuges** at about 3,200 m, a walk of around 5 to 6 hours.

From the refuges, several 4,000 m peaks are within reach. Toubkal's south cirque is the usual ski route to the summit, with a descent of about 1,000 m back to the huts. The twin summits of **Ouanoukrim** (just over 4,000 m) and the cols around **Tizi n'Ouanoums** add couloirs and wide, open slopes.

The snow is variable: in a good year the touring is big, wild and spectacular, with views toward the Sahara on clear days, and in a bad year there may be too little snow to ski from the huts. Spring, when the snow has settled into corn, is usually the best time.

Most trips take about a week, with a few days based at the refuges.
highatlas.beyond: Imlil and the surrounding valleys have terraced fields, walnut groves and mud-brick villages. Staying in a village guesthouse, with mint tea and tagine, is part of the trip. Marrakech is about 2 hours away.
highatlas.know:
Marrakech airport is about 2 hours from Imlil. Since 2019, a licensed local guide has been required for the climb to Toubkal, so book one in advance.

There is no avalanche forecasting service. Wind slabs and icy spring snow are the main hazards, and the altitude matters: allow time to acclimatise. Snow cover varies a lot from year to year, so check conditions with a local operator before booking.

sierranevada.skiing:
Sierra Nevada is Europe's southernmost major ski resort, with slopes reaching nearly to the summit of **Veleta** (3,396 m). On clear days you can see across the Mediterranean to the mountains of North Africa. It hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships in 1996.

The resort, based at **Pradollano**, has around 100 km of pistes, mostly wide, sunny and intermediate, spread across open slopes above the tree line. There's a big terrain park and night skiing on some evenings. The sun is strong, so mornings can be icy and afternoons slushy: start early and follow the sun around the mountain.

For tourers, the **Corral del Veleta** cirque and the ridges toward **Mulhacén** (3,479 m), the highest peak in mainland Spain, offer long, open descents. The southern slopes, above the Alpujarra villages, are quieter and wilder.

Snowfall varies a lot from year to year, but the resort relies heavily on snowmaking.
sierranevada.beyond: Granada and the Alhambra are about 1 hour away, and in Granada's bars a free tapa still comes with each drink. The white villages of the Alpujarra, on the southern side of the range, are beautiful, and the coast is about 1.5 hours away.
sierranevada.know:
Granada airport is about 1 hour away; Málaga about 2. Buses run from Granada to Pradollano, and the road can need chains after storms.

Weekends and Spanish holidays are very busy. The upper slopes are exposed to strong wind. Off-piste, wind slabs and spring wet slides are the main hazards.

crete.skiing:
Crete's White Mountains (**Lefka Ori**) rise to 2,453 m at **Pachnes**, the island's second-highest peak. Above about 1,800 m lies a high, lunar karst plateau, with limestone sinkholes, ridges and long, open slopes, offering ski touring in a setting like nowhere else in Europe, with the Libyan Sea glittering below.

The usual base on the north side is the **Kallergi refuge**, above the Omalos plateau, from which tours lead up onto the high peaks. Pachnes can also be climbed from the south, from the village of Anopolis, with a long approach but a huge view down to the sea.

**Psiloritis** (Mount Ida, 2,456 m), in the centre of the island, is Crete's highest peak and the other option, usually climbed on skis from the **Nida plateau**.

The snow is variable and often hard or wind-blown, but in a good winter the touring is unforgettable. Touring days often end with a drive down to a village taverna or the beach.
crete.beyond: Psiloritis is the mythical birthplace of Zeus, in a cave on its slopes. The Samaria Gorge, one of Europe's longest, cuts through the Lefka Ori (open in summer). Chania's old Venetian harbour is a lovely base.
crete.know:
Chania airport is about 1.5 hours from the mountains; Heraklion is closer to Psiloritis. Roads up to the plateaus can be blocked by snow.

There is no avalanche forecast. Wind slabs and spring wet-snow cycles are the main hazards, and navigation on the featureless plateau is hard in cloud. Go with a local guide or club, and check snow cover before you go: some winters have very little.

etna.skiing:
Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano, rises to about 3,350 m above Sicily and offers some of the strangest skiing in Europe. Two small ski areas sit on its flanks: **Etna Sud**, near Rifugio Sapienza above Nicolosi, with a cable car toward the upper slopes; and **Etna Nord**, at **Piano Provenzana**, with a few lifts on the north side.

The lifts are small and often closed by wind, weather or eruptions, but ski touring opens up the whole mountain. Tourers climb past steaming vents and old lava flows toward the summit area, then ski long, open slopes back down, sometimes toward the vast **Valle del Bove** on the eastern side.

The snow can be dusted with black ash from eruptions, which makes for surreal skiing, and on clear days the views stretch across Sicily to the sea. The season is short and depends on storms.
etna.beyond: Catania, at the foot of the volcano, has excellent street food and a famous fish market. The vineyards on Etna's slopes make some of Italy's most interesting wines. Taormina, with its Greek theatre, is about an hour away.
etna.know:
Catania airport is about 1 hour away. Access to the summit area is regulated and often restricted because of volcanic activity; check the current rules with the park and local guides.

The summit is very windy and cold. Volcanic gas and eruptions are real hazards: go with an authorised volcano guide for the upper slopes.

afriski.skiing:
Afriski, in Lesotho's Maluti Mountains, is one of only two ski resorts in Southern Africa, at about 3,000 m on the Mahlasela Pass. The terrain is small: a main run of about 1 km, a beginner area and a terrain park, served by a few lifts.

Most of the snow comes from snowmaking, which relies on the cold, dry winter nights at altitude. Natural snowfalls do happen, and when they do the surrounding mountains turn white and the place looks very different. The season is short, roughly June to August.

The other resort, **Tiffindell**, in South Africa's Eastern Cape, has operated on and off over the years. Neither is a destination for advanced skiers, but skiing in Africa is a unique experience, and Afriski is popular with South Africans learning to ski.
afriski.beyond: Lesotho is called the "Kingdom in the Sky": it's the only country in the world entirely above 1,000 m. Basotho people wear distinctive woollen blankets and ride ponies in the mountains. The dramatic Sani Pass, further south, has a famous pub at the top.
afriski.know:
Johannesburg is about 5 to 6 hours away by road, crossing into Lesotho at the Caledonspoort or Ficksburg border posts. The roads are mountainous and can be icy; a high-clearance vehicle helps.

South African school holidays (late June to mid-July) are busy. Bring your passport.

corsica.skiing:
The **Alta Strada** is a ski-touring traverse along the granite spine of Corsica, roughly following the GR20 hiking trail, with sea views on both sides. It takes about a week, staying in mountain refuges and shepherds' huts (*bergeries*). **Monte Cinto** (2,706 m), the island's highest peak, is on the way, and **Monte Rotondo** and **Monte d'Oro** are other classic summits.

The terrain mixes granite ridges, open bowls and couloirs, with descents that look straight down to the Mediterranean. Day tours are also possible: Monte Cinto from the **Haut Asco** valley in the north, and Monte d'Oro from **Vizzavona**, on the island's central pass.

Corsica's few small ski areas, such as Ghisoni and Haut Asco, have struggled with lack of snow and are often closed, so skiing here really means touring. The snow is very variable, and the traverse depends on a good winter.
corsica.beyond: Corsican food is a highlight: brocciu cheese, chestnut flour, charcuterie and wild boar. The coastal towns of Calvi, Bonifacio and Ajaccio are beautiful, and you can be on the beach the day after a summit.
corsica.know:
Bastia and Ajaccio airports are about 1.5 to 2 hours from the mountains. Ferries run from France and Italy. Most refuges are unguarded in winter.

Météo-France publishes avalanche bulletins for Corsica's mountains. Weather changes fast with sea storms, and the granite ridges are exposed. Go with a guide unless you know the island well.

sochi.skiing:
The resorts of Krasnaya Polyana, above Sochi, were built or rebuilt for the 2014 Winter Olympics. **Rosa Khutor**, which hosted the alpine events, has big modern lifts and long runs from about 2,300 m, with a good mix of pistes and trees. **Gazprom** (Laura and Alpika) and **Krasnaya Polyana** (formerly Gorki Gorod) add more terrain, and the resorts are linked by gondolas and buses.

There's lots of tree skiing and sidecountry, and the snow can be deep, though it's often heavy and wet thanks to the Black Sea. The base is low, so conditions vary with altitude: rain at the bottom and powder at the top is common.

The Caucasus above the resorts has big, wild terrain for touring and heli-skiing, with steep faces and long descents.
sochi.beyond: The Black Sea coast, with palm trees, is about an hour away. The Olympic Park in Adler has the old venues. Georgian and Caucasian food is excellent.
sochi.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Sochi airport is about 1 hour away. Fog and heavy snow can close lifts. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

elbrusarea.skiing:
The Elbrus region, in the Baksan valley, has huge, cheap freeride under Europe's highest peak. **Cheget** has old Soviet lifts and steep, varied terrain with views of the Donguz-Orun face; its freeride is steep and varied, with long, open descents through forest and couloirs.

**Elbrus**, on the other side of the valley, has a modern cable car to about 3,850 m, with wide open slopes, high altitude and spectacular views of the Caucasus. The upper slopes are the start of the summit climb.

The terrain is big and largely uncontrolled. Local guides know the best lines and conditions.
elbrusarea.beyond: The Balkar people live in the valley; try *khychiny*, thin pies filled with cheese and potato. The villages of Terskol and Cheget have simple hotels and cafés.
elbrusarea.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Mineralnye Vody is about 3 hours away. There's no public avalanche forecast in English; go with a local guide.

elbrus.skiing:
Mount Elbrus (5,642 m), a dormant volcano with two summits, is the highest peak in Europe, and skiing from the top is one of the world's great volcano descents. The route goes up the south side, from the top of the cable car to the barrel huts at **Garabashi** and on to the summit.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude, cold and wind make it serious. The descent from the summit to the huts is around 1,800 m, mostly on wide, open slopes.

Trips usually take about a week, with acclimatisation climbs and a summit day. Snowcats can take you part of the way, which helps with the long summit day.
elbrus.beyond: The Baksan valley and the Caucasus mountains are spectacular. The barrel huts, converted from fuel tanks, are a famous part of the experience.
elbrus.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Spring (roughly April to June) is the season. Acclimatise properly. Whiteouts on the summit plateau have killed many climbers.

dombai.skiing:
Dombai sits under dramatic Caucasus peaks like **Dombai-Ulgen** (4,046 m), with old lifts and big off-piste. Its terrain is steep and dramatic, with views of glaciers and needle-like peaks.

**Arkhyz**, nearby, is a fast-growing modern resort, with new gondolas, wide pistes and a growing village. It's gentler than Dombai, with good tree skiing.

Both are cheap, and the off-piste is big and largely uncontrolled. Freeriders come for the huge, untracked terrain around both.
dombai.beyond: The Teberda Nature Reserve surrounds Dombai. Near Arkhyz, tenth-century Alanian churches and a large Soviet telescope, once the largest in the world, are interesting stops.
dombai.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and specifically to the North Caucasus. Bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Mineralnye Vody is about 4 hours away. There's no public avalanche forecast in English. Infrastructure is improving but still basic in places, and English is rarely spoken. Go with an operator who knows the area.

khibiny.skiing:
The Khibiny Mountains, on the Kola Peninsula above the Arctic Circle, offer Arctic freeride and touring: open bowls, cirques and long spring days. The resort of **Bolshoy Vudyavr**, above Kirovsk, has modern lifts and big terrain, including open bowls, steep chutes and long valley runs.

The season is long, running into June, and in May the sun barely sets. Touring from Kirovsk opens up big terrain in the surrounding cirques, with views over frozen lakes.

The Khibiny are a compact, plateau-topped massif, with steep sides and flat tops, so the skiing is mostly on the flanks and in the cirques.
khibiny.beyond: Kirovsk and Apatity are mining towns, named for the apatite mined here. In winter, a snow village with ice sculptures and a snow hotel opens in Kirovsk. The northern lights are common in the dark months.
khibiny.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Apatity airport is about 30 minutes away. The Khibiny has one of Russia's oldest avalanche services, because of the mining.

sheregesh.skiing:
Sheregesh, in the Gornaya Shoria region of Siberia, is famous for its deep, very cold, dry snow in birch and fir forests. The trees are often coated with snow and rime, and the tree skiing can be excellent.

The resort, on **Mount Zelenaya**, has several lift areas around a single peak, with lots of tree skiing and sidecountry between them. The terrain is mostly moderate, but the snow quality is the draw: in the cold, the snow stays light for days after a storm.

Many skiers come for the off-piste, and the neighbouring peaks offer backcountry and cat skiing.
sheregesh.beyond: Sheregesh is known for its spring party, the Grelka Fest, where skiers ride in swimsuits. The Shor people are the indigenous inhabitants of the area.
sheregesh.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Novokuznetsk is about 3 hours away. Midwinter can be extremely cold, below −30 °C. The resort is popular with Russian skiers and snowboarders, and weekends can be busy. English is rarely spoken.

kamchatka.skiing:
Kamchatka, in Russia's far east, offers heli-skiing on volcanoes that run down to the Pacific. It's one of the wildest heli destinations on Earth, with huge open slopes, steaming craters and descents that end at the ocean.

Typical descents run 1,000 to 2,000 m, from the shoulders of volcanoes like **Vilyuchinsky** and **Mutnovsky** down to the coast, and the open, treeless slopes in spring give long corn runs. **Avachinsky** and **Koryaksky**, the two volcanoes above Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, are also skied, and Avachinsky is a popular ski ascent from the road.

The terrain is big and remote, and the volcanoes are active. The volcanoes steam, the sea glitters, and there's rarely another person in sight.
kamchatka.beyond: Kamchatka has hot springs, geysers and brown bears. The Valley of Geysers is one of the largest geyser fields in the world, reached only by helicopter.
kamchatka.know:
Check your government's travel advice: many Western governments advise against all travel to Russia, and bank cards issued abroad don't work there.

Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky is the nearest airport. Heli-skiing is weather-dependent, so allow for down days. Trips are usually sold as a week, run by a few operators, often with old Soviet helicopters. Spring (March to May) brings longer days and more stable snow.

skidubai.skiing:
Ski Dubai opened in 2005 inside the Mall of the Emirates, and it's still the most famous indoor slope in the world. Behind a glass wall next to the shops, a sloping hall of real snow holds five runs, the longest about 400 m with a drop of about 60 m, served by a chairlift and a tow. There's a small terrain park, and a snow park for tobogganing and snowball fights.

It's a novelty, not a ski trip: a couple of hours is plenty for most skiers. But skiing laps while it's 40 °C outside is a strange and memorable experience, and it's a good place to learn.
skidubai.beyond: The penguins are the other star: a colony lives in the snow hall, and you can book an encounter. Outside, Dubai has the Burj Khalifa, the old souks along Dubai Creek, desert drives and the beach, all within a short taxi ride.
skidubai.know:
Dubai airport is about 25 minutes away by taxi or metro; the mall has its own metro station. Tickets are sold in time slots, and jackets, boots, skis or boards are included; bring gloves and a hat, or buy them there.

Weekday mornings are quietest. It's a good stopover on a long-haul flight through Dubai.

skiegypt.skiing:
Ski Egypt, inside the Mall of Egypt on the western edge of Cairo, opened in 2017 as Africa's first indoor ski slope. It's run by the same company as Ski Dubai, on a smaller scale: one main slope of about 210 m, with sections for beginners and more confident skiers, plus tubing runs and a snow play area, all kept at about −2 °C.

The skiing itself takes an hour or two. The point is the contrast: real snow a few kilometres from the desert, in one of the hottest, driest countries on Earth.
skiegypt.beyond: Like Dubai, it has penguins: King, Gentoo and Chinstrap penguins live in the snow hall. The Pyramids of Giza and the Grand Egyptian Museum are about half an hour away, so snow in the morning and pyramids in the afternoon is a real option. Cairo's Khan el-Khalili bazaar and Nile felucca rides fill the rest of a city stay.
skiegypt.know:
Cairo airport is about an hour away, depending on traffic. Tickets usually include jackets, boots and skis or boards; bring gloves and a hat.

Fridays, Saturdays and holidays are busiest. Pair it with a trip to Cairo rather than travelling for the snow alone.

lsnow.skiing:
L+SNOW, in Shanghai's Lingang area, opened in September 2024 and was certified by Guinness as the world's largest indoor ski resort. The snow hall covers more than 90,000 m², with slopes for four levels stacked on three floors, like a mountain built indoors. The longest is an advanced run of 340 m at up to 26°, steeper than most indoor slopes, and there are beginner areas and a teaching trail.

It's still indoor skiing, with short runs and a roof overhead, but it's the closest an indoor slope gets to the real thing.
lsnow.beyond: The resort is a whole complex: about 20 snow activities, a water park, and three snow-themed hotels with close to 1,000 rooms, including ski-in, ski-out suites that open straight onto the slopes. Central Shanghai, with the Bund and the old lanes of the French Concession, is about an hour away.
lsnow.know:
Shanghai Pudong airport is about an hour away. It's busiest in Chinese school holidays and on summer weekends, when people come to escape the heat.

The official site and booking are mainly in Chinese, so plan ahead or book through an agent.

kachina.skiing:
The San Francisco Peaks rise to about 3,850 m just north of Flagstaff, the remains of a large volcano that once stood even higher. **Humphreys Peak**, the highest point in Arizona, and its neighbours ring a collapsed caldera called the **Inner Basin**, and their upper slopes hold real alpine terrain: open bowls, avalanche paths and glades well above the surrounding pine forest.

The Kachina Peaks Wilderness covers most of the range. **Arizona Snowbowl**, on the western side, is the main access point, and the terrain above and beside it is the most popular backcountry. The Inner Basin, reached from the **Lockett Meadow** side to the east, is a longer, quieter approach into the heart of the old volcano.

The snow is unreliable. In a big year the Peaks get several metres and the bowls are deep and wintry; in a dry year there's barely enough to ski. When it's good, though, skiing high above the desert, with views to the Grand Canyon on clear days, is a rare experience.
kachina.beyond: Flagstaff is a lively mountain town on old Route 66, with Lowell Observatory (where Pluto was discovered) and some of the darkest skies of any US city. The Grand Canyon's South Rim is about 1.5 hours away, quiet and often snowy in winter, and Sedona's red rocks are 45 minutes south.
kachina.know:
The San Francisco Peaks are sacred to the Hopi, Navajo and more than a dozen other tribes; treat them with respect.

The snowpack is thin and often has weak layers. Wind loading is strong above treeline, and the wilderness area has strict rules: check Coconino National Forest guidance on access points and closures before you go.

The Kachina Peaks Avalanche Center, a small non-profit, forecasts the area. Altitude is high, so take it easy on the first day.

lasals.skiing:
The La Sal Mountains rise to nearly 3,900 m just east of Moab, an island range of peaks above the canyon country. In winter they hold real mountain terrain: bowls, chutes and glades on peaks like **Mount Tukuhnikivatz** ("Tuk" to locals), **Mount Mellenthin** and **Mount Peale**, the highest in the range.

The main winter access is the **Geyser Pass** road, plowed to a trailhead at around 2,900 m, from which a groomed Nordic track and skin tracks lead toward **Gold Basin**, the heart of the backcountry. From there, tours range from mellow tree runs to steep lines off the summits, with views over the red-rock desert hundreds of metres below.

There is no ski area and no services. The Utah Avalanche Center's Moab forecast, supported by local volunteers, is the only regular source of conditions, and the community of skiers is small and friendly.
lasals.beyond: Arches and Canyonlands national parks are a short drive away and wonderfully quiet in winter, sometimes with snow on the red arches. Moab has good cafés and restaurants, cheap off-season lodging, and mountain biking and hiking on dry days in the desert below.
lasals.know:
The snowpack is thin and often weak, so careful terrain choices matter. Storms can be infrequent, so check recent conditions before driving out.

The Geyser Pass road is plowed to the winter trailhead; the last part can be icy, so bring a vehicle that can handle it. The Moab Nordic ski club grooms some trails near the trailhead, and a small yurt there is sometimes available.

Moab is about 4 hours from Salt Lake City and 2 from Grand Junction.

wallowas.skiing:
The Wallowa Mountains, in the remote northeast corner of Oregon, rise abruptly from the farmland of the Wallowa Valley to peaks near 3,000 m. Locals call them Oregon's "Little Switzerland", and the comparison is fair: steep alpine faces, deep valleys and, in winter, a cold, drier snowpack than the Cascades.

Most of the range is the **Eagle Cap Wilderness**, with no roads and no lifts, so skiing here is human-powered. The best-known way in is with **Wing Ridge Ski Tours**, which runs backcountry yurts in the southeastern part of the range; guests spend several days touring open bowls and glades from the yurts.

**Ferguson Ridge**, near Joseph, is a tiny volunteer-run ski area with a T-bar, a wonderful old-fashioned community hill. The peaks above Wallowa Lake and the slopes near **Salt Creek Summit** also offer day tours.
wallowas.beyond: Joseph is an art town known for its bronze foundries and sculptures along Main Street. Wallowa Lake is beautiful in winter, and Hells Canyon, the deepest river gorge in North America, is nearby. The area is also the homeland of the Nez Perce, and Chief Joseph's story is told in local museums.
wallowas.know:
The Wallowas are a long way from anywhere: about 5 hours from Portland or Boise. Services are limited in winter, and Ferguson Ridge runs only on some weekends.

The yurts are booked through Wing Ridge Ski Tours; guided and self-guided options exist. The Wallowa Avalanche Center, a small non-profit, forecasts the range.

centraloregon.skiing:
**Mount Bachelor** is a volcano with lifts all the way to the summit, about 2,760 m, so when the top lift runs you can ski off the peak in any direction, round the cone, onto big open faces and into the trees. The mountain gets plenty of snow, and the season often runs into late spring. Wind and fog can close the summit, but on clear days the views across the Cascade volcanoes are huge.

Around it are some of the best spring volcano tours in Oregon. **Tumalo Mountain**, across the road from Bachelor, is a popular short skin with a view of Bachelor's whole cone. **Broken Top**, a jagged, eroded volcano, has steeper, more alpine lines, and **South Sister**, at about 3,160 m, is a big spring climb and descent from Devils Lake.

The Central Oregon Avalanche Center forecasts the area, and the volcanoes' open slopes are exposed to wind and sun.
centraloregon.beyond: Bend is one of the West's great outdoor towns, with dozens of breweries, a river trail and a lively restaurant scene. Smith Rock, a famous climbing area, is nearby, and the High Desert Museum has wildlife and history. Lava caves and lava fields are a short drive.
centraloregon.know:
Bend is about 30 minutes from Mount Bachelor, and the road is paved and maintained. Redmond airport is the closest; Portland is about 3.5 hours.

Mount Bachelor is on the Ikon Pass at the time of writing; check before going. The Cascade Lakes Highway beyond Bachelor closes in winter, which limits access to the wider backcountry until spring. Sno-park permits are required in Oregon.

mccall.skiing:
McCall sits on the shore of Payette Lake in west-central Idaho, with two very different ski areas nearby. **Brundage Mountain**, just north of town, is known for some of the lightest, deepest snow in the region, with tree-skiing and views to the Seven Devils; it also runs cat skiing in the backcountry beyond the resort. **Tamarack Resort**, about 30 minutes south, is newer, with a large base village and long, wide runs above Lake Cascade.

The backcountry around McCall is extensive and mostly quiet. Locals tour from pass trailheads and forest roads into rolling, timbered terrain with some bigger alpine objectives, and the Payette Avalanche Center forecasts the area.

It's a relaxed, uncrowded place to ski: not a destination resort, but a good one for a week of powder with few lines.
mccall.beyond: McCall's Winter Carnival, held for about 10 days in late January to early February, fills the town with huge snow sculptures, parades and fireworks. The town has good restaurants and a frozen lake for walking, skating and ice fishing. Burgdorf Hot Springs, reached by snowmobile or skis in winter, is a rustic soak in the forest.
mccall.know:
Boise is about 2 to 2.5 hours by road. McCall has lodging of all kinds, and Tamarack has slopeside rooms.

Check pass affiliations with each resort before going. Brundage's cat skiing books up early.

whitefish.skiing:
**Whitefish Mountain Resort**, on Big Mountain above the town of Whitefish, covers about 1,200 hectares of trees, bowls and long cruisers, with views east to the peaks of Glacier National Park. Its upper slopes are often in cloud, and the trees there are coated in thick rime, forming the strange "snow ghosts" the mountain is known for.

The snow is reliable, the atmosphere relaxed, and the lifts rarely busy. Whitefish is a good choice for a week of skiing with a real town to come back to.

The Flathead Avalanche Center covers the surrounding ranges, and locals tour in the Whitefish Range, the Swan Range and, most of all, at **Marias Pass**, on the southern edge of Glacier National Park, where US-2 climbs to the Continental Divide.
whitefish.beyond: Whitefish is a lively small town with good restaurants and bars. Glacier National Park is about 30 minutes away; the Going-to-the-Sun Road is closed in winter, but you can ski or snowshoe in along it from West Glacier. The historic Izaak Walton Inn at Essex, a railway hotel, has cross-country trails and rooms in old railway cars.
whitefish.know:
Glacier Park International is about 30 minutes away, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops in Whitefish, a scenic way to arrive.

The Flathead Avalanche Center forecasts daily. Marias Pass and the park are big, avalanche-prone terrain; the railway and highway corridors also have their own control work.

jasper.skiing:
**Marmot Basin**, about 30 minutes from the town of Jasper, is the main ski area in the vast Jasper National Park. It's smaller and quieter than the resorts around Banff, with a mix of groomers, glades and high, open terrain, and the lift lines are short or non-existent most days.

The backcountry is big and wild. The **Bald Hills**, above Maligne Lake, have gentle, open touring with wide views. Further south, the **Columbia Icefield** on the Icefields Parkway has glacier skiing and ski-mountaineering on peaks like Mount Athabasca, best in spring with a guide.

The snowpack is typically Rockies: shallow and cold, with persistent weak layers, so the Parks Canada forecast is essential.
jasper.beyond: Jasper is a Dark Sky Preserve, with superb stargazing. You can walk on the frozen bottom of Maligne Canyon on a guided ice walk, and see elk, bighorn sheep and sometimes wolves. A wildfire in 2024 burned part of the town; it's rebuilding, so check what's open.
jasper.know:
Jasper is about 4 hours from Edmonton and 4.5 hours from Calgary (via the Icefields Parkway, which can close in storms). A national park pass is required.

VIA Rail's Canadian stops in Jasper, a scenic way to arrive. Lodging can be limited in the wake of the fire; book ahead.

kananaskis.skiing:
Kananaskis Country, just south-east of Banff National Park, is the closest big touring area to Calgary. **Nakiska**, its ski area, hosted alpine events at the 1988 Winter Olympics, but most people come for the backcountry along the Smith-Dorrien / Spray Trail road.

The classic tours start from roadside trailheads: **Burstall Pass**, a long, gentle approach to a high pass with views into Banff National Park; **Chester Lake**, a popular tour with good bowls above it; and **Rummel Lake** and other easier options for unstable days. There's terrain for every level, from meadow skiing to steep alpine faces.

The snowpack is classic Rockies: thinner and colder than in BC, often with weak layers deep down, so careful terrain choices matter. Chinook winds can bring sudden warm spells.
kananaskis.beyond: Canmore, on the edge of Kananaskis, is a lively mountain town with good food and coffee. The Kananaskis Nordic Spa offers hot pools in the mountains. Banff is about 30 minutes away, and Calgary about an hour.
kananaskis.know:
A Kananaskis Conservation Pass is required to park in the area. The Smith-Dorrien road is gravel and can be rough. Highway 40 over Highwood Pass is closed in winter.

Kananaskis Country Public Safety forecasts daily on avalanche.ca. Trailheads can be busy on weekends.

pinepass.skiing:
Pine Pass carries Highway 97 over the northern Rockies between Prince George and the Peace River country. It's a low pass, under 1,000 m, but it catches a lot of snow, and the mountains on either side offer roadside touring in deep, reliable powder.

**Powder King**, near the pass, is a small, snowy ski area with a big reputation for snowfall. Around it, locals tour on treed slopes, open ridges and alpine bowls, often with very few people around.

The area is remote, with long distances between towns and limited services, so it's best for self-sufficient groups. Avalanche Canada's North Rockies forecast covers the region.
pinepass.beyond: The drive along Highway 97 passes lakes, forests and the occasional moose. Prince George is the nearest city, with an airport and services. Mackenzie and Chetwynd are small towns on either side of the pass.
pinepass.know:
Prince George is about 2 hours away. Lodging is limited, so plan ahead. Highway 97 is a major road, but winter conditions can be severe.

Powder King's operations have varied over the years, so check its status before going.

northshore.skiing:
The North Shore Mountains rise straight above Vancouver, with three ski areas you can see from downtown. **Cypress Mountain** hosted the freestyle and snowboard events at the 2010 Olympics and has the most terrain; **Grouse Mountain**, reached by a big aerial tram, has views right over the city; and **Mount Seymour** is the smallest, with a lot of local character.

All three offer night skiing, and you can go from office to lift in under an hour. The snow is coastal and heavy, and rain at the bases is common, but in a good spell the skiing can be excellent.

The backcountry above the resorts is popular for short tours, especially from Seymour, where routes lead to **Pump Peak** and **Tim Jones Peak**, and from Cypress toward **Black Mountain**. The terrain is small but steep, with cliffs and creek gullies, and North Shore Rescue is regularly called out for people lost beyond the resort boundaries.
northshore.beyond: Vancouver is one of the world's most beautiful cities, with Stanley Park, great food and the ocean at your doorstep. Whistler is about 2 hours away along the Sea to Sky highway, and the Capilano Suspension Bridge is on the North Shore.
northshore.know:
The ski areas are 30 to 45 minutes from downtown by car or shuttle bus. Night skiing is the local favourite.

The terrain beyond the boundaries is steep and dangerous, with cliffs and creeks; don't follow tracks out of bounds without knowing where they lead.

vanisland.skiing:
Vancouver Island's mountains catch storms straight off the Pacific, and in a good year the snow is very deep. **Mount Washington**, above the Comox Valley, is the island's main resort, with a big snowpack, ocean views and a wide mix of terrain. In the island's far north, **Mount Cain** is a small community-run ski area with steep, open terrain and a loyal following.

**Strathcona Provincial Park**, next to Mount Washington, is the island's wilderness core. From the **Paradise Meadows** trailhead, Nordic and ski-touring routes lead into the Forbidden Plateau, with gentle terrain near the trailhead and bigger peaks deeper in.

The snowpack is coastal, heavy and deep, and the weather can be wet and windy. Avalanche Canada publishes a Vancouver Island forecast.
vanisland.beyond: Tofino, on the island's wild west coast, is famous for winter storm watching and surfing. Courtenay and Comox are friendly towns with good food. Whale-watching and old-growth forests are nearby.
vanisland.know:
Comox airport is about 40 minutes from Mount Washington, and ferries connect the island to Vancouver. Mount Cain runs on weekends and holidays; check its schedule.

The weather is wet, so pack waterproof gear.

shames.skiing:
Northwest BC is one of the snowiest, most remote ski regions in North America. **Shames Mountain**, near Terrace, is a community co-op ski area, saved from closure by the town and run by its members. It gets huge amounts of snow, and the lift-served terrain and the touring terrain beyond it are steep, deep and often empty.

The Shames backcountry, reached directly from the top of the lifts, offers big alpine bowls, glades and couloirs with very short approaches. Avalanche Canada's Northwest Coastal forecast covers the area.

Further north, near **Stewart** and **Bell 2**, heli-skiing operations offer some of the largest heli-ski terrain in the world, in the Skeena and Coast Mountains, with long glacier runs and deep, coastal snow.
shames.beyond: Terrace is a small working town on the Skeena River, with good fishing and hot springs nearby. The Nisga'a Memorial Lava Bed Park, to the north, is the site of a lava flow from the 18th century, and the Highway 37 drive north to Stewart passes glaciers and wildlife.
shames.know:
Terrace is about 40 minutes from Shames; flights connect to Vancouver. Lodging is limited. The weather can be long and stormy, so allow flexible days.

The heli-ski operations book up a year ahead.

whitepass.skiing:
White Pass carries the Klondike Highway from Skagway, at sea level in Alaska, up to the British Columbia and Yukon border at about 870 m. It's the route of the Klondike Gold Rush, and today it's the main backcountry area for skiers from Whitehorse and Skagway.

The terrain is open and alpine right from the road, with rolling ridges, bowls and steeper lines on the surrounding peaks. The pass catches snow from coastal storms, and the snow is often wind-affected but plentiful. Spring brings long days and corn snow.

Avalanche Canada forecasts the White Pass area. Services are minimal, and the weather can change fast.
whitepass.beyond: Skagway is a preserved gold-rush town, with wooden boardwalks and the historic White Pass & Yukon Route railway, which mostly runs in summer. Whitehorse, the Yukon capital, has hot springs nearby and good chances of seeing the northern lights.
whitepass.know:
Whitehorse is about 2 hours' drive; Skagway is about 30 minutes from the pass. You cross an international border (US–Canada), so bring a passport.

The road can close in storms. Bring everything you need; services are minimal.

hatcherpass.skiing:
Hatcher Pass sits in the Talkeetna Mountains about 1.5 hours north of Anchorage, above the towns of Palmer and Wasilla. The road climbs past the old buildings of **Independence Mine**, a gold mine from the 1930s and 1940s, into a wide alpine bowl ringed by rocky peaks.

The touring is mostly above treeline, on open slopes and couloirs of every angle, with short approaches from the road. The snowpack is colder and shallower than at Turnagain Pass, so the snow often stays light longer, but it also tends to have more persistent weak layers. Wind is a constant factor.

The road over the pass itself closes in winter, but the access road to the Independence Mine area is plowed, and on a good day the views over the Matanuska-Susitna Valley are huge.
hatcherpass.beyond: Independence Mine State Historical Park preserves the old mining camp. Palmer is a farming town with the Musk Ox Farm and a famous state fair. The Matanuska Glacier, about 1.5 hours away, can be walked on with a guide in winter.
hatcherpass.know:
Anchorage is about 1.5 hours away; Palmer has services. The road above the Independence Mine area closes in winter.

The Hatcher Pass Avalanche Center, a small non-profit, forecasts the area. The snowpack can have deep weak layers, so check the forecast carefully.

bavaria.skiing:
Germany's Alps are a narrow strip along the Austrian border, but they pack in a lot. **Garmisch-Partenkirchen** has the Garmisch-Classic area, with the **Kandahar**, one of the toughest downhills on the World Cup circuit, and the **Zugspitze**, Germany's highest peak at 2,962 m, has a small glacier ski area reached by cog railway and cable car, with views over four countries.

Further west, the **Allgäu** has **Oberstdorf**, with the Fellhorn, Kanzelwand and Nebelhorn areas, and the Nebelhorn's long off-piste and its famously steep run from the top. The Allgäu catches a lot of snow from the north-west and has a strong freeride and touring scene.

The Bavarian Prealps between Garmisch and Berchtesgaden are one of the busiest ski-touring regions in Europe, with easy, friendly tours from almost every village. The **Spitzingsee** area, about an hour from Munich, is a classic, with tours like the **Rotwand** and dozens of others.
bavaria.beyond: Garmisch-Partenkirchen hosted the 1936 Winter Olympics and has painted houses and beer gardens. Neuschwanstein Castle is about an hour west, and Munich, with its museums and beer halls, is close for a city day. Oberstdorf has the Heini-Klopfer ski-flying hill and good cross-country trails.
bavaria.know:
Munich airport is about 1.5 hours from Garmisch, and trains run from Munich to Garmisch and Oberstdorf. Weekends are busy with day-trippers from Munich, and the roads can be slow.

The Bavarian avalanche service forecasts daily. Many Bavarian resorts allow uphill skiing on marked routes; rules vary, so check before you go.

gastein.skiing:
The Gastein valley, in the Hohe Tauern, combines several ski areas with around 200 km of pistes. The main area, **Stubnerkogel–Schlossalm**, links Bad Gastein and Bad Hofgastein with long, wide runs and big views. **Graukogel**, above Bad Gastein, is a small, old-fashioned area with tree-lined runs and an Olympic history.

**Sportgastein**, at the head of the valley at about 1,600 m, is the high, wild end of the valley. Its lifts climb to about 2,700 m on the Kreuzkogel, and the terrain is open and snowy, with some of the best lift-served freeride in the Salzburg Alps and long off-piste descents.

The valley catches storms from both north and south, so Sportgastein often has good snow when other areas don't. The surrounding Hohe Tauern also offer ski touring, with routes into the national park from Sportgastein and the side valleys.
gastein.beyond: Bad Gastein is a striking belle-époque spa town, built on a steep slope around a waterfall that crashes through the centre. Its grand hotels, some empty for years, have been restored as creative, boutique places. The thermal baths (Felsentherme in Bad Gastein, Alpentherme in Bad Hofgastein) and the radon "healing gallery" in an old mine make the valley a classic spa destination.
gastein.know:
Salzburg is about 1.5 hours away, and trains run straight to Bad Gastein and Bad Hofgastein on the main line. The Ski amadé pass covers Gastein and many other areas in the region.

The Salzburg avalanche service forecasts daily. Off-piste at Sportgastein is uncontrolled; a guide helps.

montafon.skiing:
The Montafon is a long valley in Vorarlberg, at the western end of Austria, with several ski areas on one pass. **Silvretta Montafon**, the biggest, links Schruns and St. Gallenkirch with around 140 km of pistes and lots of easy off-piste between the lifts. **Golm** is a smaller family area with views of the Rätikon's limestone peaks, and **Gargellen**, in a side valley, is small, snowy and quiet.

Gargellen is also the start of the **Madrisa-Rundtour**, a classic day tour: you climb over the border into Switzerland, ski down to Klosters, take the lifts up the Madrisa, and tour back over to Gargellen. It's a great introduction to ski touring.

The valley is the gateway to the Silvretta and Rätikon huts for longer tours, and the area is popular with tourers for its friendly terrain and good snow.
montafon.beyond: Ernest Hemingway spent two winters in Schruns in the 1920s, writing and skiing; the Hotel Taube, where he stayed, still remembers him. The Montafon's villages are traditional, with wooden houses and good food. The Lünersee and the Rätikon's limestone towers are spectacular.
montafon.know:
Zurich is about 2 hours away; Friedrichshafen and Innsbruck are closer for some flights. A train runs from Bludenz up the valley to Schruns.

The Vorarlberg avalanche service forecasts daily. For the Madrisa-Rundtour, carry a passport and a Swiss lift ticket; it's best done with a guide the first time.

dachstein.skiing:
Schladming is the heart of the **Schladming-Dachstein** region, part of the huge Ski amadé pass with hundreds of kilometres of pistes. Four linked mountains (**Hochwurzen**, **Planai**, **Hauser Kaibling** and **Reiteralm**) offer long, wide, perfectly groomed runs, and the **Planai** hosts the famous World Cup Nightrace each January.

Across the valley, the **Dachstein** massif rises above Ramsau to about 2,995 m, with a small glacier ski area reached by cable car. The glacier offers early- and late-season skiing and access to classic ski tours on the high plateau.

The limestone plateaus of the Dachstein and the nearby Totes Gebirge are some of the most interesting touring terrain in Austria, with wide, karst landscapes, sinkholes and big views. Ramsau, below the Dachstein, is also one of the best cross-country areas in the Alps.
dachstein.beyond: The Dachstein Skywalk and suspension bridge at the top of the cable car offer dizzying views, and the Ice Palace inside the glacier is a curiosity. Hallstatt, on the other side of the massif, is one of Austria's most beautiful lake villages, and the Dachstein ice caves are nearby.
dachstein.know:
Salzburg is about 1 hour away, and Schladming has a train station. The Ski amadé pass covers the region and more.

The Styrian avalanche service forecasts daily. Plateau tours need good navigation: the karst terrain is featureless in cloud, with hidden holes.

jasna.skiing:
Jasná, on the slopes of **Chopok** (2,024 m) in the Low Tatras, is the biggest ski resort in Slovakia and one of the best in Central Europe. Cable cars link its north and south sides over the summit, so you can ski both faces of the mountain on one pass.

The **north side** is the main area, with steeper runs, the base at Jasná and the lively Biela Púť village. The **south side** is sunnier and gentler, with long runs down toward Srdiečko and Krupová. Jasná has marked freeride zones, controlled but ungroomed, which make it one of the easiest places in the region to get into off-piste skiing.

The Low Tatras ridge, east and west of Chopok, also offers ski touring with big views over the High Tatras.
jasna.beyond: The Demänovská valley below the resort has show caves, including the Demänovská Ice Cave. Liptovský Mikuláš, the nearest town, has the Tatralandia aquapark and thermal pools. The High Tatras are about an hour away.
jasna.know:
Poprad airport is about an hour away; Kraków and Bratislava are about 3 and 4 hours. Prices are good compared with the Alps.

The Slovak avalanche service (laviny.sk) forecasts daily. The summit is windy and the cable cars over the top close in strong wind.

krkonose.skiing:
The Krkonoše, or Giant Mountains, run along the border between Czechia and Poland and rise to **Sněžka** (1,603 m), the highest point in Czechia. They're not high, but they're exposed to wind and weather from the north, with treeless summit plateaus, rime-coated trees and glacial cirques where real avalanches happen every winter.

**Špindlerův Mlýn** is the main resort, with the most lifts and the steepest runs in Czechia, and **Pec pod Sněžkou** sits below Sněžka. Both are busy and lively, and lift tickets are cheap by Western standards.

The cirques, like **Obří důl** under Sněžka and the Labský důl at the source of the Elbe, are the area's backcountry, steep and wind-loaded. The national park restricts off-trail skiing, so most visitors stick to marked routes; check the rules before going.
krkonose.beyond: The Krkonoše have a long ski history, with old wooden mountain huts (*boudy*) serving hearty Czech food and beer. Prague is about 2 hours away, and the Polish side has Karpacz and Szklarska Poręba. Cross-country skiing on the summit ridges is very popular.
krkonose.know:
Prague is about 2 hours away by car or bus. Prices are low.

The Czech Mountain Rescue Service forecasts avalanches in the Krkonoše daily. Fog, wind and icing are common on the ridges, and the national park has strict rules on where you can ski.

formigal.skiing:
The Aragonese Pyrenees have Spain's biggest ski area and two of its oldest resorts. **Formigal**, in the Valle de Tena, is linked with **Panticosa** under the Aramón brand, with around 180 km of pistes on wide, open slopes. Formigal's terrain is big and varied, with good off-piste and a famous après scene.

Further west, near the Somport pass and the French border, **Candanchú** and **Astún** sit side by side. Candanchú is one of Spain's oldest ski resorts, with steep, varied terrain; Astún is more modern, with wide, open slopes.

The mountains around both are classic ski-touring country. The Valle de Tena and the area around Candanchú have dozens of tours, from easy summits to steep couloirs, and the high peaks around the **Balaitús** and **Pico de Anayet** offer bigger objectives with views across to France.
formigal.beyond: Jaca has a big 16th-century citadel and a Romanesque cathedral, and its tapas bars are lively. The Valle de Tena's villages are stone-built and traditional. The Ordesa canyon, a UNESCO site, is nearby, and dinners start late, Spanish style.
formigal.know:
Zaragoza is about 2 hours away; Pau, in France, is about 1.5 hours over the Somport. Spanish weekends and holidays are busy.

AEMET publishes the Pyrenees avalanche bulletin. Off-piste is uncontrolled.

gransasso.skiing:
The **Gran Sasso** rises to 2,912 m at **Corno Grande**, the highest point of the Apennines, and holds the remains of the **Calderone**, once the southernmost glacier in Europe. Below it, **Campo Imperatore** is a vast high plateau, sometimes called "Little Tibet", with a small ski area at its edge and huge open touring terrain all around.

The ski touring is the real draw. Corno Grande has steep gullies and faces, and the rounded peaks around Campo Imperatore offer easy, open tours with views to the Adriatic on clear days. Storms from the east can bring huge snowfalls, and big cornices form on the ridges.

To the south-east, the **Majella** massif, with **Monte Amaro** (2,793 m), has wide, open slopes and long descents. **Roccaraso**, further south, is the biggest ski area in the southern Apennines.
gransasso.beyond: The hotel at Campo Imperatore is where Mussolini was held in 1943 before a famous German glider raid freed him. L'Aquila, rebuilt after the 2009 earthquake, has a beautiful old centre. Abruzzo's hill villages, like Santo Stefano di Sessanio, are stunning, and the food (arrosticini lamb skewers, pecorino, saffron) is excellent.
gransasso.know:
Rome is about 2 hours away; Pescara is about an hour. The Campo Imperatore road and cable car can close in storms.

Meteomont, run by the Carabinieri, forecasts the Apennines. Cornices and wind slabs are the main hazards. Fog can roll in fast on the plateau.

fagaras.skiing:
The **Făgăraș** mountains are the highest range in Romania, with **Moldoveanu** (2,544 m) and a long ridge of steep, alpine peaks and glacial cirques. In winter, the Transfăgărășan road is closed, but a cable car from **Bâlea Cascadă** climbs to **Bâlea Lac**, a frozen glacial lake at about 2,030 m, giving access to steep, open terrain all around.

The skiing around Bâlea Lac is serious: couloirs, cirques and big avalanche paths. Each winter an ice hotel is built on the lake. Spring is the best time, when the snowpack settles and the days are long.

The **Bucegi** mountains, closer to Bucharest, have a high plateau above **Sinaia** and Bușteni, with cable cars and a few lifts. The plateau offers easy touring, and the steep valleys on its eastern edge are a serious freeride and touring challenge.
fagaras.beyond: Sibiu, near the Făgăraș, is a beautiful Saxon town. Sinaia has Peleș Castle, one of the most striking royal palaces in Europe, and Bran Castle ("Dracula's castle") is close. Brown bears live in these mountains, as do wolves and lynx.
fagaras.know:
Sibiu is about 1.5 hours from Bâlea Cascadă; Bucharest is about 2.5 to 3 hours from Sinaia. Prices are low.

Romania's national meteorology service publishes avalanche bulletins. Rescue resources are limited in remote areas, so go with a local guide.

mercantour.skiing:
The Mercantour is the southernmost range of the Alps, rising behind Nice to more than 3,000 m. It gets big, irregular storms from the Mediterranean, the famous *retour d'est*, which can dump a metre of snow in a day, followed by long spells of sun.

**Isola 2000** and **Auron** are the main resorts, both about 1.5 hours from Nice. Isola 2000 sits high, at about 2,000 m, close to the Italian border, and catches the most snow; Auron is a sunnier, more traditional village.

The ski touring is wild and quiet, in a national park where you're more likely to see ibex or chamois than other people. The **Cime du Gélas** (3,143 m), the highest peak of the range, is a classic spring tour from the **Madone de Fenestre**, and the **Vallée des Merveilles**, with its Bronze Age rock engravings, is a beautiful area for touring.
mercantour.beyond: Nice and the Riviera are about 1.5 hours away, so you can ski in the morning and walk on the seafront in the afternoon. The perched villages of the Vésubie and Roya valleys are stunning, and the Vallée des Merveilles has tens of thousands of prehistoric rock carvings.
mercantour.know:
Nice airport is about 1.5 hours from the resorts. Storm Alex in 2020 badly damaged the Vésubie and Roya valleys, and some roads have been rebuilt or changed since, so check access.

Météo-France forecasts the Mercantour massif. The snowpack can be thin and weak, so check conditions carefully.

hemavan.skiing:
Hemavan and Tärnaby, in southern Swedish Lapland, are the home of Swedish alpine racing: Ingemar Stenmark grew up in Tärnaby, and the valley has produced several other world champions. **Hemavan** is the bigger ski area, with open, treeless slopes on the Hemavan fell; **Tärnaby** is smaller and steeper, with tree skiing.

The real draw for many is the touring. The **Norra Storfjället** massif, right above Hemavan, rises to about 1,767 m and has big, open slopes and steeper faces. **Syterskalet**, a dramatic U-shaped valley through the massif, is one of the classic spring tours in Sweden, and Hemavan is the southern end of the **Kungsleden** trail.

Spring is the season, with long days, corn snow and stable weather.
hemavan.beyond: Tärnaby has a museum about its skiing legends. The area is Sámi land, with reindeer herding, and the Norwegian coast at Mo i Rana is about 1.5 hours away.
hemavan.know:
Hemavan has its own airport, with flights from Stockholm. Mo i Rana, in Norway, is about 1.5 hours away.

The Swedish avalanche forecast covers Södra Lapland. Wind and whiteouts are common on the open fells.
