harjedalen.skiing:
Funäsfjällen, in western Härjedalen near the Norwegian border, is a group of ski areas around Funäsdalen, including **Tänndalen**, **Ramundberget** and **Bruksvallarna**, on one lift pass. They're modest in size, but snowy and friendly, with tree skiing and open fells, and very good cross-country trails.

The big draw for tourers is **Helags**, at 1,797 m the highest peak in southern Sweden, with the southernmost glacier in the country. The STF **Helags mountain station** sits below it and is a classic base for day tours, and the area is part of the **Jämtland triangle**, a popular hut-to-hut route.

The fells are open and rounded, with plenty of easy touring and some steeper faces on the bigger peaks. Spring is the best time.
harjedalen.beyond: Funäsdalen is a lively little town with good food. Röros, across the border in Norway, is a UNESCO-listed mining town with wooden houses. Sámi reindeer herding is active in the area.
harjedalen.know:
Röros airport, in Norway, is about 1 hour away; Östersund is about 2.5 hours. A car helps.

The Swedish avalanche forecast covers Västra Härjedalen. Wind and whiteouts are common on the fells.

trollheimen.skiing:
Trollheimen, between Trondheim and the west coast, is a compact range of rounded and steep peaks, with a famous trio of huts: **Gjevilvasshytta**, **Jøldalshytta** and **Trollheimshytta**, linked by the "Trekanten" (triangle) route. It's a classic Norwegian hut tour, with a day's skiing between each hut and optional summits along the way.

**Snøtinden** (1,668 m) is the highest peak, and the terrain ranges from gentle valleys to steep faces. The huts are traditional and welcoming, with good food at Easter, when they're staffed.

To the west, **Innerdalen**, often called Norway's most beautiful valley, is a car-free valley under the steep pyramid of **Innerdalstårnet**, with good touring and a small lodge. The western peaks are steeper and more alpine.
trollheimen.beyond: Trondheim is a lively university city with the Nidaros Cathedral, the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world. Oppdal, on the eastern edge, has a big ski area and good cross-country trails.
trollheimen.know:
Trondheim is about 2.5 hours away. DNT huts are staffed at Easter; at other times, some are self-service and need a DNT key.

Norway's Varsom forecasts Trollheimen. The weather can change quickly.

salten.skiing:
Salten, the region around Bodø, is a quiet alternative to Lofoten and Lyngen, with steep coastal peaks, deep fjords and, inland, the big **Sulitjelma** glacier on the Swedish border. Locals tour from the road all around the region, and the skiing ranges from summit-to-sea lines on the coast to big glacier tours inland.

The **Børvasstindan**, just outside Bodø, are jagged peaks with steep couloirs and big views over the sea. Further inland, the old mining town of **Sulitjelma** sits below a glaciated massif with long, open tours.

The region is little known to visiting skiers, so the peaks are quiet, and the long spring days bring the best conditions.
salten.beyond: Saltstraumen, near Bodø, is the strongest tidal current in the world, with whirlpools forming as the tide pushes through a narrow strait. Bodø, a European Capital of Culture in 2024, has a lively harbour and an aviation museum. Sulitjelma has a mining museum.
salten.know:
Bodø has flights from Oslo and ferries to Lofoten. A car is essential.

Norway's Varsom forecasts Salten. Coastal weather changes fast.

eastfjords.skiing:
Iceland's Eastfjords are a string of deep fjords lined with steep mountains, with small fishing villages at the head of each. The peaks are mostly under 1,200 m but rise straight from the sea, with steep gullies and open faces, and they see very few visiting skiers.

**Seyðisfjörður**, with its colourful wooden houses, sits at the end of a long fjord below the **Fjarðarheiði** pass, and the small **Stafdalur** ski area is on the pass above. Further south, **Oddsskarð**, above Eskifjörður, is another small ski area with steep slopes and sea views.

The touring is wild and quiet, with tours from the pass roads and from the villages. Local guides are few, so this is a place for self-reliant groups or for joining one of the small local operators.
eastfjords.beyond: Seyðisfjörður is an artsy village, with galleries and the rainbow-painted street to its blue church. The Norröna ferry from Denmark docks here, making it the one place in Iceland you can arrive by sea with your car. In 2020, landslides hit the town, and it has been rebuilding since.
eastfjords.know:
Egilsstaðir airport, with flights from Reykjavík, is about 30 minutes from Seyðisfjörður. The Fjarðarheiði pass can close in storms.

The Icelandic Met Office forecasts the Eastfjords. The fjords have a long history of avalanches, so check the forecast carefully.

minakami.skiing:
Minakami sits on the main ridge of Honshu, where Sea of Japan storms meet the mountains, so it gets very heavy snowfall, yet it's less than two hours from Tokyo by Shinkansen. Several small resorts surround the town, and **Tanigawadake** (1,977 m), above it, is the big draw.

The **Tenjindaira** ropeway climbs Tanigawadake's flanks to a small ski area with access to serious backcountry, with steep, open slopes and gullies above the trees. The mountain is notorious in Japan: its steep walls and sudden storms have made it one of the deadliest climbing mountains in the world, and the skiing deserves respect.

Other resorts around Minakami, like **Hodaigi**, are good for storm days, with wide, snowy slopes.
minakami.beyond: Minakami is a hot-spring town, with dozens of onsen in the surrounding valleys, including old ryokan with riverside baths. Takaragawa Onsen has huge outdoor baths along a river, beautiful in snow.
minakami.know:
From Tokyo, take the Jōetsu Shinkansen to Jōmō-Kōgen (about 1 hour 15 minutes), then a bus. A car helps to move between resorts.

The snowpack is deep and heavy, with storm slabs and glide cracks. Go with a local guide for the backcountry, and file a climbing plan.

taranaki.skiing:
Taranaki Maunga (2,518 m), a near-perfect volcanic cone on the west coast of the North Island, is one of New Zealand's most striking ski peaks, and very few skiers ever come here. On its eastern slopes, the tiny **Manganui** club ski area runs rope tows on steep, open terrain, reached by a short walk and a footbridge from the road end.

The real draw is the ski descent from the summit. In spring, after a good winter, skiers climb the cone and ski long, open, steep slopes down to the ski area or the road. The snow is usually icy on top and corn lower down, so timing matters.

The mountain sits close to the Tasman Sea and catches storms, so snowfall can be heavy but conditions change fast. In 2025 Taranaki Maunga was granted legal personhood, in recognition of its significance to local iwi.
taranaki.beyond: New Plymouth, on the coast, has the Len Lye Centre and good surf. Egmont National Park has beautiful walks and waterfalls.
taranaki.know:
New Plymouth airport is about 1 hour away. The summit is icy and exposed, with frequent fatal accidents: carry crampons and an ice axe and turn back in poor weather.

The New Zealand Avalanche Advisory covers the mountain. Manganui is a small, volunteer-run field, so check whether it's open before you go.

fiordland.skiing:
Fiordland, in the far south-west of the South Island, has some of the wildest ski touring in New Zealand, and few skiers know about it. The Milford Road, which crosses the Darran Mountains through the Homer Tunnel, gives road access to steep, glaciated alpine terrain.

**Homer Hut**, owned by the New Zealand Alpine Club, sits just below the tunnel and is the base for most trips. From there, skiers tour into the cirques around the head of the Hollyford valley and up to **Gertrude Saddle**, a steep, dramatic pass with views down to Milford Sound.

The terrain is steep and big, with granite walls and couloirs. The snowfall is huge, but the weather is very wet, and storms come straight in from the Tasman Sea. When it clears, the scenery is some of the most spectacular in the world.
fiordland.beyond: Milford Sound, at the end of the road, is one of New Zealand's most famous sights. Te Anau, the nearest town, is on a big lake and is the base for the Great Walks.
fiordland.know:
Queenstown airport is about 4 hours away; Te Anau about 1.5 hours. The Milford Road has its own avalanche control programme and is often closed after storms, so check the road status before you go.

The New Zealand Avalanche Advisory covers Fiordland. The terrain is serious and avalanche-prone: go with experience or a guide.
